News.title: Miracle poodle hauled from rubble of collapsed building in Venezuela 29 DAYS after double-earthquake horror
News.content:
A POODLE has miraculously been hauled from the rubble of a collapsed building nearly a month after the deadly Venezuela earthquake.

Beyli was fortunately rescued from the site of his ruined family home near Playa Grande on Tuesday as emergency services scoured for bodies.



The dog’s owner, Victoria Rengel, 11, survived the terrifying 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude double-earthquake horror last month.

But her mum and grandmother were both killed by the successive tremors.



Beyli was found 29 days after the two earthquakes next to Victoria’s mum’s body.

The young dog-owner told local media: “He wanted to protect her.

“I will remember how much he loved my mum.”

The catastrophic quakes on June 24 left over 5,500 dead and 17,000 injured – with many more still missing.



Rescue teams are still working to find survivors in La Guaira – with locals also joining efforts using pickaxes and electric hammers.

After Beyli was transferred to a veterinary clinic, vets gave the miracle dog an intravenous drip.

He is expected to make a full recovery – despite surviving without food or water for 29 days.



The dog’s vet said: “It is a miracle everything that has happened with him.

“He has some ulcers in the eyes, but soon he will be fine.”

It comes after a spate of fortunate rescues from the rubble in the wake of the disastrous double tremor.

Days after the horror, a young boy was found alive in the rubble and international teams rescued a mum and 18-day-old baby.

Tragically, the body of a model was pulled from the rubble still clutching her beloved pet on June 30.



Oriana Usatariz, 25, was found clinging tightly to her dog in the crumbled remains of a collapsed building.

Her body was discovered during frantic search efforts at the Moisés building in the San Bernardino district of Caracas.

The fashion model, known for distinctive red curly hair, was the last person still unaccounted for from the apartment block.

The United Nations estimates at least 50,000 people could still be unaccounted for, despite momentous rescue efforts.

News.title: Two children, 6 & 11, rushed to hospital after being mauled by dog in playground – as CCTV released in hunt for woman
News.content:
DOG ATTACK Two children, 6 & 11, rushed to hospital after being mauled by dog in playground – as CCTV released in hunt for woman

TWO children have suffered bites to their legs and thighs after being mauled by a dog.

Cops have released CCTV images in a bid to track down a woman they want to speak to.



The kids were at a playground on Vernon Street, near Newfoundpool, Leicester, on April 19 when they were injured.

Cops said the victims, aged six and 11, were bitten and later treated in hospital.



Leicestershire Police have now appealed to the public in their attempt to identify a woman who they believe could help with their investigation.

A spokesperson for the force said: “Enquiries have been ongoing since the incident was reported to us and we hope the public can help us move the investigation on.

“We know the images are not the best quality, but we hope someone will recognise the woman or the dog.

“If this is you or you have any suspicions about who the woman may be, we would urge you to get in touch.”

Anyone with any information is asked to contact PC 4630 Samuel Senior on 101, quoting crime number 26*224111.

News.title: Shocking moment huge brawl erupts in street with spade & bat-wielding men swinging at each other in mystery row
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a huge brawl breaks out in a street as men armed with spades and bats swing at each other.

The chaos was caught on camera after tempers on an estate spiralled out of control with a huge fight kicking off.



A large group of men clashed on Dallow Road in Luton, Bedfordshire, armed with a variety of items whilst exchanging blows in broad daylight.

Shockingly, kids in the park near the road watched on in horror as the brawl spiralled out of control.



A man in a blue shirt and white trousers can be seen joining the fight armed with a massive shovel.

He can then be seen holding it over his head before slamming it down on one of the others involved in the brawl.



Following this, one man can be seen grabbing a plastic chair from outside a local shop to try and use as a weapon.

The clip surfaced on July 27 with a passer-by capturing the scenes on camera.



The video racked up over 117,000 views online.

Members of the public were left disgusted by the brawl.

One person said: “All it takes to stop a bad man with a stick is a good man with a shovel.”

Another viewer wrote: “Looks lovely.”

A third added: “The parking on the pavement is a nice touch.”



While another responded: “There should be a dedicated police unit in every estate like this.

“Zero tolerance.”

One other person said: “Embarrassed what a large part of the town has become.

“Surely the guy with the shovel can be arrested for attempted murder.

“Hitting someone with a shovel is only going to end up one way.”



A spokesperson for Bedfordshire Police said: “Police were called at 9pm on Tuesday 21 July to a group of men fighting near Brantwood Road Recreational Ground.

News.title: Man, 32, stole ambulance from outside hospital while patient was being treated in the back before dumping it near woods
News.content:
AMBO HEIST Man, 32, stole ambulance from outside hospital while patient was being treated in the back before dumping it near woods

A MAN stole an ambulance from outside a hospital while a patient was being treated in the back.

Staffordshire cops said they were called to a report of a man taking the emergency vehicle from the Royal Stoke University Hospital at about 8.15pm on March 25.



The ambulance was parked in a triage bay at the hospital in “run lock” mode, which keeps the vehicle running but allows paramedics to remove the keys from the ignition, the force said.

While a paramedic was treating a patient in the back of the ambulance, 32-year-old Marshall Leese got inside and drove away.



Appearing at Stoke-on-Trent Crown Court on Tuesday, Leese, from Hanley, pleaded guilty to false imprisonment and the aggravated vehicle taking of the Fiat Ducato ambulance and driving it dangerously between the hospital and London Road, in Chesterton, Newcastle-under-Lyme.

Leese, who wore a grey Nike tracksuit, smiled and waved at a woman in the public gallery at the start of the hearing.



He also pleaded guilty to failing to provide a specimen for analysis at Wolverhampton New Cross Hospital and using a motor vehicle without third party insurance on March 25.

Staffordshire Police said officers tracked the ambulance, which cuts off after a period of time in “run lock” mode.

Leese ran off into woodland after abandoning the ambulance at an Esso petrol station and was bitten on the hand by a police dog after failing to comply with instructions.

In his police interview, Leese denied the offences and instead said that he was cycling in the area and looking for a friend before he was approached by the police dog and bitten.



Judge Sally Hancox, who said the case was “unusual”, adjourned sentencing to a date to be fixed.

She told Leese, who spoke only to confirm his name and enter his pleas during the hearing: “Thank you for coming to court this morning.

“I will now formally adjourn this case for sentence.

“You are remanded into custody.”

News.title: Incredible helmet cam footage shows brave firefighters tackling France inferno as huge flames rip through trees
News.content:
JAW-dropping footage shows the moment a team of brave firefighters battles a vicious inferno in France as huge flames rip through a forest.

Terrifying video showed emergency workers hosing down a massive fire as it swallowed up trees in Gironde on Monday.



It comes as a series of wildfires tear through France, Spain and several other European nations amid record-breaking heatwaves.

In the astonishing clip, a group of firefighters can be seen using a red hose to douse the roaring blaze.



The extraordinarily large inferno appears to barely falter when initially hit by the water, as powerful gusts fan the flames.

Plumes of smoke can be seen billowing over the forest during the apocalyptic battle to contain the wildfires.



The inferno seemingly dies down towards the end of the footage as a result of the firefighters’ efforts.

It comes after French President Emmanuel Macron warned the wildfires are the country’s biggest challenge since World War Two.



Macron warned the coming weeks will be some of the toughest yet as the country braces for another 40C heatwave.

Currently, 2,500 firefighters, 1,500 military personnel and around 1,200 police officers have been deployed in Gironde, the south-western area worst affected by the fire.

Officials say fire crews have been “overwhelmed” by the ferocity of the flames and remain “far from” bringing them under control.



Two people have died due to the wildfires so far with at least 88, mainly firefighters, injured.

Dozens of homes have been burnt to the ground with an estimated 220,000 people displaced and forced to live in shelters while the flames remain high.

On Monday, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the flames that had decimated 42,000 hectares of land was stable but not contained.



It comes amid fears Bordeaux could be reduced to ashes as authorities battle “apocalyptic” flames less than seven miles away from the ancient city.

Around 360,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in France and Spain as infernos tear up neighbourhoods and forests.

In Spain, a new heatwave is set to begin on Wednesday.

Madrid earlier said temperatures would soar and humidity levels drop across Spain.

This would cause the fire risk to “surge to very high or extreme levels across almost the entire country”.



The European Union said it would deploy additional aircraft to Spain to help combat the fires.

Footage shows two Greek Canadair CL-415 firefighting aircraft spraying water across a number of locations devastated by wildfires in Spain.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Reacting to the forecast, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said: “I ask for understanding and call on all citizens in all the country to exercise extreme caution and take every possible precaution.”

It comes after Gironde firefighting Chief Eric Brocardi compared the battle to contain the inferno as a “David-versus-Goliath scenario”.

News.title: Scots mum killed & husband found dead in suspected ‘murder-suicide’ at country home

POLICE are investigating a suspected murder-suicide amid claims a husband killed his wife before taking his own life.

The bodies of Jim Mair, 43, and his wife Stacy, 35, were found on Corsliehill Road, on the outskirts of Houston, Renfrewshire, yesterday.



Cops locked down a detached cottage on a rural single-track lane as a major probe got underway.

Sources claim a firearm was also found at the country home.



More than a dozen police vehicles flooded the scene today.

Uniformed officers stood guard outside a rundown outhouse next to a small trailer.



The secluded country lane was sealed off at both ends, with one tape cordon halfway up Corsliehill Road.

Another squad car sat guarding the bottom of the street at the junction with Barochan Road.

Officers were alerted to a concern for a person in Corsliehill Road around 7.50am on Monday.

Mercy crews raced to the scene but Mrs Mair and her husband, who wedded in May 2019, were found dead.

News.title: Terrifying moment female cop is pepper-sprayed in face & left temporarily blind after knocking on thug’s door
News.content:
THIS is the terrifying moment a female cop is pepper-sprayed in the face, leaving her temporarily blind after knocking on a thug’s door.

PC Hollie and PC Molly had gone to an address in Luton, Bedfordshire, following reports of a domestic assault when they were attacked on May 17.



Ionut Spanache opened the door and assaulted the officers with a PAVA-like spray, a synthetic pepper spray substitute, causing them to run from the property.

The bodycam footage shows PC Hollie stating that she could not see, with the toxic substance causing the officer to experience temporary blindness as well as breathing difficulties.



PC Molly was also experiencing a burning sensation to her face and hands but quickly came to her colleague’s aid by clearing the substance from her eyes and mouth.

PC Hollie said: “Neither of us could have anticipated what happened next; there was no time to protect ourselves.

“As we ran from the property, I could feel a burning sensation that progressively got worse until I couldn’t see and began struggling to catch my breath.

“My initial thought was that we’d been attacked with acid.



“It’s hard to describe how painful and distressing this experience was, but I am grateful for the immediate actions of PC Molly, paramedics and those who witnessed the aftermath.

“The support I received from colleagues was crucial in getting back to work, and I’m pleased to have been present at Spanache’s sentencing and share first-hand the impact of assaults on officers.”

Spanache, 31, from Luton, pleaded guilty to two counts of assault on an emergency worker, possession of a weapon for the discharge of a noxious liquid, and actual bodily harm.

He was sentenced at Luton Crown Court on July 17 to two years’ imprisonment.

Superintendent Rachael Glendenning said: “Last month, we saw 33 officers seriously assaulted over the course of just seven days, with a number of officers requiring hospital treatment.



“Our officers regularly place themselves in challenging and unpredictable situations to protect others.

“However, no one should be subjected to violence of any degree, and we will always pursue offenders who think this is an acceptable response to police intervention.”

Almost 30 Bedfordshire Police officers are assaulted every month while on duty.

News.title: Benefit claimants set to rake in £4.5k a year if their child starts an apprenticeship under Andy Burnham’s latest plans
News.content:
PARENTS on benefits will get up to £4,500 a year if their child takes up an apprenticeship under Andy Burnham’s plans to get more youngsters into work.

The new bursary is designed to stop families being left worse off when a teenager starts earning.



The move comes as more than one million young people are currently not in education, employment or training.

From August, the Government will also fully fund apprenticeship training for all eligible under-25s.



Small firms will receive up to £8,000 to help take on young apprentices as ministers aim to create 50,000 new youth apprenticeships by the end of this Parliament.

An extra £287million will also create more than 22,000 new college places, including expanded construction courses to train future bricklayers, plumbers and decorators.



The announcement follows the PM’s wider plans to overhaul education by giving teenagers more technical learning, work experience and courses designed around local employers.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said: “Every young person deserves the chance to build a future they can be proud of.

“Our welfare system should be a springboard to opportunity, not a barrier to it.”

It comes as Labour MPs threatened a fresh welfare rebellion after Mr Burnham warned benefit claimants they could face tougher hurdles to get their cash.



The PM is considering making support conditional on under-25s engaging with work, education or community projects as ministers battle Britain’s soaring £333billion welfare bill.

But left-wing backbenchers warned they would oppose any “punitive” reforms, raising the prospect of another Commons revolt.

Liverpool Riverside MP Kim Johnson told Bloomberg: “If the new leadership believes it can revive the failed politics of welfare cuts instead of asking the wealthiest to pay their fair share, it will be repeating not only Keir Starmer’s mistakes but 14 years of Tory austerity.

“If the first instinct of a new leadership is to target disabled people and low-income families rather than challenge the wealth and inequality at the top of society, then nothing has been learnt.”

Former shadow chancellor John McDonnell insisted welfare reform should be based on “positive support” rather than “punitive sanction”.



The warning comes after Sir Keir Starmer was forced into a humiliating climbdown last year when more than 100 MPs rebelled against plans to tighten disability benefit rules.

Despite the backlash, Mr McFadden insisted there should be an “expectation to engage” if young people are offered opportunities through the welfare system.

News.title: Trump live: Zelensky and Netanyahu at White House as Donald set to quiz Putin
News.content:
Donald Trump is holding crucial talks at the White House with Volodymyr Zelensky and Benjamin Netanyahu, who are both in Washington DC for the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham

Donald Trump is set to hold crucial talks with Volodymyr Zelensky and Benjamin Netanyahu at the White House today - just days after Zelensky accused Russia of helping Iran target US troops.

Both the Ukrainian president and Israeli prime minister are in Washington DC to attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, who died earlier this month aged 71.

Zelensky has said he plans to discuss strengthening Ukraine's anti-ballistic missile defences with Trump. It comes after the Ukrainian leader said on Saturday that Kyiv has intelligence indicating Russia shared satellite imagery with Tehran, enabling Iran to target US military bases in the Middle East. Trump said that he will "find out if that's true" and "ask Putin about it".

After meeting Zelensky, Trump will hold talks with Netanyahu - marking their first in-person meeting since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28.

News.title: France wildfires live: Thousands of tourists evacuated from coast near Bordeaux
News.content:
Flames are nearing the French Atlantic Coast with raging wildfires now nine miles from Bordeaux as the city's mayor says he's prepared for 'all eventualities'

More than than 4,000 tourists have been evacuated from an area near the French Atlantic Coast as inferno wildfires burn nearby.

Holidaymakers have been forced to leave campsites, tourist homes, holiday villages and leisure parks around Lacanau, which is around 40 miles from Bordeaux. The order comes as firefighters race against time to bring the fires under control before the country's south-west is blasted by a forecast 40C heatwave tomorrow (Wednesday).

Officials say the largest blaze has "stabilised" but have warned it could still burn out of control again as temperatures rise and humidity falls.

French President Emmanuel Macron says the wildfires are the "most difficult situation" his country has dealt with since World War Two, with more than 260,000 people now evacuated from their homes in the south-west.

The mayor of Bordeaux, Thomas Cazenave, says he is preparing for "all eventualities" and that authorities are preparing to "accommodate a large number of people should further evacuations be ordered".

Meanwhile in Spain, 63,000 people have been evacuate from their homes near Madrid, with the country's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez calling it "the most painful expression of the climate emergency".

News.title: Donald Trump urged to help end one war and intensify another as he meets Zelensky and Netenyahu
News.content:
Donald Trump urged to help end one war and intensify another as he meets Zelensky and Netenyahu

Trump met Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky and Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu one after the other at the White House as they both arrived in Washington DC to attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham

View Image Trump met with Volodymyr Zelensky and Benjamin Netanyahu one after the other (Image: UKRAINIAN PRESIDENTIAL PRESS SERVICE/AFP via Getty Images)

Donald Trump was urged to help end one war and intensify another as he met with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky and Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu.

‌



Trump met the two leaders one after the other at the White House as they both arrived in Washington DC to attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham.

‌



Graham had, separately, been an ally to both Zelensy and Netanyahu - acting as a go-between and helping to help Ukraine and Israel to better understand the thinking of Trump's White House.

‌



Both meetings were closed to the press.

In a post on social media after the meeting, Zelenskyy thanked Trump for the “good meeting” and the Republican administration's efforts to aid Kyiv in the long-running war, which began more than four years ago when Russia invaded Ukraine.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said both the Zelensky meeting and a separate, later sit-down with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu were "positive and productive."

‌



Trump welcomed Zelenskyy to the White House as the Ukrainian leader traveled to Washington to honor Graham, whose final act as a public official was visiting Kyiv and securing an agreement on a package of sanctions that seek to punish countries that purchase Russian oil, gas and other exports.

In a TV interview on Tuesday, Trump said senator Graham's support for Ukraine never wavered. He said it was Graham who suggested it was time to make a deal with Iran but had no similar suggestion for the Russia-Ukraine war.

“Ukraine, he's very militant about,” Trump told Fox News. "I mean, Lindsey liked war, to be honest with you."

Article continues below

Ahead of the meeting, Zelensky also warned that Russia has been aiding Iran as the war persists by capturing satellite imagery of US bases in the Gulf region that later appeared in Iran. The Ukrainian president also asserted that there was a "clear correlation" between Russia's images and subsequent Iranian strikes.

"The purpose is clear," Zelensky said earlier this month. "None of us in the world should turn a blind eye to one very simple fact: Evil always seeks ways to make things worse and spread further."

News.title: Japan earthquake live: Dozens still missing as search for survivors continues overnight
News.content:
Multiple people have died while more are missing after a shopping centre collapsed following a huge 7.1 magnitude earthquake on the Japanese island of Kyushu

Dozens of people are still reported missing following the horror collapse of a shopping mall in Japan that caused 'many fatalities' after being struck by a powerful earthquake.

Up to 30 others remain missing at the Aeon Mall in Kumamoto, while employees are also missing at the nearby Nippon Paper Industries Yatsushiro Plant. Several people travelling in a high speed train were also injured after a chimney stack from the paper company fell on them during the quake, local media reports.

“People are coming in with burns and fractures from being trapped under objects due to the earthquake, and ambulances are constantly bringing in injured people,” a hospital employee told national broadcaster NHK.

“Inside the hospital, there are water leaks and electrical system failures,” they added.

The massive quake measured at the highest possible level seven on Japan's own Shindo "scale of shaking" and has left tens of thousands without power. Kumamoto Airport has been closed indefinitely after the earthquake rocked its runway.

Kumamoto was hit with a deadly quake in 2016 that left more than 50 people dead, 1,800 injured and tens of thousands of homes damaged or destroyed.

News.title: The Buck Moon: Rare chance to catch glimpse of spectacular Full Moon this week
News.content:
The Buck Moon: Rare chance to catch glimpse of spectacular Full Moon this week

Brits hoping to catch a glimpse of one of the year's most spectacular Lunar displays will have a good opportunity to enjoy the Buck Moon when it appears on the horizon this week

View 5 Images Juky's supermoon will trace a path through the night's sky this Wednesday (Image: Geoffrey Swaine/REX/Shutterstock)

The Buck Moon will lay down another impressive July Lunar display as it arrives this week, with the spectacular Full Moon set to materialise during clear skies.

‌



The phase, also known as the Thunder Moon or the Hay Moon, is a massive presence in the sky during midsummer, when it looms large in the night's sky. A global phenomenon - which is believed to impact people based on their star signs in some circles - it also has more than one name, and even varying cultural significance stretching back several hundred years.

‌



The Buck Moon can be seen from around the world, including the UK, where it will land in a matter of hours during what is expected to be one of the hottest weeks of the year.

‌



How to see July's full Buck Moon in the UK as it rises on Wednesday READ MORE :

View 5 Images The Buck Moon is July's only full moon (Image: Zeynep Demir Aslim/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

What is the Buck Moon?

The Buck Moon owes its unique name to Native Americans, who noted that male deer - known as bucks - who shed their antlers, tend to regrow them during the late summer. It has been variably known as the Thunder Moon, after the season's tendency for thunderstorms, and the Hay Moon, a name used mostly by farmers as the annual hay harvest lands every July.

Most people will know the Moon for its incredible size, which has its own scientific roots based it's relation to the Earth at the time, which produces an illusion

‌



The Moon will be low-hanging and full, and especially large when it takes pride of place on the horizon over the next couple of days, but won't have physically grown at all, or be closer to the Earth. Instead, its position on the horizon will make it look much larger as it sits in front of foreground objects.

The Buck Moon will also look yellow - or orange, depending on where it is being viewed from - again due to its position on the horizon.

While it is particularly low, sunlight will bounce off the Moon's surface and pass through the Earth's atmosphere, which is especially thick at this point. The atmosphere will filter blue and violet light, meaning what is left behind is solely on the yellow and orange section of the spectrum.

‌



View 5 Images The Buck Moon is named after male deer (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

When will the Moon rise?

We know the Buck Moon will be present on the horizon this week, but at different times depending on where would-be viewers are living.

The Moon is expected to reach its peak illumination in the UK at around 3.36pm BST, but at this point it will be sitting just below, rather than on, the horizon. It will at the time still appear like a golden or orange orb, and visible to the naked eye despite having not yet reached full fruition.

‌



According to EarthSky, it will appear lowest - and by extension look its largest - in the Northern Hemisphere, while those living in the Southern Hemisphere have a good view of the high Full Moon, but to a lesser extent.

Full Moons tend to follow the same path through the night's sky as the Sun does during the daytime, meaning it will get steadily higher after people get their first glimpse on the satellite. As it does so, it may cause some tricks of the light, such as appearing to develop a halo in cloudier weather.

View 5 Images The Moon is expected to be especially spectacular in the east (Image: PA)

‌



Where is the best place to see the Buck Moon?

The easiest way for budding astronomers to see the Buck Moon is by moving to high ground when the object hits its peak on Wednesday.

Noah Petro, the chief of the Planetary Geology, Geophysics and Geochemistry Lab at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Centre, told CNN people will have "flexibility" to see the Moon. But this is provided they're "in a place that’s free of bright lights" and "have a fairly clear view of the sky”.

In the UK, the best places to watch the Buck Moon is the west country, where conditions are expected to be largely clear, with little in terms of cloud cover.

‌



Key viewing points include the Troopers Hill Nature Reserve in St George, Bristol, Clifton Observatory in the same city, and Victoria Park, which sits between Bedminster and Totterdown. Gloucestershire is another good viewing area, including Cleeve Hill and Painswick Beacon, as is Wiltshire, specifically around the ancient Avebury Stone Circle and Barbury Castle.

View 5 Images Clifton Observatory, provided it isn't cloudy, is expected to be a good viewing point for the Buck Moon (Image: PA)

What is the weather forecast for Wednesday evening?

The UK continues to experience a prolonged heatwave, which will extend until Wednesday, when temperatures are expected to hit a sweltering 33C in some parts of the country.

‌



The unnaturally warm weather, while unwelcome for many given it has now been several weeks without rainfall for some areas, comes with a positive, as it will be clear on Wednesday evening in most parts of the country. The forecast for London and the South East shows that part of the country will see the highest temperatures, even heatwave conditions.

Wales and eastern Scotland will also see a dry week with sunny conditions, with western Scotland and northwest England cloudier on Tuesday.

The areas may even see rain or drizzle, and there remains a chance that heavy showers could also develop - obscuring people's views of Wednesday's Buck Moon. According to weather maps from the Met Office, cloudy conditions could also take hold in the southwest, around Exeter and Plymouth, most of Wales, parts of Yorkshire, and the northeast coast.

Article continues below

West country viewing points like those listed above seem likely to remain largely clear for the day, although some cloud may arrive in the evening - after the Buck Moon has reached its most illuminated state.

News.title: Mystery deepens after 14 elephants found dead in 'mysterious' circumstances
News.content:
Mystery deepens after 14 elephants found dead in 'mysterious' circumstances

The dead elephants were of various ages and sexes and were found close to the Amboseli National Park in the south of Kenya in eastern Africa

View Image Authorities are investigating whether the deaths occurred due to poisoning, disease or other factors (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

An investigation has been launched after 14 elephants were mysteriously found dead near a national park in Africa.

‌



The carcasses were discovered across different locations around 15km to 30km from the boundaries of the Amboseli National Park. The area, known as the Amboseli ecosystem, is located in the south of Kenya in eastern Africa.

‌



Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) said experts are examining the bodies. The BBC reports that tissue samples have been sent to laboratories to establish what caused the death, with hypotheses such as disease and poisoning considered.

‌



This is the first time in decades that elephant deaths on this scale have been recorded in the African region. Poaching - the illegal hunting, killing or capturing of wild animals - has successfully been tackled in the area.

There is currently no evidence that a single cause of death is what took the lives of all 14 elephants, KWS said. The dead animals include elephants of various ages and sexes which suggests the deaths are not limited to a single family or age group.

Article continues below

Investigators probing the deaths from the University of Nairobi have reportedly discovered a suspected toxin in some of the creature's corpses. Samples are currently being analysed to determine whether it played a role in the fatalities, local news sources claim.

The KWS is also investigating a range of environmental factors, including water sources and other potential contaminants, to determine whether the elephants were exposed to a common source.

The Amboseli ecosystem is a wide area on the border with Tanzania, a country famous for its wildlife. Figures for the Amboseli Trust for Elephants shows more than 2,000 elephants were in the ecosystem as of last year.

News.title: The moment Tuesday's powerful earthquake hit Japan
News.content:
A powerful earthquake struck Japanâs Kyushu island on 28 July, forcing more than 150,000 people to evacuate. The quake caused power outages, damaged roads, brought down part of a castle wall, and destroyed a footbridge. More than 40,000 households are without power and several people are missing after a chimney collapsed at a paper factory in the Kumamoto prefecture, according to the police who are being cited by Japan's public broadcaster NHK.

News.title: Some parents on benefits to get up to £4,500 for child starting apprenticeship
News.content:
Some parents on benefits will be given up to Â£4,500 a year to encourage their children to start apprenticeships, the government has said.

Under plans to encourage young people into work, families will be offered a bursary to replace Universal Credit payments lost by starting jobs.

The payment is expected to benefit an estimated few thousand households, who currently face losing between Â£17 and Â£330 a week if their children start apprenticeships.

The Conservatives welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's support for apprenticeships, but criticised his plans to fund the bursaries.

The bursary will be paid for from a Â£30m pot, funded through the growth and skills levy, a tax on employers with annual wage bills over Â£3m.

It followed the publication of a Social Security Advisory Committee report, external which warned of the "perverse effects" of the benefits system on young people's employment choices.

It said, for example, single parents with a disabled child could lose up to Â£340 per week in benefits if their child started an apprenticeship, exceeding the expected apprenticeship salary of Â£258 per week.

Because they are classed as paid employment, benefit payments are reduced to households where young people take on apprenticeships.

The committee said the system was hampering government efforts to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).

In a recent report, former Health Secretary Alan Milburn warned that one in six young people could be Neet in the next five years unless urgent action is taken.

Official figures show more than a million people aged 16 to 24 are currently Neet.

The government said its new bursary would remove a barrier to young people taking on apprenticeships, allowing them to "earn and learn".

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said: "By providing bursaries to those who need them most and fully funding apprenticeship training, we are making sure cost is not the reason someone misses out."

It is part of a wider package of support for apprenticeships, including funding for apprenticeship training for under-25s and additional support for employers taking on apprentices.

Helen Whately, the Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary, said: "I'm glad Burnham agrees: apprenticeships are a good thing, and we need more of them."

But she said the plan was "uncosted".

"It is spending money already committed elsewhere. So, either it is another unfunded announcement, or Andy Burnham is not being straight with us about his plans."

Burnham has said he is "on a mission" to reduce the number of Neets.

"The trend is rising at the moment, so the first thing I've got to do is to stop that rise," he said.

As he continues a flurry of early policy announcements, Burnham on Tuesday set out plans to strike a balance in the education system between prioritising academic and technical skills.

News.title: Funeral director 'left baby's remains on floor for two years'
News.content:
This story contains details some might find distressing.

The remains of a stillborn baby were left on the floor of a funeral home for almost two years and his grieving parents given the wrong ashes, a court has heard.

Former undertaker Robert Bush admitted 67 offences, including failing to bury and cremate people at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in Hull.

Jasmine Beverley told Hull Crown Court that learning her baby Sunny-Beverley Conlin was discovered in a brown paper bag on the floor of the Hessle Road parlour in March 2024 "will stay with me for the rest of my life".

Addressing Bush through tears, she told him: "I trusted you with the most precious person in my life."

News.title: Naga Munchetty to leave BBC Breakfast after 17 years
News.content:
Munchetty, 51, is among the best-paid presenters on the BBC's star salaries list, earning about Â£360,000 a year, according to the latest accounts.

She has interviewed major celebrities and politicians on the programme over the years ranging from Hillary Clinton and Michelle Obama to Sir Keir Starmer, Sir David Attenborough and Sir Rod Stewart.

In 2016, she appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing.

She has also been at the centre of some controversies during her time on BBC Breakfast.

In 2019, she was initially found to have breached the BBC's guidelines over comments she made about a social media post from Donald Trump about four female politicians of colour.

However, the BBC's director general then reversed that finding after deciding her words were not "sufficient to merit" upholding part of the complaint.

In 2021, Munchetty and co-presenter Charlie Stayt were "spoken to and reminded of their responsibilities" after complaints about their reaction to a government minister's flag. Munchetty apologised for liking "offensive" tweets about the exchange.

In June 2025, the Sun reported details of two alleged incidents which the paper said caused BBC bosses to speak to Munchetty about her conduct.

That came amid reports of behind-the-scenes tensions on the show, and at the same time as the programme's editor Richard Frediani took extended leave following allegations about his behaviour.

Frediani returned to work two weeks later and remains editor of BBC Breakfast.

At the time, the BBC said it did not comment on individual cases but took all complaints about conduct at work extremely seriously. Munchetty and Frediani did not comment on the reports.

The programme won a Bafta TV Award last year for best news coverage for a special about the Post Office scandal.

News.title: Powell says student loan system at top of in-tray
News.content:
Lucy Powell has said she wants to make sure the student loans system is "fair" and that the issue is at the top of her in-tray as the new education secretary.

Labour's deputy leader told the BBC she stood by comments she made in February that the interest rates graduates with Plan 2 loans were paying were "egregious".

She said she was committed to looking at the issue, although acknowledged she "can't make any promises" about changes.

Plan 2 loans were taken out by students in England between September 2012 and July 2023, and are still issued in Wales. Graduates pay back what they earn above the repayment threshold at a rate of 9%.

In November last year, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves said the repayment threshold for students with Plan 2 loans would be frozen at Â£29,385 between 2027 and 2030, instead of rising with inflation.

The change would result in students starting to repay their loans sooner than they would otherwise have done, and their rising salaries leading to greater repayments.

Campaigners have called for that decision to be reversed.

Reeves later said the government's measures were "fair and proportionate" for getting "the balance right between tax and spending".

In April, the government said interest on some student loans in England - including Plan 2 - would be capped at 6%.

Speaking to Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live, Powell said she was "very familiar" with the issue as her eldest child has a Plan 2 loan.

She said: "I think it's not just about the threshold of when people start to pay it back, but also the interest rate which is RPI [retail prices index] plus 3%.

"I think I've called it in the past egregious and I'm not going to change my opinion on that just because I'm now the secretary of state.

"The government has committed to a review of that, it's very much at the top of my in-tray as the secretary of state, and I want to make sure we look at this so it's fair for students."

Powell described it as a "real cost-of-living issue" for young people, adding: "They're paying high repayments and never, ever paying off the capital of their student loan."

Pressed on whether it is something she will look at, Powell replied: "Yes. I can't make any promises, but it needs looking at."

MPs on the Treasury Committee this month said comparing student loan repayments to phone contracts or cinema tickets "amounted to mis-selling" by government.

It came after a BBC investigation found the government compared student loan repayments to Â£30-a-month phone contracts in promotional presentations to teenagers a decade ago.

Earlier this year, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would cut the rate of interest charged on Plan 2 loans, capping it at RPI only. The current RPI rate is 3%.

News.title: Richard Hammond fined £999 for  speeding offences
News.content:
Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has been fined Â£999 after being caught speeding twice in three weeks while driving luxury cars.

The 56-year-old was captured driving his Porsche Taycan Cross Turismo at 68mph in a 50mph limit on the A40 in Pencraig, Herefordshire on 2 December.

He was later clocked driving his Bentley Continental GT at 82mph in a 70mph limit on the M50 Rudhall Overbridge, also in Herefordshire, on 22 December.

Hammond pleaded guilty to two speeding charges through his solicitor. Two further charges that he had ignored the police letters and failed to identify himself as the guilty driver were withdrawn by police.

He was also given seven penalty points for his licence at the hearing last week.

Magistrate Ann Minton ordered him to pay a total of Â£1,771, comprising two fines of Â£333 and Â£666, Â£240 in costs and victim surcharges totalling Â£532.

News.title: Odyssey translator writes scathing review of Nolan film adaptation
News.content:
Sir Christopher Nolan's latest film, The Odyssey, may have won rave reviews from critics and done storming business at the box office - but one person is definitely not happy.

Emily Wilson, the academic whose 2017 translation of Homer's Odyssey was cited by the director as an influence on his adaptation of the poem, has written a scathing review of the movie.

Published in the London Review of Books, external, Wilson said she "would be ashamed to have written any of this script", describing the film's narrative structure as "gimmicky."

"The writing is abysmal," she said. "None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible."

News.title: Can Burnham's vision for Manchester's schools really work for the rest of England?
News.content:
Two years ago, I stood at the back of a conference room in Manchester Hall, sipping a coffee and watching Andy Burnham unveil his vision for transforming technical education in Greater Manchester.

He had announced plans for the Manchester Baccalaureate, or MBacc, the year before, and, armed with PowerPoint slides and guest speakers, was running through the ins and outs in front of a room full of education and business leaders.

Now, as prime minister, Burnham has announced plans to make that idea national, and overhaul the technical education system across the whole of England.

The details are still scarce at this stage. We know it will involve giving pupils the option to study more vocational courses and take up work experience from Year 10, but how it will work in practice is still up in the air.

One thing that is certain is that the thinking behind it, and the ambition, is the same as that which underpins the MBacc: a determination to give teenagers a clear, step-by-step route into more practical and technical jobs.

The trouble is, the MBacc itself can be quite a difficult concept to get your head around if you're not familiar with it.

Let's be clear from the start: it's not another type of qualification, like the T-levels and V-levels announced in England in recent years.

Instead, it's a framework that aims to give teenagers a "clear line of sight to good jobs" in vocational and technical areas.

The best way to think about it is a step-by-step route - picture a flow chart - that teenagers can follow from school into any given technical career.

It's set up in parallel to a more clearly defined academic route. During that conference event in July 2024, Burnham and other speakers made clear that those who want to go on to desk jobs can follow a well-trodden path of GCSEs, A-levels, and a university degree.

But for those who want more practical careers, the landscape is much more complicated.

The MBacc is best seen as an effort to simplify that landscape, spelling out for teenagers who want to go into more vocational or technical careers which courses they can study, and ensuring they have the opportunity to study them along with hands-on work experience.

It spells out routes to careers in seven different categories:

Construction and the green economy

Creative, culture and sport

Digital and technology

Education and early years

Financial, business and professional services

Health and social care

Manufacturing and engineering

Its success is difficult to measure, since the MBacc is still in its infancy.

It's not until 2030 that it seeks to achieve its mission of guaranteeing every young person a clear path to good jobs. By 2035, the aim is for every young person to have 45 days of work experience by the time they're 19.

According to the most recent data, the MBacc has been rolled out across 101 secondary schools and colleges in Greater Manchester - about 40% of the total.

The Greater Manchester Combined Authority says 1,405 young people accessed workplace experiences during its second year.

Time will tell, as those teenagers leave school and enter the world of work, how transformative it will be.

News.title: Schools to offer technical subjects to pupils from age 14 in England, Burnham says
News.content:
Secondary school pupils in England will be able to study subjects like manufacturing and AI in addition to core academic learning under reforms outlined by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The government said the courses, which would be available from Year 10, would be linked to local industries and designed to give children a clearer pathway into work.

Data published this year showed more than one million young people across the UK were not in education, employment or training, the highest level in more than 12 years.

Few details have been published about how the new vocational courses would work in practice and it is not clear how they would operate in areas with low industrial activity.

The BBC understands that the government expects the new pathways into work to be up and running in some areas by 2028.

Later on Tuesday, the government also announced a new bursary of up to Â£4,500 for some families who would lose out on money if their children wanted to do an apprenticeship, because the child benefit they would lose out on would be worth more than the apprenticeship starter salary.

Speaking at a train manufacturing site in Derby, Burnham said: "We've had a system built for too long around the university route and it sends a message to some young people that they're some kind of second-class citizens, and it's just not right.

"They need an education system that works for them as well, that offers a path to all young people, that's balanced between academic and technical."

The prime minister said he was "on a mission" to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training - known as "Neet" - but declined to put a target date on his ambition.

"The trend is rising at the moment, so the first thing I've got to do is to stop that rise," he said.

"It's hard to put a firm date on the moment when you can say there are fewer than now."

However, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said while there was a "broad consensus" on improving vocational education, it was "not a big bold announcement".

She told BBC Breakfast: "What's going on there is a drastic shortage of jobs because Labour's policies over the last couple of years have killed job opportunities for young people. This announcement will not solve that."

News.title: Fourth heatwave grips parts of UK with 35C forecast
News.content:
A fourth heatwave of the year is now under way for parts of the UK, with temperatures expected to climb into the mid-30s Celsius later this week.

This latest spell of heatwave threshold-level temperatures is expected to peak on Wednesday in the south-east and east of England.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has warned the rising temperatures could increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.

It has issued amber heat health alerts, external for much of eastern England that come into force on Wednesday.

News.title: Laughter and tears at Dame Penelope Keith funeral
News.content:
Dame Penelope Keith's funeral has been hailed as "wonderful, beautiful and absolutely amazing" by her friends.

The actress, who starred in The Good Life and To The Manor Born, "died peacefully whilst living with cancer at her home" on 29 June at the age of 86.

Crowds lined the streets to say their goodbyes to the "very special lady" as her coffin travelled through her home town of Milford in Surrey before the service at Guildford Cathedral.

Broadcaster, writer and former politician Gyles Brandreth said the funeral was "filled with a mixture of sadness but laughter and gratitude as well because we were celebrating a great actress".

"It was a wonderful way to remember a remarkable person," he told BBC Radio Surrey.

Posting on X later, he said: "There was laughter and tears at Guildford Cathedral this morning - a truly beautiful and deeply moving funeral service for Dame Penelope Keith - what a lady and what a perfect service.

"It caught her completely. She was very special."

News.title: Unsolved Suzy Lamplugh case 'haunts' detectives
News.content:
Police officers investigating the disappearance of estate agent Suzy Lamplugh in west London say they remain "haunted" by the case, four decades after she went missing.

Lamplugh, 25, vanished after leaving her Fulham office to meet a client on the afternoon of 28 July 1986. She never returned and her body has never been found.

As the Metropolitan Police investigation is due to be mothballed next year, cold case detectives say they are troubled by the continuing mystery.

To mark the 40th anniversary of her disappearance, the Lamplugh family has released previously unseen photographs featuring her siblings Lizzie, Tamsin and Richard and her parents Paul and Diana.

In releasing the intimate family images, her siblings described her as "a truly beautiful person inside and out".

News.title: Hundreds of thousands of women get morning-after pill via free pharmacy service
News.content:
The morning-after pill, known as emergency contraception, external, is medication designed to prevent unwanted pregnancies. It usually has to be taken within three to five days of having unprotected sex. The sooner it is taken, the more effective it is.

It works by delaying or preventing the release of an egg, but will only prevent pregnancy if ovulation has not already happened.

Alternatively, women can visit a doctor or nurse to have a coil or intrauterine device (IUD) fitted to prevent pregnancy at any time during their menstrual cycle. To be effective, it needs to be fitted within 120 hours or five days of unprotected sex.

The government said making the morning-after pill available free from pharmacies would end the "unfair" barriers and postcode lottery some women faced - with access varying dramatically depending on where they live.

Under the scheme, women can visit their local pharmacy and have a confidential consultation with a pharmacist or trained pharmacy technician, before receiving the medication on the same day.

Prior to this, women had to book an appointment with their GP, sexual health clinic or pharmacy to get the morning-after pill. Women could also access it privately, as they still can now.

In 2024/25, there were around 150,000 NHS prescriptions for the morning-after pill - far fewer than under the new service.

Dr Sue Mann, NHS National Clinical Director for Women's Health, said the pharmacy service was a "major step forward for women's health", with "no appointment, no waiting and no judgement".

"This service is already making a real impact, particularly for women living in more deprived communities, by making contraception easier to access closer to home," she added.

Women can check online, external to find their nearest participating pharmacy. All pharmacists and pharmacy technicians delivering the service have received specialist training to provide emergency contraception and wider contraceptive care.

News.title: Man guilty of murdering two men found in woods
News.content:
A man has been found guilty of murdering two men he met in a homeless shelter.

James Desborough had previously admitted preventing the lawful burial in 2025 of 57-year-old Claudio Aquilino and 43-year-old Daniel Coleman.

A jury at Winchester Crown Court heard the 40-year-old, of Old Oak Woods, Lower Sticker, Cornwall, dismembered his victims' bodies, tried to burn their remains and hid them in woodland in Sticker where he owned a cabin. He is due to be sentenced on Wednesday.

Earlier this year, Desborough was found guilty of murdering his cellmate in Exeter Prison while on remand for the Aquilino and Coleman trial. He was sentenced to life with a minimum tariff of 19 years over that killing.

The court heard Aquilino was last seen alive on 18 April 2025 and Coleman was last seen on 3 June 2025.

Both men had suffered from serious addictions and were seen in the company of Desborough on pub CCTV in Newquay and Truro respectively.

Prosecutors said both men were likely killed by Desborough soon after they were last seen.

News.title: Chairman stole £22k from junior football club to fund cocaine habit
News.content:
A former junior football club chairman stole Â£22,491 from accounts and faked HMRC documents to feed his cocaine habit.

Karl Morecroft, 45, lied to club members at RTB Ebbw Vale while taking home the payments over the course of 15 months.

The club in Blaenau Gwent supported 330 children and relied on the goodwill of fundraisers, parents and volunteers to raise the money to keep going after the fraud.

Morecroft was given a 20-month jail term suspended for two years at Cardiff Crown Court on Monday, and must complete 180 hours of unpaid work and 50 rehabilitation days.

He was also ordered to pay Â£21,259 within three years and a default order of 12 months in prison if he failed to do so was imposed.

News.title: The 10 most overcrowded commuter trains revealed
News.content:
The most overcrowded train service in England and Wales last autumn was a Thameslink morning rush hour service between Bedford and Three Bridges in West Sussex, according to the Department for Transport (DfT).

Second on the list was a West Midlands service from London Euston to Crewe, Cheshire, departing at 17:46, the government figures reveal.

Overall, they show overcrowding on commuter trains serving major English and Welsh cities fell slightly, for the first time since 2020, due to an increase in capacity.

Only 1.1% of peak-time travellers were on an overcrowded train, the DfT said. More than 1.2 million of the average 1.9 million journeys on a typical autumn day were in London.

The DfT says work is under way to improve capacity where there are pinch points during peak hours.

The Thameslink service which topped the list had a "load factor" â meaning how full the train was â of 176% at London St Pancras shortly after 08:00.

The West Midlands service to Crewe had a load factor of 170%. It was busiest when it departed Euston.

The third most crowded train was a Transport for Wales service from Bridgend to Rhymney, with a load factor of 161%. It was busiest at Llanishen.

Four of the top ten services were operated by South Western, and Thameslink appeared twice more.

President Trump has never let negotiating world affairs get in the way of one of his other main tasks in office: posting on Truth Social.

On an unusually busy day in Washington — with White House visits from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, plus a memorial ceremony for the late senator Lindsey Graham — the president was unusually busy on social media, firing off more than 20 posts around these marquee events on the schedule.

At times, the messages, which ran the gamut from commentary on AI to false claims about the 2020 election being “rigged,” came just a single minute apart.

It’s unclear if the posts were pre-scheduled or made live, but they gave little indication of the president’s day full of high-stakes meetings that touched on two of the globe’s most pressing conflicts.

In fact, none of his posts on Tuesday on Truth Social had to do with Ukraine or Israel , and his only reference to Graham was a post about the campaign of Sen. Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham’s sister, who has temporarily been appointed to her brother’s vacant Senate seat and is running for a full term with Trump’s surprise endorsement.

President Trump fired off numerous social media posts on Tuesday in between attending meetings with the leaders of Israel and Ukraine and visiting the memorial service of the late senator Lindsey Graham ( Reuters )

Instead, the president made posts about last week’s victory parade for the Spanish World Cup team, where game-winner Ferran Torres wore a red, MAGA-style hat with the slogan “Make Spain Great Again.”

He also shared what appeared to be an AI-made image of Sen. Elizabeth Warren holding a machine gun, plus a post claiming he was the “#1 most followed and watched world leader on TikTok,” with videos under the Trump hashtag allegedly receiving more than 425 billion views.

Later in the morning, after his meeting with Netanyahu, Trump posted about a heroic young lifeguard who pulled a child out of the waves in Santa Cruz, California.

“We’re going to bring this heroic young man, and his family, into the White House with, perhaps, the boy he saved, to give him a High Civilian Honor,” Trump wrote. “Very brave, he deserves it!”

This is a breaking news story and will be updated with new information.

News.title: Trump has launched a new ‘Red Scare’ in the US – a favorite tactic of the right
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

President Donald Trump’s recent speech at the Mount Rushmore National Memorial was a key moment in his carefully choreographed America 250 weekend. Though partisan and rambling in typical Trumpian style, the speech stood out for its focus on a theme which has increasingly dominated his rhetoric over recent months: the dangers of communism.

Communism is back, the US president argued – a resurgent menace and mortal threat to American liberty.

He linked the fight against communism to the upcoming midterm elections in November. Trump’s Republican party is presently on course to lose at least one and possibly both houses of Congress. Meanwhile, the president’s personal job approval ratings continue to plummet.

This attack on communism might seem so ludicrous as to be easy to dismiss. It is partly a response to the success of Zohran Mamdani, who was elected last year as the mayor of New York on a Democratic Socialists of America ticket.

Neither Mamdani nor any of his Democratic Socialists colleagues are remotely close to being communists. But Trump has clearly decided that the best strategy for the midterm elections is to whip up a new Red Scare.

open image in gallery Trump has linked the fight against communism to the upcoming midterm elections in November ( AFP via Getty Images )

He may well be right. Anti-communism has huge appeal within American political culture – particularly for the generation of voters who, like Trump, grew up on a diet of cold war propaganda.

Ironically, given the connections Trump has regularly made between communism and immigration, it also appeals to some voters from immigrant communities. For much of the Latin American diaspora in the US, particularly from places such as Cuba and Venezuela, anti-communism is even more politically powerful than it is for the rest of the country.

When we think about the history of anti-communism, we probably think first about McCarthyism and America’s last major Red Scare in the 1950s. But anti-communism was not limited to the US or the cold war. It was one of the most powerful global political projects of the 20th century.

Anti-communism drove Britain and its allies to invade Russia 1919, and provoked a rightwing backlash against the rise of the Labour party in the 1920s. It fuelled Christian politics and parties in the interwar period, particularly in the Vatican.

Anti-communism also underpinned the rise and popular appeal of fascism throughout Europe in the 1920s and ’30s. It drove Britain’s murderous fight against Malaysian independence in the 1950s, caused up to 1 million deaths in the Indonesian genocide of the 1960s, and was used to justify mass torture and disappearances during the Latin American dictatorships of the 1970s.

About the author David Brydan is a Senior Lecturer in the Modern History of International Relations, King's College London. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article .

It also underpinned many features of 20th-century politics that are widely regarded as progressive. The UK’s welfare state, for example, was built to encourage the working classes to resist the siren call of communism. Social democratic parties existed to offer a reformist alternative to revolutionary parties to their left. Many trade unions, in Britain and elsewhere, pursued the fight against communist rivals with even greater urgency than the fight against their bosses.

Anti-communism, in short, was a far more persistent and powerful force in 20th-century history than anti-fascism.

Manufacturing an ‘enemy within’

There are three reasons why anti-communism was, and remains, such a powerful project. The first is the ease with which hatred or fear of communism can be yoked to hatred or fear of other outsider groups.

For Trump, the link is between communists and illegal immigrants. For the Nazis, it was between communists and Jews. Hitler’s deranged obsession with “Judeo-Bolshevism” culminated in the Holocaust.

The second reason is the ability of anti-communism to unite people across the political spectrum, from traditional conservatives to the wildest fringes of fascism.

open image in gallery This attack on communism might seem so ludicrous as to be easy to dismiss. It is partly a response to the success of Zohran Mamdani, who was elected last year as the mayor of New York on a Democratic Socialists of America ticket ( Getty Images )

In the Spanish civil war, fear of communism proved a more powerful ideological glue for Franco’s supporters than fear of fascism did for the fractured Republican side. And throughout history, there have been plenty of examples of liberals and social democrats who, when push came to shove, chose to line up on the side of the fascists when the threat of communism loomed.

The third reason is that anti-communism doesn’t require the existence of actual communists to retain its power.

Many of those being tarred with the brush of communism, like Mamdani, are no more than moderate social democrats by historical standards. Similarly, most of those killed in the anti-communist massacres in Indonesia and Latin America weren’t card-carrying party members. And while there were plenty of Jewish communists and socialists in early 20th-century Europe, the idea that all Jews were communists was nothing more than an antisemitic fever dream.

We can see all of this at play in the rise of the global far right over recent decades. Former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro declared at his first inauguration that Brazil’s flag would never be red. Colombia’s president-elect, Abelardo de la Espriella, denounced his reformist opponent as a “radical left Marxist”.

Even mainstream UK conservatives such as Suella Braverman are prone to sharing “cultural Marxism” conspiracy theories.

For all these reasons, it’s important not to be blinded by the seeming absurdity of Trump’s anti-communist rhetoric. Anti-communism is back – indeed, it never went away.

It survived the end of the cold war, embedded itself within some of the most extreme ideological currents of the far right, and is now reemerging as a central plank of global politics. It is powerful, persuasive and dangerous, and we need to take it seriously.
