Marie Nickle has been working her whole life, and now approaching 61, she has been thinking more and more about what her dream retirement looks like.

“I would like to spend more time with my family and my husband. We don't really spend a whole lot of time together because everybody is at work most of the time,” she said. “We like to travel, we like to go to the beach, and we like to camp.”

But for Nickle, retirement may remain a dream. She is one of millions of Americans in their 60s who fear they’ll never be able to retire due to a mountain of student loan debt. Some are still carrying debt from their own college years decades ago, while others took out loans for their children or went back to school themselves later in life.

“We want to retire so we can enjoy life, but we can't, and I don't know when or if we ever can,” Nickle, who went back to school to earn a master’s degree in special education when she was 49, told The Independent.

Student loan debt is commonly thought of as a young person’s problem. But borrowers aged 35 and older outnumber them, according to the latest Department of Education data on federal student loan debt. There are 24.6 million borrowers aged 35 and older compared to 20.2 million under that age, the data shows.

open image in gallery Marie Nickle, 61, is one of the millions of Americans who fears they’ll never be able to retire due to their student loan debt. Nickle, pictured with husband Joe, returned to school in 2015 so she could qualify as a special education teacher ( Marie Nickle )

Older people also owe more money than younger people, on average. Americans over 50 have approximately $47,500 in student loan debt compared to an estimated $27,300 for under-35s, according to the data.

Collectively, 9.5 million Americans over-50 owe close to half a trillion dollars in federal student loan debt.And there are 1.5 million more people over 62 years old with student loan debt today than a decade ago, according to the education department.

“Borrowers are taking longer to repay their loans, and that's why we're seeing more older borrowers,” explained Betsy Mayotte, president and founder of The Institute of Student Loan Advisors, a nonprofit that offers free advice to consumers.

Another reason, Mayotte said, is the rise in non-traditional students. “So, not someone right out of high school going to college, but someone in their 30s or 40s going back to college trying to get better employment,” she said.

The Independent spoke with three Americans in their 60s who are entering their golden years with punishing amounts of student loan debt.

The three, all members of the grassroots advocacy group Student Loan Justice, said that despite making tens of thousands of dollars in repayments, their student loan balances have swelled due to interest accumulated over the years.

In addition to accruing interest, others have been hit with steep penalties for falling behind on payments, leaving them with balances in the six figures. A record 9.5 million Americans are more than nine months behind on their student loan payments, analysis from The Associated Press revealed this week.

The student loan system also saw a major change this month by the Trump administration,limiting the amount Americans can borrow while restricting their repayment options. The overhaul also axed the Saving on a Valuable Education, or SAVE plan, a Biden-era initiative that calculated monthly payments based on income and a borrower’s family size.

“I have been working in this industry in a policy and advocacy role for over 25 years,” Mayotte said. “I have researched student loan policy back to the 60s, and I could say truthfully, without feeling like I'm being dramatic, that the past five years have been the most chaotic policy in the history of the program.”

She added: “It's even difficult for experts to keep up lately. So, if it's hard for experts to keep up, how do we expect the general consumer to?”

‘People need to understand how this is really tearing lives apart’

Nickle, from Pennsylvania, went back to school in 2015 to make the jump from teaching assistant to special education teacher, and took out a federal student loan for $73,000 to cover her studies.

The mom, 60, said she was inspired to get her master’s because of her son, Alex, 37, who is disabled. “If I have a child in my classroom with a disability, I'll fight for them,” she told The Independent.

open image in gallery Nickle is one of 9.5 million Americans over 50 who collectively owe approximately $456.5 billion in federal student loan debt. She has paid back more than $75,000 of a $100,600 balance, but still owes approximately $25,000 ( Marie Nickle )

Despite making monthly payments of around $250, the accrued interest saw the balance peak at $100,600. Nickle said she has paid back more than $75,000 but still owes approximately $25,000.

“It's sad…I'll talk about it with my husband and we say we’ll never be able to retire unless I can get something done about this loan,” Nickle said. “People need to understand how this is really tearing lives apart.”

Under the Biden-era SAVE plan, Nickle said her payments were manageable. “It was an affordable payment. It was wonderful,” she said. But the Trump administration ended the SAVE plan July 1 - and Nickle, like millions of others, has seen her payments jump: in her case, to $600 a month.

open image in gallery Nickle said the Saving on a Valuable Education plan — a Biden administration initiative that calculated monthly payments based on income and a borrower’s family size — was a huge help until it was recently axed by the Trump administration ( AFP/Getty )

‘There are people who have the funds. I was a single parent’

Between 2011 and 2016, single parent and teacher Diane took out Parent PLUS loans totaling approximately $60,000 on behalf of her children, now 29 and 26, to cover their undergraduate degrees at four-year colleges in business management and physical therapy, respectively.

Parent PLUS loans tend to come with a higher interest rate and limited repayment options, something Diane said she wished had been made clearer to her at the time. Her balance stands at approximately $120,000, she told The Independent.

“The loan will outlive me. It's just the way it is,” the 61-year-old who lives in Torrance, California, and asked The Independent that her last name not be used for privacy reasons.

The Parent PLUS loan program was launched in 1980 and aimed at higher-income parents sending their children to more expensive private schools. But over time, more lower and middle-income families started using the loans as the price of public education increased.

It left many parents saddled with debt they’ve been unable to pay off. In 2016, more than 200,000 families earning less than $40,000 took out a Parent PLUS loan, according to an NBC News report at the time, citing federal data.

“There are people who have the funds. I was a single parent, I didn't have it. I wanted to give my children an education, so I didn't have much of a choice,” Diane said.

open image in gallery Betsy Mayotte, president and founder of The Institute of Student Loan Advisors, said the last five years have been ‘the most chaotic policy in the history of the program’ in her more than 25 years of research ( AFP via Getty Images )

Diane, a transitional kindergarten teacher at a Title 1 school — a federally funded program which supports children from low-income families — is currently on an income-driven repayment plan. Her monthly repayments are around $80.

“Luckily, my payments are totally manageable,” she said. “But [the total debt] is going to outlive me.”

She added: “I would love to do a little bit of travel, and not have to worry about working forever. But I don't see retirement in my future.”

Diane said that being a part of the Student Loan Justice community, which describes the system as “viciously predatory,” has made her realize she’s not alone.

“For a long time I did feel like, what a stupid thing I did. How could I have done this?” Diane said. “But now I'm like, ok, I'm not the only one.”

“It makes me want to do something for the future and ask, ‘How can we move forward and try to change things?’” she added, calling for clearer guidelines and more support from the government to navigate the complex system.

Mayotte said that consumers have to make decisions based on the information in front of them.

“There definitely is some personal responsibility with respect to finances,” she said of the negative judgement older borrowers often experience when it comes to decisions they made decades ago.

“But with what's been going on with student loans for the past five or six years, even borrowers that do pay close attention to their finances and what's going on, they could not have predicted what happens with SAVE and some of this other stuff.”

‘I'm just gonna die with student loan debt’

Arizona grandmother Carol Henderson-Dahms, 60, graduated with a bachelor’s degree in advertising in 1990 before returning to school in 2002 for her master’s, which left her with approximately $28,000 in student loan debt overall.

Over the course of her working life, she has made minimum monthly payments and despite paying back more than $100,000 - she still has a balance of $82,000 today because of the amount of interest accumulated.

“I honestly feel I'm just gonna die with student loan debt. I've always paid, I've never defaulted,” she said. The 60-year-old said the only time she didn’t make a payment was, like millions of others, during the pandemic.

“Whatever choices were available to me, I always chose the lowest payment,” said the self-employed consultant, whose clients include non-profits and the federal government.

And while Henderson-Dahms doesn’t regret going to college, she wonders what she would have done if someone sat her down at 18 years old and warned her of the potential pitfalls of only paying back the lowest monthly amount.

open image in gallery Arizona grandmother Carol Henderson-Dahms loves to work but believes she will die with student loan debt, she told The Independent. She described her debt as ‘snowballing’ over the decades, having been passed around so many different federal student loan servicers ( Carol Henderson-Dahms )

“I think when I was 18, if somebody said, ‘Hey, this is like credit card debt. Your interest builds up, and don't stay on those low payments very long…I don't know what I would have done because of life, rent, kids, childcare and everything else. But I think there could have been a middle ground,” she said.

She described her debt as “snowballing” over the decades, having been passed around so many different federal student loan servicers—companies who are contracted by the government to handle the loan on its behalf.

“They have switched me through so many servicers that I can't even count,” Henderson-Dahms said. “The interest just keeps capitalizing.”

Now she has moved to an income-driven repayment plan and pays just over $300 a month. In 11 months, she said the monthly repayments will jump to anywhere between $800 and $1,100 because her income was higher this year.

“At this age, I’m trying to think about putting more in my 401k so I can actually retire; my husband's retired already. But with having a payment of that size, something would have to give,” she said.

When she thinks of her ideal retirement, it still involves working with the causes she supports now.

“I love to work,” Henderson-Dahms said. “I help a food bank, a crisis pregnancy center, a senior center... so basically, I would do what I still do, just volunteering. But at some point I feel like the debt is something that's going to infringe on my ability to decide when it's time to stop.”

Mayotte said that student loan debt policies are being written “with the assumption of a younger person being the borrower.” She also raised concern that policymakers do not understand the scale of the problem for older Americans.

“Today in 2026, when people think student loan debt, the picture in their mind is a 20-something,” she said. “And that's just not the case.”

News.title: Jailhouse calls reveal Georgia school shooter’s obsession with online notoriety after attack
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

After killing two students and two teachers at Apalachee High School in Georgia, the teenage gunman spoke frequently with his mother from jail about his online notoriety, with his mother at one point saying she would create a shrine in his honor.

Prosecutors played recordings of those conversations between Colt Gray and his mother during the 16-year-old’s sentencing hearing Tuesday. Gray pleaded guilty Friday to 55 counts, including murder, for the Sept. 4, 2024, shooting at the school, located about 45 miles (73 kilometers) northeast of Atlanta. The discussions raised enough concern among officials that Gray’s mother was later prohibited from communicating with him.

In Georgia, murder carries a minimum sentence of life in prison. Barrow County Superior Court Judge Nicholas Primm must decide whether Gray will have the possibility of parole after reviewing testimony and evidence from both prosecutors and the defense. Tuesday marked the third day of a sentencing hearing that began Friday.

open image in gallery Gray spoke frequently with his mother, Marcee Gray, by phone from a youth detention center in the months after the shooting ( Jason Getz/Atlanta Journal-Constitution via AP )

Teachers Richard “Ricky” Aspinwall, 39, and Cristina Irimie, 53, and students Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo, both 14, died in the shooting. Another teacher and eight more students were wounded, seven of them hit by gunfire.

A jury in March convicted Gray's father, Colin Gray, on charges including second-degree murder and involuntary manslaughter. He is scheduled to be sentenced Thursday. Prosecutors said he gave his son the assault-style rifle used to open fire at the school.

Colt Gray wanted to know if people were talking about him

Ashley Gilleland, an investigator with the district attorney's office, testified that Gray idolized other mass shooters, talking about them online with other members of the “true crime community,” a group of young people online who are fascinated with such attacks. He chatted with other people online about gaining notoriety through a school shooting and his admiration for previous mass shooters.

There were aspects of his preparation and behavior before and after the Apalachee High School shooting that mimicked other mass shooters, Gilleland testified.

He spoke frequently with his mother, Marcee Gray, by phone from a youth detention center in the months after the shooting. During those phone calls, portions of which were played in court, he would direct her to look up what people were saying about him online. When she described “fan art” drawings depicting him or comments people made about him, he asked her how much engagement those posts were getting and seemed excited when they were getting a lot.

Marcee Gray repeatedly told her son she would print some of the images and bring them to him, and during at least one conversation said she was also going to print some photos for herself.

“Have you made the shrine?” Colt Gray asked his mother, indicating that he wanted her to make a shrine to him. His mother responded that she needed to go get some photos printed. “Then I'll make my Colty shrine,” she said.

When Marcee Gray described a request she'd gotten just over a month after the shooting from a journalist who wanted to make a documentary about the case, Colt Gray told her, “Yes. Go for it.”

He also repeatedly asked his mother to communicate with one of the people he'd been speaking to online before the shooting to pass along messages to their online community. His mother assured him she would.

open image in gallery Gray also repeatedly asked his mother to communicate with one of the people he'd been speaking to online before the shooting to pass along messages to their online community ( Arvin Temkar/Atlanta Journal-Constitution via AP )

In February 2025, about five months after the shooting, it came out during a court hearing that the district attorney's office was aware of their calls. Marcee Gray told her son that she didn't believe they'd talked about anything inappropriate but that she was being accused of encouraging her son.

Barrow County District Attorney Brad Smith has asked investigators questions designed to discredit claims Colt Gray made during two interviews with investigators the day of the shooting. The teenager talked about hearing people tell him to do things, having uncontrollable urges and acting spontaneously.

When a sheriff's office investigator asked him if he was seeking attention, Gray said no and said he thought it was “really childlike” when mass shooters did that.

But his online conversations, a notebook that included a step-by-step plan for how he would carry out the shooting and the conversations with his mother contradicted his claims and showed careful planning of the attack and his intention to survive it, Gilleland said under questioning by Smith.

State official says Colt Gray seemed to improve with treatment

Candice Broce, who is director of the state Division of Family & Children Services and commissioner of the Georgia Department of Human Services, was called to testify by Colt Gray's attorney. She managed Gray's case after he was put in foster care while in detention because he was a minor and his father was in prison and there were concerns about his mother's contact with him.

Broce testified that Colt Gray had suffered abuse and neglect and that her agency had opened investigations into the family several years before the shooting. During her initial assessment, she tried to find health records for Gray but said he was unable to recall ever going to a doctor.

“I was really surprised by the complete absence of care,” Broce said.

She testified that Gray appeared to show improvement while being treated. After Marcee Gray was barred from speaking with her son by a July 2025 no-contact order and he started taking medication, staff at the youth detention center later told Broce it “changed him essentially into a different child,” she said.

News.title: Let’s see what the ‘Burnham bounce’ can do for us all
News.content:

Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. A little over a week since he was appointed prime minister, Andy Burnham has his very own “bounce”. The boing in his personal ratings in the opinion polls has been more pronounced than that of his party, and it is undeniably dramatic.

Truth be told, his immediate predecessor’s approval ratings were never that high, even while Labour was running double-digit leads over its rivals, but by the time Sir Keir Starmer left office, they were running at dismal, historical lows.

Now, Mr Burnham is the most popular of the party leaders – and while Burnhamania has not yet quite gripped Britain, he has made the change in mood he promised. Unless something strange happens, on Thursday, he will cement a solid debut with an emphatic Labour victory over a floundering Reform UK in the Greater Manchester by-election for a new mayor. Quite the transformation from the May elections.

As is now universally accepted, perhaps even by Sir Keir himself, Mr Burnham does indeed possess superior communication skills. His critics, notably Kemi Badenoch, dismiss the appeal of Mr Burnham as mere long-lashed, Manc “vibes”, and some certainly are tiring of “government by TikTok”.

Yet Mr Burnham has brought a confidence and a rare fluency to No 10 – the one in Westminster, as well as his new North branch office. Even more impressive, where Sir Keir made the error of being so downbeat as to depress the nation in his early days in power – endless gloom about the notorious “black hole” – Mr Burnham has restored hope.

He is by nature a brighter, more relaxed personality than most frontline Labour politicians, and more at ease in front of a camera. In terms of his command and understanding of the essential media skills of his age, he is comparable only to Boris Johnson, Tony Blair and Harold Wilson over the last half century or so.

He knows, however, that this is not enough, and will not by itself propel either him or his party to victory at the next general election. He cannot rely either on Reform UK or the Greens always making the kind of disastrous misjudgements they have in recent months to boost his popularity.

What he needs are policies and, as he claimed he had during his leadership election, a plan. He needs to imbue his administration with a sense of purpose, and one clearly visible to the electorate. Sir Keir got tangled up in an incoherent matrix of missions, pledges and phases that even his own advisers struggled to keep up with. Without a compelling narrative, Mr Burnham will in due course struggle just as badly as Sir Keir did to hold public trust and support.

Rishi Sunak and Sir Tony Blair, among many others, have publicly counselled their successor that a prime minister enjoys maximum leverage during their first days in power. That is the moment to expend political capital and the best moment to make a mark on history.

In terms of his choice of personnel, Mr Burnham has selected some excellent lieutenants to be by his side, notably John Healey in the Treasury, Shabana Mahmood pursuing crucial reforms on asylum at the Home Office, and the redoubtable Pat McFadden to deal with the highly combustible challenge of welfare reform – whose failure sank Sir Keir’s premiership.

Mr Burnham may have marginalised the Starmerites, but his cabinet feels better balanced than Sir Keir’s team. The appointment of Bridget Phillipson as party chair is at least a gesture of reconciliation to the ancien régime.

The policy decisions taken in the early days of power can define a premiership, for good or ill. Some get it right, as in 1997, when the Blair administration in its first week decided to make the Bank of England operationally independent. John Major took the first step to abolishing the poll tax.

Others misjudge recklessness for bravery, as when Liz Truss assured the country on her first day that: “I have a bold plan to grow the economy through tax cuts and reform.”

Others do something right and symbolic, but which achieves limited resonance with the public, which is what happened with the cancellation of the Rwanda plan for migrants by Sir Keir as his first act – now forgotten even by him as part of his “legacy”.

Mr Burnham’s early days can be characterised as small actions and big talk. As a former mayor, and now a seasoned politician, he responded to public concerns about the cost of living with modest moves that nonetheless showed that he has indeed been listening in recent weeks.

Bringing in a temporary cut in VAT on domestic electricity bills, cutting bus fares to £2 a ride and the 20 per cent reduction in business rates for pubs and clubs were eye-catching and popular. In macroeconomic terms, they were irrelevant. In the political calculus, they yielded a far more lucrative return – the Burnham Bounce.

Now, Mr Burnham has an opportunity to do something big, something to match the soaring rhetoric we sometimes hear from him. He is to pick up where he left off when he was health secretary under Gordon Brown and relaunch nothing less than his “National Care Service”.

It is a fitting project for a Labour government, an echo of the foundation of the National Health Service – and an attractive one for him because he could succeed where predecessors in all parties have had to abort their plans to “fix” the issue. That includes Sir Keir and the former health secretary, Wes Streeting, who spoke the same sort of language, but, rather than taking action, chose to postpone it during yet another review of the system, this time by Dame Louise Casey.

That work is being brought forward by Mr Burnham, and he at least is trying to build a cross-party consensus on the way forward. It will take time, as he is sensible enough to admit – but at least something is being done.

A real sense of momentum is at last being felt, in Whitehall and beyond. If Mr Burnham keeps it up, he’ll deserve a great deal of credit.

Evan Rachel Wood has opened up about her disappointment about not being invited to return for the upcoming sequel to Practical Magic.

Wood, 38, was just 11 when she appeared in the beloved 1998 movie as the youngest daughter of Sandra Bullock’s character Sally Owens.

A sequel is set to be released this September, with 26-year-old Joey King taking over Wood’s role.

Speaking to Entertainment Tonight, Wood said she “hadn’t had the chance to connect” with King about playing the character.

The new film is based on Alice Hoffman’s 2021 novel The Book of Magic, the follow-up to her own 1995 novel which inspired the original film.

Evan Rachel Wood says she’s ‘sad’ not to have been invited to reprise her role in the ‘Practical Magic’ sequel ( Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images )

Wood added: “You know, I read the book and it seems like they’re not following the book... I think in the book it would have made sense to bring me back. I think in the way that they’re redoing it, and approaching it, it didn’t make sense.”

The Westworld star continued: “It is sad because when you’re acting, truth is found money. We bonded with that cast so much as children, so to miss out on the opportunity to look at that cast, and look at that house, as an adult and see the history in our eyes is something that can’t be faked.

“I’m sad that that doesn’t get to exist, especially for the fans, but I wish them all the best and obviously wish Joey the best. I hope she had a great time, and I still have really fond movies of being in the original.”

Wood was speaking at the premiere of The Shards, the new FX series created by Ryan Murphy and Bret Easton Ellis, based on Ellis' semi-autobiographical novel of the same name.

The first Practical Magic film starred Bullock and Nicole Kidman as sisters Sally and Gillian, who are descended from a long line of witches. Raised by their aunts after the death of their parents, they are taught the practical uses of magic.

Alexandra Artrip starred alongside Wood as Sally’s eldest daughter, Antonia. Artrip has also been notably left out of the Practical Magic 2 cast.

While the original film initially received mixed reviews, it’s since become a beloved cult classic and is particularly well-remembered for its soundtrack, which includes both a score by Alan Silvestri and Stevie Nicks’ original song “If You Ever Did Believe” as well as a re-recording of her song “Crystal.”

The forthcoming sequel will welcome back Bullock and Kidman, as well as Stockard Channing and Dianne West as their aunts Franny and Jet.

News.title: Recovery aids and building muscle: Welsh weightlifter Laura Hughes answers your questions
News.content:
Laura Hughes first discovered weightlifting while training at her local Crossfit gym, making the transition from amateur gym-goer to competitive lifting.

Now a member of the Welsh national weightlifting squad, the 33-year-old holds the Welsh record for both the snatch and the clean and jerk (the two official competitive lifts in weightlifting) and is currently third overall in the women’s Welsh rankings. Hughes won bronze at the 2018 Commonwealth Games in Australia and was selected again for this summer’s Games in Glasgow.

We caught up with her for our Readers Ask series, where industry specialists answer questions from our Telegraph Recommended Reader Panel.

Who inspired you to get into weightlifting?

Olamilekan, South East

Originally, it was lots of different people, particularly general gym goers who were doing weightlifting at my gym. As I’ve grown as an athlete and become more competitive, I’ve had other inspirations.

Most notably, coming into [the Commonwealth Games], it has to be Gareth [Evans], our coach. Looking back at his performance in 2018 when he won his gold medal is so inspiring. [English lifter] Emily Godley was another competitor in 2018. She won the gold medal in my category and I just remember thinking that she was on fire that day.

What are the best exercises for you to build muscle mass?

Norman, Wales

We spend a lot of time doing our main lifts, so snatches, clean and jerks, but we also do lots of pulls and squats. I spend a lot of time doing accessory work to make sure that my body stays healthy, especially being an older athlete. I’ve put on quite a lot of muscle in this last block just from going heavier and pushing my limits with my main lifts.

What advice would you give to people who want to improve their strength?

David, North West

The most important thing is consistency. As long as you’re doing something, do it regularly, even if it’s twice a week. Don’t be afraid of picking up some dumbbells. If you’ve got somebody that can teach you how to lift weights properly, that’s going to be the best option. Do it safely, do it consistently, and don’t be afraid to try new strength exercises.

News.title: Explosive mpox outbreak causes 3,000 cases in Madagascar
News.content:
More than 3,000 cases of mpox have been recorded in Madagascar after the virus spread from a single port city to some of the country’s busiest coastal hubs.

A total of 3,022 cases and 20 deaths have been recorded as of this week, with cases in Toamasina and Taolagnaro accounting for more than half of all diagnoses.

The outbreak has been linked to Clade 1b mpox, a strain that emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare a global public health emergency at the time.

“The main factor driving the continued spread of the disease is human mobility, seeding new outbreaks in areas where the virus has not circulated before,” Professor Carlos Maluquer de Motes of the University of Surrey told The Telegraph.

“Under-reporting is likely, with the real number of cases exceeding what is being reported.”

News.title: Chelsea in 10-goal thriller as ‘Alonso ball’ brings risk and reward
News.content:
Chelsea’s first match under the management of Xabi Alonso was a 10-goal thriller in Australia, as the Premier League side eventually showed their class in a 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers.

Star striker João Pedro, who was controversially left out of Brazil’s World Cup squad, scored a nine-minute hat-trick after coming off the bench with half an hour of the friendly remaining.

Alonso had selected a youthful team for the first hour before bringing nine senior players, including João Pedro, into the side in the second half. According to Transfermarkt, Chelsea’s squad is valued at over £1.3bn while their opponents a more modest £5.86m.

Teenage signing Dastan Satpayev, midfielder Dario Essugo and winger Jamie Gittens also found the net for Chelsea, who were defensively vulnerable for long spells for the game.

Here are five things Telegraph Sport learned from Alonso’s first match.

João Pedro picks up where he left off

João Pedro scored 13 goals in the second half of last season and his impressive performances resulted in the 24-year-old being named Chelsea’s player of the campaign. It was something of a surprise, then, when he was left out of Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil squad this summer.

The good news for Chelsea is that João Pedro’s absence from the World Cup has given him plenty of time to recover ahead of the new campaign, and he looked thrillingly sharp in his second-half performance against Western Sydney Wanderers. The difference in class between João Pedro and Liam Delap, the man he replaced, was clear for all to see.

Two of the Brazilian’s three goals were classy, composed finishes — and he also created a goal for Gittens after surging past three defenders on the left wing. João Pedro looks like he means business.

News.title: China’s chip breakthrough triggers global tech rout
News.content:
China has achieved a breakthrough in developing technology crucial to the AI boom, overcoming US efforts to limit Beijing’s access to the systems.

China’s chip giant Shanghai Yuliangsheng has started production of deep ultraviolet lithography machines, according to The Information, a tech publication.

These machines, which can reach the size of a double-decker bus, use high-powered lasers to imprint designs on to silicon wafers, which are used to make chips.

Until recently, only Western companies and allies of the US had the capability to produce these machines.

The most advanced versions of the technology have largely been the preserve of companies such as Dutch giant ASML and Japan’s Nikon.

These machines have been cut off from China by US export controls, preventing their production of advanced chips as Washington seeks to slow the development of AI in the country.

Semiconductor stocks plunged on the report. Trading was briefly halted on South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index after it suffered a collapse of nearly 11pc overnight, following a bleak day on Wall Street.

Advanced semiconductors, such as those used in AI chips, rely on minuscule circuits, invisible to the naked eye. They can only be manufactured by directing tiny lasers onto microchip wafers, a process known as ultraviolet lithography.

News.title: Ramsay-Peaty ‘human first, athlete second’ as he settles for second bronze
News.content:
So a pair of bronze medals for the man who once only dealt in gold. Not that Adam Ramsay-Peaty thinks that is necessarily such a bad trade when he also computes the wider price of sporting domination.

“I’ve been that person who wins all the time, and it costs you pretty much everything, and I won’t say it’s worth it,” Ramsay-Peaty said after his return to international competition continued in his now favoured 50m breaststroke with a second podium place at these Commonwealth Games. “That period of time, where I was undefeated for eight years, it was athlete first, then human,” he added. “Now it’s human first, then athlete, which is a very fair price to pay.”

Aged 31, and with a baby girl on the way with wife Holly Ramsay, Ramsay-Peaty’s order of priorities might be understandable, but it was still another performance to raise questions over whether he can again climb to the top of a major podium.

Swimming is not kind to the over-30s – Michael Phelps was the first man in 2016 to win an Olympic gold in the pool even at the age Ramsay-Peaty is now – and we still have another two years until the Los Angeles Olympics. It would be the greatest achievement even of the Englishman’s extraordinary career to win his third individual Olympic title.

He trailed from the start here and was almost exactly a second outside his world record – set almost a decade ago – as Australia’s Sam Williamson completed a breaststroke double ahead of South Africa’s Michael Houlie in second. “As you get older, it gets harder,” said Ramsay-Peaty, before adding a crucial caveat, “but I’m enjoying it more…in my head, I’m getting fresher.”

News.title: Musk passed ‘slow death sentence’ on HIV patients by cutting US spending, says head of UNAIDS
News.content:
The world’s richest man has passed a “slow death sentence” on an untold number of people with HIV by cutting US spending on the disease, according to the head of UNAIDS.

In an interview with the Telegraph, Winnie Byanyima, executive director of the UN body, said Elon Musk’s claim that the cuts made to US aid had resulted in “zero” deaths was born of ignorance.

“I do not know where Elon Musk gets his data from, but he [is] showing ignorance of the disease”, Ms Byanyima told the Telegraph at the opening the 26th International Aids Conference in Rio de Janeiro.

“This disease is not like a bullet shot in the head and you die. This is an attack on the immune system.” Withdrawing medication is a “a slow death sentence,” she said.

Data released by UNAIDS show that reductions to international funding and cuts to HIV prevention and community services threaten a resurgence of the epidemic.

In 2025, 1.2 million more people became infected with HIV and 570 000 more people died of Aids-related illnesses as the world fell short of global targets.

Although new HIV infections and Aids-related deaths are at their lowest levels in more than 30 years, an 18 per cent cut to total international funding means previous gains are now at risk, say experts.

News.title: Europe faces energy crisis as gas stockpiles sink
News.content:
Britons face a winter of surging energy bills as Europe struggles to secure enough gas to fill its storage tanks.

A squeeze on Qatari gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has pushed European gas stockpiles into “energy crisis territory”, analysts at Wood Mackenzie warned.

The Continent’s storage tanks are barely 50pc full, a historical low for this time of year. Fresh tension between the US and Iran has cut the chances of more tankers sailing anytime soon.

Wood Mackenzie now forecasts that Europe will enter the winter with its gas storage tanks no more than 75pc full, compared with a five-year average of 90pc.

This could drive up prices, as Europe competes with Asia to buy extra gas, mostly from America on the spot market.

“Europe is approaching energy crisis territory,” Wood Mackenzie warned on Monday.

Meanwhile, Britain, which no longer stores significant amounts of gas, faces paying even more than rival buyers.

“The UK’s market model is that we’ll always pay more than anyone else, rather than relying on storage,” said David Lewis, an energy analyst at Wood Mackenzie.

“If other markets are going to struggle, it just means that the UK price will be even higher.”

Last week British Gas boss Chris O’Shea warned the country risked shortages over winter because of low levels of storage.

European gas prices fell at the fastest pace in a month on Monday after a pause in attacks between the US and Iran over the weekend, dropping to about €58 per megawatt hour.

Goldman Sachs expects the price to remain at about this level for the next three months, which is 80pc higher than the pre-war price of €32.

But the US investment bank warned the price could hit €100 next year if Middle East energy exports were slow to get back to normal.

The pressure from lost Qatari supply is being compounded by the EU’s plan to prohibit imports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) from next year.

This will leave Europe in a bidding war with Japan and China for US LNG supplies.

Britain produces half its own gas and imports the rest, mostly via pipeline from Norway. But the Norwegian gas will largely track global LNG prices.

Laura Page, of the analysis firm Kpler, said Britain’s heavy reliance on Norway left it perilously exposed to any supply interruption.

“If there was a pipeline outage in Norway, or a problem with the gas field, that could cause prices to increase,” she said.

Mr Lewis said the Norwegians were postponing as much maintenance on their gas rigs as possible, to keep the supply flowing for Europe’s depleted stockpiles.

“But the problem is the same as in the UK: these are mature fields, they require a lot of maintenance, a lot of careful management,” he said.

Goldman Sachs said Europe had “only small room for error” in its gas stockpiling, and capacity could be as low as 28pc by the winter’s end.

Mr Lewis said the Netherlands and Germany were particularly exposed. “They might struggle to actually deliver the gas during peak demand days,” he said.

The El Nino weather pattern that will prevail for the rest of this year might come to Europe’s aid, delivering a milder winter than usual.

“It’s going to be an expensive winter unless we have a mild winter, which is what everybody’s hoping for at the moment. Fingers crossed,” Mr Lewis said.

Sports.title: Son of Man Utd and England legend finally lands new club and admits ‘my career’s gone full circle’
Sports.content:
TOM INCE has completed a free transfer to Tranmere Rovers in a “full-circle” move.

The veteran winger, son of former Manchester United and England star Paul Ince, has penned a two-year deal with the League Two side.



Ince, 34, had been a free agent since it was announced in May that Watford would not be renewing his contract.

He now links up with his new club, and could be in line to make his debut this Saturday as they host Rochdale in the Carabao Cup preliminary round.



Upon completing the move back to Merseyside, former Liverpool starlet Ince told Tranmere’s club media: “It’s a great feeling, bit full circle for me. I’m looking forward to it.

“It’s always great when you come to a club like this. The good thing about it for me is that I have that hunger and that desire still.



“I think that’s what’s allowed me to have the career that I’ve been able to have, the amount of games I’ve been able to play and the level I’ve been able to reach.”

Former England youth international Ince started at Liverpool, another of his dad’s former clubs, and made one first team appearance for the Reds.

Following a loan spell at Notts County he signed for Blackpool, going on to impress for the Tangerines and even playing for his dad during his final season.

Ince scored 33 goals in 113 appearances for the Bloomfield Road club, and spent the second half of the 2013-14 campaign on loan at Premier League side Crystal Palace.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Upon the expiry of his Blackpool contract in the summer of 2014, Ince sensationally turned down Inter Milan to sign for Hull City.

He has since played almost all of his football in the Championship; representing Nottingham Forest, Derby County, Stoke City, Luton Town, Reading and Watford in the second tier.

Ince did get one more crack at the Premier League, playing 33 times for Huddersfield during the 2017-18 campaign.

He still played relatively regularly at Championship level last term – scoring four goals in 27 appearances for Watford – and could represent something of a coup for League Two Tranmere.



Rovers boss Darrell Clarke said: “Tom is a player who brings real quality and experience to the group. He’s played at a very high level throughout his career.

“He’ll give us creativity, composure and versatility in the final third, while his experience will be invaluable to some of our younger players and we believe he’ll be an excellent addition to what we’re building here.”

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino plotting shameless plan to SELL World Cup as furious Uefa blast ‘it’s not Fifa’s to sell’
Sports.content:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino is plotting an outlandish move to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

The scheme, which would involve forming a company to control the World Cup and Club World Cup and potentially earn Infantino tens of millions of pounds, has already been blasted by Uefa.



European chiefs have launched a furious statement saying the idea “crosses a line”, adding that football is “not Fifa’s to sell”.

Potential investors have reportedly been briefed on the plot that would also see each of Fifa’s 211 member associations handed a £15m share of the company that they could choose to sell themselves.



According to The Times, figures close to Donald Trump’s administration are amongst those consulted about the plans.

Joshua Kushner’s Thrive Capital is expected to lead the proposed investor group and JP Morgan is set to be Fifa’s financial advisor for the project.



Kushner, 41, is the younger brother of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Fifa would assume the majority ownership of the company, with private investors owning up to 30 per cent initially – costing them billions of pounds.

The money-making plot could also see Infantino appointed as an effective “commissioner” of the company once his final presidential term ends.

Infantino is set to be re-elected unopposed until 2031.

Reports have suggested that a commissioner role could carry an annual salary worth around £48MILLION.

The blueprint would likely drive Fifa – currently a non-profit organisation – to focus more on commercial revenue due to outside pressure from investors.

That could see the World Cup expanded from 48 teams to 64 and prioritising host nations based on their commercial potential.

There could also be pressure to hold the tournaments more often than every four years to increase revenue.



The Times report that Fifa’s 2022-2026 World Cup cycle is expected to have raked in £11.3BILLION in its current format.

A Fifa statement read: “Fifa is always on the lookout for innovative projects that can boost the development of football around the world and is always open to reviewing proposals submitted to it. We are starting a consultation process.

“As the Fifa President stated on July 18 during a meeting with all Fifa member associations, the priority now is to, ‘unleash the commercial potential and opportunity that Fifa has,’ after Fifa World Cup 2026 success.



“Fifa makes its decisions democratically, and a proposal that Fifa has received and is currently reviewing will soon be presented to the 211 Member Associations and the Fifa Council, who will be the sole final decision-makers on the matter.”

The project has already received major backlash, including the stern statement from Uefa. It read: “This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross. Uefa takes it extremely seriously.

“So should every National Football Association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game.

“The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade – especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA’s to sell.”

This battle is the latest in football’s ongoing civil war that could tear the game apart.

Sports.title: Lisandro Martinez and Alexis Mac Allister employ private security after Argentina’s heated World Cup win vs England

Martinez has developed a cult following since he joined United in July 2022 and their matchgoers have chanted “Argentina” in support of their Argentinian players over the last 25 years.

A ‘We’re not English, we’re Scouse’ banner is frequently seen at Liverpool matches while a ‘United>England’ banner is permanently pinned up at Old Trafford.

View 2 Images Vinicius Jr will reportedly remain at Real Madrid amid interest from Arsenal. (Image: Photo by Fran Santiago/Getty Images)

Real Madrid head coach Jose Mourinho has intervened and Arsenal target Vinicius Junior will not leave the club, according to reports. Sky Sports have claimed that the former Chelsea and Manchester United manager is keen to keep the Brazilian in the Spanish capital, scuppering Mikel Arteta's hopes of a landmark signing.

‌



The forward is into the last 12 months of his deal at the Bernabeu and uncertainty had been cast over his future at Madrid with the prospect of losing him on a free transfer. However, Mourinho has stepped in and Los Blancos will reportedly not sanction a sale while there is confidence that he will sign a new deal with the club.

‌



The Gunners had shown a genuine willingness to fund a move for the 26 year old after identifying the winger as a considerable upgrade on their current options, according to football.london.

‌



UEFA hit back at FIFA plan to SELL World Cup in bitter war of words READ MORE :

Arteta's side had been assessing the feasibility of pushing through a deal, with the Premier League-winning manager giving his blessing for the transfer to go ahead.

Arsenal had been on high alert regarding the prospect of snapping up Vinicius, with the two-time Champions League winner entering the final 12 months of his contract at the Bernabeu.

However, the Gunners will now be forced back to the drawing board, with Mourinho determined to keep his prized assets available as he prepares for his first season back at the helm.

‌



FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

It is understood that Vinicius and the Spanish giants are poised to enter fresh discussions, with the Brazilian international fully expected to put pen to paper on a new long-term contract.

Club president Florentino Perez is reportedly central to the negotiations and has made no secret of his determination for the forward to stay. Real Madrid head into the upcoming season aiming to topple rivals Barcelona from the top spot, after Hansi Flick's side cruised to La Liga glory with relative ease.

‌



Despite falling short of domestic honours, Vinicius remained integral to Real Madrid's attacking play, contributing 22 goals and 14 assists across all competitions. BBC Sport revealed earlier this week that the forward was open to staying at the club but wished 'to feel loved' with his new contract reflecting his significance to the side.

View 2 Images Vinicius Jr celebrates winning the 2023/24 Champions League with Real Madrid (Image: Getty Images Europe)

Mourinho's team have been active this summer following the signings of Ibrahima Konate and Bernardo Silva on free transfers, while they secured Marc Cucurella and Denzel Dumfries from Chelsea and Inter Milan respectively.

‌



Arsenal begin their Premier League title defence against newly-promoted Coventry City on August 21 as they seek to successfully retain their top-flight trophy.

Christos Tzolis became the most recent summer acquisition after finalising his switch from Club Brugge. This summer's transfer window has proved a challenging market to navigate following the missed opportunities for Morgan Rogers and Jeremy Monga.

Chelsea and Manchester City moved swiftly to secure the two highly-regarded additions following Arsenal's public chase of the duo. Vinicius' standing could mean that any transaction for his services will surpass £100million.

Article continues below

Any transfer would almost certainly have implications for Gabriel Martinelli's future, with the club understood to be willing to entertain offers this summer.

Sports.content:
Man Utd handed Aurelien Tchouameni timeline hint amid Real Madrid agreement mystery

Real Madrid star Aurelien Tchouameni continues to be linked with a summer move to Manchester United as Michael Carrick looks to bolster his midfield options

View 2 Images Man Utd are interested in Real Madrid and France star Aurelien Tchouameni (Image: Getty Images)

Manchester United could potentially sign Real Madrid star Aurelien Tchouameni in August - if Rodri joins the Spanish giants by then. The French midfielder has reportedly signed a contract extension at Los Blancos, but the La Liga side are yet to confirm it, leading to hope at Old Trafford.

‌



The Red Devils are open to signing a third midfielder this summer after Casemiro's departure and Manuel Ugarte's serious injury during the recent World Cup. United have signed Andrey Santos from Chelsea and Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa so far, but Michael Carrick's squad lacks a specialist defensive midfielder.

‌



That has led to links with former Monaco star Tchouameni. It is understood that United have conducted background checks on the 26-year-old several months ago and are keen on a deal should he become available.

‌



Chelsea hoping to repeat Man Utd and Liverpool's inspired transfer deals with latest moves READ MORE :

Ruben Amorim admits to Man Utd mistakes and explains how sacking has changed him READ MORE :

And despite confusion over whether the No.8 has signed a contract extension at the Santiago Bernabeu, Real have been linked with a big-money move for Manchester City star Rodri and may need to drum up funds.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

The Spanish giants have stepped up their interest in the 30-year-old, who is into the final year of his City contract. Rodri has been offered fresh terms by the Blues, but the deal remains unsigned, and his future this summer remains uncertain.

‌



The Spanish World Cup winner has undergone surgery and is expected to remain out of action for a few weeks. When back to full fitness though - Real could make their move and sign him.

View 2 Images Rodri could hold the key to Man Utd signing Tchouameni (Image: Getty Images)

That means United could then have an opening to acquire Tchouameni in mid-August. Carrick's men have until the summer transfer window closes on September 1 to sign him.

At City, new Blues manager Enzo Maresca has insisted that Rodri would 'be back with us' and that he was not concerned by the transfer speculation surrounding his star midfielder.

Sports.title: Xabi Alonso drops telling hint over Chelsea’s Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck transfers
Sports.content:
Xabi Alonso drops telling hint over Chelsea’s Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck transfers

Chelsea have been linked with moves for veteran Premier League stars Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck and boss Xabi Alonso has spoken out on deals for the pair

View 2 Images Xabi Alonso took charge of his first Chelsea match on Tuesday (Image: Getty Images)

Xabi Alonso has refused to confirm Chelsea are interested in signing Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson - but hinted that the Blues want to add more experience. The Blues have been linked with moves for the veteran stars over the past few days.

‌



Reports have suggested that Henderson, 36, will be allowed to leave Brentford on a free transfer just a year after moving to West London. It has also been suggested that Chelsea are already in talks with Brighton regarding a move for Welbeck.

‌



Asked about potential deals following Tuesday’s 6-4 victory against Western Sydney Wanderers, new Chelsea boss Alonso remained tight-lipped.

‌



He said: “No, I'm sure that from today until the last day of the transfer [window] there will be a lot of rumours, so to be commenting on all of them. It's going to be a hard task, but for sure we need proper balance in terms of qualities, in terms of positions, in terms of balance.

“We want to have a complete squad and we want to make a good team. For that we have an idea, we have a plan and let's see how we set it up until the start of the Premier League.”

Chelsea hoping to repeat Man Utd and Liverpool's inspired transfer deals with latest moves READ MORE :

Xabi Alonso left with easy transfer decision as Chelsea win Western Sydney Wanderers goalfest READ MORE :

Chelsea’s moves for Henderson and Welbeck are huge departures from their previous approach in the market. Having preferred to sign youth with promise in previous windows, the Londoners now appear to be prioritising experience.

‌



Chelsea have of course already been busy in the window this summer. Morgan Rogers arrived from Aston Villa for £117m earlier this summer, while Marco Palestra was signed from Atalanta.

Elsewhere, Geovany Quenda and Emmanuel Emegha arrived at Stamford Bridge on pre-agreed moves. The Blues have already earned considerable sums back, with Andrey Santos and Marc Cucurella having joined Manchester United and Real Madrid respectively.

View 2 Images Chelsea are interested in signing Jordan Henderson (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Tyrique George has signed permanently for Everton following last season’s loan spell, while Alejandro Garnacho has been allowed to move to Aston Villa on loan. Another star who could leave before the end of the transfer window is striker Liam Delap.

The 23-year-old endured a difficult debut season with Chelsea, having netted on just three occasions. On the striker, Alonso added: “Every player that is involved is doing well, Liam as well. It was 60 minutes when he had to battle hard against the centre-backs, a good few lays off, so he's doing well and preparing for the season.

“I see him in a good mood, in a good desire to get proper fitness, proper football feeling good, and he's doing well.”

Sports.title: UEFA hit back at FIFA plan to SELL World Cup in bitter war of words
Sports.content:
UEFA hit back at FIFA plan to SELL World Cup in bitter war of words

FIFA president Gianni Infantino is reportedly planning to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors but European football’s governing body have fired back at that plot

View 2 Images Gianni Infantino faced severe criticism throughout the World Cup (Image: Getty Images)

UEFA have taken aim at FIFA and said that football is ‘not theirs to sell’ in the face of their outrageous plan. Recent reports have suggested that world football’s governing body is planning on selling stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

‌



The scheme could see FIFA president Gianni Infantino earn millions if a deal is rubber-stamped. The administration of US President Donald Trump has reportedly been consulted.

‌



And while the plan is still being mulled over by those within the organisation, it has not gone down well within UEFA.

‌



A statement from the Champions League organisers on Tuesday afternoon read: “This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross.

Roberto Mancini named new Italy manager as Claudio Ranieri makes shock return READ MORE :

“UEFA takes it extremely seriously. So should every National Football Association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game.

“The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade - especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA’s to sell.”

‌



FIFA have already explained their plan in detail. In a statement, they confirmed that FIFA intends to expand football development funding to over $10 billion (£7.49 billion). That funding would then be available to all 211 associations that are members of FIFA.

View 2 Images Trump's administration have already been told about FIFA's plan (Image: Getty Images)

FIFA would remain as majority stakeholders in the World Cup, with private investors buying 20 to 30 per cent, and the member organisations would receive a small stake totalling 20 per cent.

‌



The Times has reported that one senior figure within the game has labelled FIFA’s plan as a "nuclear bomb" for the game.

FIFA President Infantino has regularly courted controversy this summer, particularly when it comes to the World Cup. Supporters took aim at him for the sky-high ticket prices during the tournament.

He was also criticised for his role in the decision to reverse Folarin Balogun’s ban for a red card. The American forward was initially suspended after being sent off, only for that decision to be reversed following a phone call from US President Trump.

Article continues below

On the criticism he faced, Infantino said : “You were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all. To those behind their pens and papers, behind their screens spreading hate and false rumours, I want to say that while you are sitting behind, we at Fifa are on the front lines organising, working hard, and delivering ‌the best show in the ‌world. We experienced no violence, no incidents, 100% safety and security, only joy and happiness.”

Man Utd learn Iliman Ndiaye asking price in transfer battle for Everton star

Manchester United are considering a move for Iliman Ndiaye, who also has interest from Saudi Arabian side Al-Hilal, but Everton are set to ask for a hefty transfer fee

View 2 Images Iliman Ndiaye is in demand (Image: Michael Regan/Getty Images)

Everton will demand around £70million for in-demand star Iliman Ndiaye amid interest from Manchester United and Al-Hilal. Ndiaye, 26, is a wanted man after a couple of eye-catching seasons on Merseyside.

‌



The forward is open to leaving Everton and his camp would encourage a bid from the Saudi Arabian side. But United are also in the running, with left wing among their priorities this summer.

‌



Michael Carrick's side have shortlisted Ndiaye and are tracking his situation. The Athletic report that Everton are aware of Al-Hilal's interest, although no talks between clubs have taken place.

‌



It's added that Everton are expected to ask for a fee similar to the £70million that Barcelona paid Newcastle United this summer for Anthony Gordon. Ndiaye also has three years left on his contract and the Toffees are in no rush to sell him.

Ndiaye has come to the forefront of United's options after Morgan Rogers went to Chelsea for £117m and Yan Diomande indicated that he wants to join Real Madrid. However, their search for a left winger isn't as pressing as other areas, with Marcus Rashford due to be integrated back into the squad after a season on loan at Barcelona.

‌



There have been claims that Everton would like to hand Ndiaye an improved contract in order to fend off interest, but he's rejected their proposals. The Toffees paid £15m for Ndiaye two years ago when he arrived from French giants Marseille.

The former Sheffield United star has scored 17 goals and provided three assists in 71 appearances for Everton. Ndiaye went to the World Cup with Senegal, starting one of their four games as they reached the last 32.

Sports.title: Roberto Mancini named new Italy manager as Claudio Ranieri makes shock return
Sports.content:
Roberto Mancini named new Italy manager as Claudio Ranieri makes shock return

Italy have finally ended a week of turmoil by appointing Roberto Mancini as Claudio Ranieri is hired as technical director - replacing Paolo Maldini

View 2 Images Roberto Mancini, who won Euro 2020, is back in charge of Italy (Image: getty)

Italy's manager search has ended with Roberto Mancini taking charge for a second spell - and Claudio Ranieri coming in as the country's technical director.

‌



Monday proved a pivotal day as Azzurri legend Paolo Maldini quit after only 16 days in the job after Andrea Pirlo was blocked from taking over the four-time World Cup winners. Some senior figures at the Italian Football Federation (FIGC) shied away from his appointment due to ties to a Russian betting firm.

‌



Pirlo was the third man to be eyed for the job after Pep Guardiola and Carlo Ancelotti both said no. Mancini is the fourth man they've gone after a finally a deal has been agreed with Ranieri sitting in a senior role.

‌



The FIGC president, Giovanni Malago, said on the appointment: “Mancini is the coach. I believed that the best person to become head coach was ‌Roberto Mancini.”

Liverpool's Milos Kerkez explains why he chose to keep distance from Andy Robertson READ MORE :

Chelsea hoping to repeat Man Utd and Liverpool's inspired transfer deals with latest moves READ MORE :

Ranieri replaces ⁠Maldini and will oversee technical operations and elite football development across Italy’s national team structures. He's most heralded for leading Leicester to the Premier League title but has also managed Juventus, Roma and Inter Milan.

“I needed someone with whom I could share ‌the decision on the coach, because without that shared view my reasoning would have carried little weight,” Malago said. “So consequently, we have a new coach and a new technical director for Italy.”

‌



In hiring Mancini they bring back the last man to lead Italy to tournament glory, although either side of that they've been wholly disappointing. The former Manchester City boss replaces Gennaro Gattuso, who ⁠left the post in April after Italy failed to qualify for a third World Cup in succession. He held the job from 2018 to 2023 and claimed Euro 2020 glory following a penalty shootout victory over England at Wembley.

View 2 Images Italy have bought in Claudio Ranieri as technical director

Mancini ultimately presided over the Azzurri's world record 37-game unbeaten run, but couldn't qualify for the 2022 World Cup - losing to North Macedonia in a play-off - before resigning in August 2023.

‌



Italy became the first World Cup winners ever to miss out on three tournaments successively having not played at the finals since 2014, when they were knocked out in the group phase. That was also the case in 2010, marking a dire run since they claimed the World Cup in 2006.

Italy start their Nations League campaign on 25 September at home to Belgium before travelling to face Turkey three days later.

Sports.title: Mandhana fires Manchester Super Giants to victory over SunRisers Leeds
Sports.content:
Smriti Mandhana dazzled with an imperious 88no to fire Manchester Super Giants to a four-wicket win over SunRisers Leeds at Headingley.

SunRisers looked to have the upper hand after strong performances from Australian stars Phoebe Litchfield (31 off 26) and Annabel Sutherland (35 off 24) - aided by a brilliant cameo from captain Dani Gibson (18 off 6) - to give the home side a defendable score of 142, having lost just four wickets over their 100 balls.

The home bowling attack looked to have consolidated that prominent position with a brilliant second-innings spell which yielded four wickets for 10 runs, to leave the Super Giants reeling at 71-5 having been 61-2, but Mandhana held firm, with the opener reaching her half-ton from just 33 balls.

Image: Dani Gibson made 18 off 6 at the end of the SunRisers innings

Image: Smriti Mandhana made an imperious 88no to guide her team to victory

Leeds looked to have taken the pivotal wicket 91 balls in, but Mandhana was dropped on the boundary on 71, and made no mistake with her remaining balls as she smashed two straight sixes to win the game for her side with five balls remaining.

The win preserves the Super Giants' unbeaten record, putting them second with 10 points in the Hundred table, while a second loss for the SunRisers leaves them fifth on four points.

Sports.title: Scandinavia retains Goodwood Cup crown after eventful race
Sports.content:
Scandinavia confirmed his superiority over Trawlerman to defend his Al Shaqab Goodwood Cup title in fine style at Goodwood.

Aidan O'Brien's son of Justify and his John and Thady Gosden-trained adversary had served up a thriller in the Gold Cup at Royal Ascot and another titanic tussle looked on the cards on the Sussex Downs.

Sent off the 6-5 favourite, Ryan Moore was always hot on the heels of Trawlerman who headed affairs in the hands of William Buick, in a race that had early drama when Amiloc unshipped Hector Crouch leaving the stalls.

Amiloc would again play a key role after Buick had set sail for home heading downhill into the straight and with the two Ascot rivals knuckling down for another battle, the loose Amiloc cut across the pair, checking Trawlerman's momentum and allowing Scandinavia to scorch clear.

He galloped on eight and a half lengths into the distance as Trawlerman finished second once again to his Ballydoyle foe, with Roger Varian's Rahiebb third.

"I'm delighted, I'm thankful to everyone around him. He's a great horse, he's a real top stayer," said O'Brien.

"He's a high cruising speed, he relaxes and finds his momentum. Ryan said he finds the minute he starts asking him, he starts coming alive underneath him.

Image: Ryan Moore rode Scandinavia to Goodwood Cup success

"We were a bit worried coming to Ascot because we've never been two and a half (miles) and you're never sure until you do it.

"We felt he's really gone the right way since Ascot. It's a great race to win, very prestigious.

"It's great that Trawlerman came and all the horses were there, it's what we all want to see - win, lose or draw.

"We thought that Trawlerman was going to make it, we were hoping that he would so Ryan could just follow him as he did in Ascot.

"It was going to be very simple, was he good enough or not? Obviously there was a little bit of drama, Trawlerman was a bit slowly away and Ralph's (Beckett) horse (Amiloc) was loose.

"It was a bit eventful, but it was still a great race at a great track. It was a spectacle to watch and going two miles, you get a great chance to look at it and take it in."

Of Scandinavia's future, O'Brien added: "He's very sound, he loves what he's doing and the lads love having him.

"When you get a horse like this that can race year in, year out, that's what makes it special.

"They're very hard to find, impossible really. I would imagine he'll keep racing as long as he stays safe and sound.

"He could (emulate Yeats, four-time winner of the Gold Cup), he's a natural cruiser. He's easy to train, he's a great mind and as he's by Justify, he has that great rhythm."

Moore said: "It was nice for him to have a horse to follow all the way, he probably thinks he got beat!

"His stride never shortened, he just kept galloping all the way to the line - what more can you say?

"He likes fast ground, he's a high-class horse and hopefully there's a few more good days to come."

Kaiya Fraser shines with Vintage performance

Kaiya Fraser produced a brilliant ride to land the Coral Vintage Stakes at Goodwood aboard the unbeaten Dr Rascal and celebrated the biggest victory of his career in the process.

The winning jockey had endured the nasty experience of being pulled from the saddle of the Oliver Cole-trained colt by the bite of a loose horse before remounting to win at Ascot earlier this month.

On this occasion the 23-year-old held his nerve to squeeze through a narrow gap on the rails on the inside of David Egan on Pikachu a furlong from home, delivering the son of Sottsass to land the spoils at 13-2 by half a length from the Aidan O'Brien-trained Haffner.

Favourite Al Hudaiba once again looked a difficult ride, with William Buick struggling to get him going before finishing a close third.

Fraser said: "It means everything, this is what we wake up for every morning.

Image: Dr Rascal claimed Group 2 gold at Goodwood

"I've put so much hard work in to get where I am today and all the people around who have helped me - my agent James Forrest and all the owners and trainers who put me up.

"I'm very grateful to them and I wouldn't be here if it wasn't for them."

He added: "You saw today, he had to get a push into the stalls because he obviously had that experience last time out where he got a bit nervous, but luckily he's a willing horse and he went in with a bit of encouragement and he got out and got the job done."

This was a first victory for Cole in a race his father Paul won three times with Putra (1996), Central Park (1997) and Strategic Prince (2006).

He said: "I was always quietly confident, he's a very good horse.

"I wasn't very nervous before the race which was quite a good thing because I have a lot of faith in this horse.

"He's a very fast horse… another unlucky run really because he got loose before Ascot and then he's just got mullered coming up there in the straight and he's still won.

"We'll probably look to the Dewhurst or something like that; he's got so much class and so much speed and he's very well bred, we're very lucky to have him in our stable.

"We're not used to these kinds of horses so back to the drawing board (for plans). The Royal Lodge probably not. I'll have to go away and have a think about it.

"It means a lot (to follow in his father's footsteps). My first complete year as a trainer, it means a lot. It's not just me, there's a big group at home that work so hard - I'm very proud of all of them."

The stewards did have a look afterwards, but found Fraser and Dr Rascal had gone through a legitimate gap on the inside of Pikachu.

Fraser said: "My horse slightly came off his line and I just had to straighten him up, didn't cause anything.

"I'm delighted, first Group winner - in a Group Two on a very nice two-year-old, so I'm looking forward to the future."
