World.title: Kenya: Court Lifts Shisha Ban in Major Blow to Government Crackdown
World.content:
Nairobi — The High Court has lifted the ban on shisha, ruling that continued enforcement of the prohibition is unlawful and unconstitutional after the government failed to regularise the underlying regulations.

In a judgment delivered Tuesday, Justice Bahati Mwamuye held that the Public Health (Control of Shisha Smoking) Rules, 2017 ceased to have legal effect after the government failed to comply with a 2018 court order requiring the regulations to be regularised within nine months.

The judge ruled that state agencies could no longer rely on the lapsed regulations to enforce the ban, declaring unlawful a February 3, 2025 Ministry of Health press statement and an April 14, 2025 directive ordering a nationwide crackdown on shisha outlets.

Justice Mwamuye further found that the continued enforcement of the expired regulations violated the constitutional rights of members of the Novel Tobacco Products Association, and issued orders restraining the government from enforcing the 2017 rules and the subsequent directives against the association.

The ruling effectively removes the legal basis that authorities had relied on to sustain the ban, pending any fresh lawful regulatory action by the government.

World.title: Cote d'Ivoire: Over 400 Liberians Left Homeless After Demolition of Communities Outside Abidjan
World.content:
Abidjan — More than 400 Liberian nationals have been left homeless and stranded after a large-scale demolition exercise carried out by Ivorian authorities destroyed hundreds of homes in the Vridi Canal community on the outskirts of Abidjan, according to leaders of the Liberian diaspora in Côte d'Ivoire.

The demolitions, which took place approximately three weeks ago, formed part of the Ivorian Government's ongoing urban redevelopment and settlement clearance program aimed at addressing unauthorized structures and improving urban planning in rapidly expanding areas surrounding the commercial capital. However, the operation has had devastating consequences for hundreds of Liberian migrants and their families who had lived in the affected communities for decades.

Speaking on the situation, Mr. Robert Varney Zoker, Vice President of the Liberian Community in Côte d'Ivoire, described the humanitarian conditions facing displaced Liberians as dire and worsening by the day.

"The situation is extremely difficult," Mr. Zoker said. "Hundreds of Liberians have lost everything--their homes, personal belongings, businesses, and important documents. Many are now living in temporary shelters under very challenging conditions."

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

According to the community leader, the demolition exercise swept through several settlements housing migrant populations, including a large number of Liberians who had established roots in the area over many years. The affected population includes women, children, elderly persons, and individuals with special needs, many of whom now lack access to adequate shelter, food, healthcare, and sanitation facilities.

Community representatives say the destruction of homes has left many families vulnerable and uncertain about their future. In addition to housing, residents also lost household items, fishing equipment, small business assets, savings, and official documents, making recovery increasingly difficult.

In an effort to provide immediate relief, members of the Liberian community have mobilized limited resources to assist the displaced. Some families have been temporarily relocated to school buildings and other makeshift facilities, but community leaders warn that these arrangements are unsustainable.

"We took some of them to temporary shelters in schools and other locations," Mr. Zoker explained. "But conditions remain very, very difficult. People are sleeping in crowded spaces, and many families are struggling to find food and necessities."

The humanitarian impact has become particularly alarming for vulnerable groups. According to Mr. Zoker, some displaced women have been forced to give birth under inadequate conditions while taking refuge in temporary shelters.

"Imagine someone delivering a baby in a school building because they have nowhere else to go," he said. "It is heartbreaking and demonstrates the severity of the crisis facing these Liberians."

Many of the affected Liberians were residing in communities along the Vridi Canal area, a strategic zone in Abidjan that serves as a major maritime gateway connecting the Port of Abidjan to the Atlantic Ocean. The area has historically attracted fishing communities and migrant workers due to its access to economic opportunities.

Mr. Zoker noted that a significant number of those affected are fishermen and their families who have lived and worked in Côte d'Ivoire for decades, contributing to local economic activity while maintaining strong ties to Liberia. "These are people who have been living here for more than 60 years," Mr. Zoker said and added, "Most of them are fishermen who built their livelihoods around these communities. Today, they have nowhere to go."

Concerned by the deteriorating conditions, the Liberian community in Abidjan has formally appealed to the Governments of Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire, as well as humanitarian and international organizations, to provide urgent assistance.

The community is requesting emergency support in the form of temporary accommodation, food supplies, medical care, sanitation services, and psychosocial assistance for affected families. Leaders are also seeking transportation support for Liberians who wish to voluntarily return home and rebuild their lives in Liberia.

According to Mr. Zoker, a petition outlining the plight of the displaced Liberians has already been submitted to the Liberian diplomatic mission in Abidjan, urging immediate intervention and engagement with Ivorian authorities.

Community representatives have emphasized that the issue requires swift diplomatic attention to prevent further suffering and ensure that vulnerable families receive the protection and support they urgently need.

The plight of the displaced Liberians has drawn comparisons with recent interventions undertaken by the Government of Ghana. Following the same demolition exercise, Ghanaian authorities reportedly assisted approximately 327 Ghanaian nationals who had been affected by the demolitions. Among them, 228 individuals were repatriated through a special operation coordinated by Ghana's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Ghanaian officials said the intervention was designed to ensure the safety and welfare of their citizens while facilitating the transport of families and their belongings back to Ghana. The operation has since been cited by members of the Liberian community as a model that could be replicated to support Liberians facing similar circumstances.

Drawing on that example, community leaders are calling on the Government of Liberia, through its Embassy in Abidjan and relevant national agencies, to undertake a comprehensive assessment of the affected population and develop a coordinated response plan.

Recommendations include engaging directly with Ivorian authorities, documenting the number of affected Liberians, facilitating humanitarian assistance, and arranging the voluntary and orderly repatriation of those seeking to return to Liberia.

Community leaders believe that urgent diplomatic engagement and humanitarian intervention will be critical in alleviating the suffering of displaced Liberians and restoring hope to families who have lost nearly everything.

Close 

As efforts continue to determine the full scale of the displacement, many affected Liberians remain in temporary shelters, relying on the goodwill of fellow community members and local support networks. While uncertainty hangs over their future, community leaders remain hopeful that the Liberian Government, in partnership with Ivorian authorities and development partners, will move swiftly to address the crisis and provide relief to citizens affected by the demolitions.

For the hundreds of Liberians now struggling to rebuild their lives, timely assistance and coordinated action could mean the difference between prolonged hardship and a pathway toward recovery and dignity.

According to Ivorian authorities, the demolition campaign formed part of a broader government initiative aimed at eliminating structures deemed unsafe, reducing environmental and public safety risks, and reorganizing urban spaces to support modernization and sustainable city planning. Officials maintain that the exercise is necessary to improve living conditions, enhance infrastructure development, and prevent settlement in high-risk areas vulnerable to flooding and other hazards.

However, the operation has generated significant criticism from affected residents and human rights advocates, many of whom argued that the evictions were carried out with little or insufficient prior notice. Residents claim that families were given limited time to remove their belongings before demolition crews arrived, leaving many unable to salvage personal possessions, business assets, and important documents.

World.title: Kenya: Expert Debunks Kindiki Duty Transfer Claims As DP Dismisses 'Fake News'
World.content:
Nairobi — Deputy President Kithure Kindiki's brief dismissal of viral claims that he had been stripped of key government responsibilities has now received backing from a governance expert, who says the controversy is based on a misunderstanding of Kenya's legal framework rather than an actual transfer of power.

The debate erupted after social media was flooded with reports alleging that President William Ruto had reassigned Kindiki's role in coordinating intergovernmental affairs to Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi.

However, Kindiki brushed aside the reports in a short message posted on X.

"Fake news," Kindiki wrote.



His response came as speculation continued online, although neither State House nor the Office of the Prime Cabinet Secretary has issued an official statement confirming that any such reassignment has taken place.

Governance and devolution expert John Burugu argues that the claims have been exaggerated and fail to consider how Kenya's intergovernmental system is established under the Constitution and various Acts of Parliament.

According to Burugu, if any administrative adjustments have been made, they should not be interpreted as stripping the Deputy President of constitutional or statutory powers.

Instead, he says the issue highlights a long-standing administrative gap created by the absence of a substantive Cabinet Secretary responsible for Devolution.

"The perceived loss, politically, by the Deputy President is misplaced because it is a move to correct a mistake by the same administration aimed at easing operational and administrative hiccups," Burugu said.

He added that assigning certain administrative responsibilities elsewhere would merely address operational challenges rather than diminish the office of the Deputy President.

"Therefore, there is no political fodder as is being hyped over the matter," he stated.

Burugu further noted that one of the Deputy President's most significant intergovernmental responsibilities remains protected by law.

He explained that Section 187(1)(a) of the Public Finance Management Act expressly provides that the Deputy President chairs the Intergovernmental Budget and Economic Council (IBEC), the body responsible for coordinating fiscal relations between the national and county governments.

According to the expert, that position cannot change unless Parliament amends the law.

"It is expected that legal provision under the PFM Act would prevail and allow H.E. Prof. Kithure Kindiki to continue chairing this fiscal intergovernmental structure," Burugu said.

Close 

He added that only an amendment to the Public Finance Management Act could remove the Deputy President as IBEC chair.

Presidential Special Projects Head Dennis Itumbi also rejected the reports, saying the claims were based on a misunderstanding of Kenya's intergovernmental governance structure.

According to Itumbi, intergovernmental relations are shared among several legally established institutions, including the National and County Government Coordinating Summit, IBEC, the Intergovernmental Relations Technical Committee (IGRTC) and the Council of Governors.

He maintained that IBEC remains chaired by the Deputy President as required by law and argued that suggesting one office had taken over another's constitutional mandate was inaccurate.

"The claims are FAKE NEWS," Itumbi said.

"Each institution has a specific mandate. Suggesting that one office has taken over another's constitutional or statutory role is simply inaccurate."

World.title: Africa: Rethink. Rebuild. Rise. - AIDS 2026 Charts the Next Phase of the HIV Response
World.content:
Rio de Janeiro, Brazil — The global fight against HIV has never had more powerful scientific tools or faced greater political uncertainty.

More than 7,000 scientists, activists, policymakers and community leaders gathered in Rio de Janeiro for the opening of the International AIDS Conference. Global leaders warned that decades of progress against the epidemic could be reversed by shrinking international funding, geopolitical tensions and growing attacks on human rights.

The warning comes at a contradictory time in the HIV response.



Science has made breakthroughs that seemed impossible. It has changed HIV from a deadly diagnosis into a manageable condition. Researchers have developed highly effective long-acting prevention medicines and are working on simpler, longer-lasting treatment options. However, many of these gains are out of reach for millions of people because of political choices, funding gaps and rising inequalities. The science exists. The question confronting AIDS 2026 is whether the world can find the political will to deliver it.

In this context, the six-day conference began with the theme "Rethink. Rebuild. Rise." This theme calls not only for celebrating scientific progress but also for reconsidering how it is funded, delivered, and safeguarded in an increasingly uncertain world.

International AIDS Society President and AIDS 2026 International Co-Chair Professor Beatriz Grinsztejn said the meeting comes at a pivotal moment for the global HIV response, with scientific advances colliding with mounting political and financial challenges.

"We are here because the world needs us to be - Rethink. Rebuild. Rise. And by meeting here in Latin America and the Caribbean, we are showcasing the value of investing in the creativity and strength of the Global South," she said.

Grinsztejn said that the choice of Brazil as host reflected the country's long-standing commitment to universal access to HIV care and treatment. The region is one of the few in the world where new HIV infections are still rising, even as case numbers fall elsewhere. Brazil has been a global leader in adopting a science-driven, human rights-based approach to HIV. It has also played a key role in advancing HIV prevention research.

The global HIV response, she said, is being battered by converging crises, geopolitical shifts, sudden funding cuts, and rising hostility toward the communities most affected by the virus. "We gather in the shadow of decisions made by a few and felt by too many in clinics and communities across the planet," she said.

Despite those challenges, Grinsztejn said the HIV response has repeatedly demonstrated what science and political commitment can achieve. This year marks 30 years since the introduction of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), which transformed HIV from a near-certain death sentence into a manageable chronic condition. It is also 15 years since the HPTN 052 trial results, presented in Rome in 2011, established the scientific basis for the principle of Undetectable = Untransmittable.

Since then, she said, treatment has moved from complex multi-pill regimens to single daily tablets and long-acting injections; this week's program will preview a once-weekly oral treatment now in development. Prevention science, she added, has advanced just as far, with long-acting injectable tools that would have been unimaginable at the outset of the epidemic.

"These advances could bend the curve of the pandemic, if we follow the evidence on where and how to implement them, and if we make access the number one political priority," she said.

However, Grinsztejn warned that scientific breakthroughs alone cannot end the epidemic. None of it matters, she said, without access, and access, thirty years on, remains the field's unresolved problem. Nearly nine million people still cannot get life-saving treatment, a gap she attributed not to missing science but to political choices, financing failures, and a persistence of stigma and discrimination that no drug can dismantle on its own.

She also criticised the international response to financing the HIV epidemic.

Many of the countries carrying the heaviest HIV burden are simultaneously being pressured to fund their epidemic responses while servicing colonial debt.

She added that demands rebuilding the way we deliver the HIV response with a sustainable global solution, including debt restructuring and a serious reckoning with historical injustice. And social justice demands the realization of the right to health as a fundamental human right.

We must never forget that upholding democratic values is an integral part of public health.

"But to achieve that, we need political will," said Grinsztejn. "We need far greater political commitment than was demonstrated at last month's United Nations High-Level Meeting on HIV. The fact that some Member States turned their backs on the discussions and the Political Declaration itself shows just how significant the challenges ahead remain."

"AIDS 2026 will be our moment to push back," Grinsztejn said.

Grinsztejn said AIDS 2026 would put the scientific evidence on the record, hear the testimonies of communities most affected by HIV and help drive the political will needed to turn scientific evidence into policy and financing decisions around the world. She urged delegates to remain focused on the people most affected by the epidemic.

"We rise because the evidence is clear, our voices will not be silenced, and people living with and affected by HIV cannot wait," said Grinsztejn.

We are not going back

UNAIDS Executive Director Winnie Byanyima said the world was entering a new phase of the HIV response, shaped by shifting geopolitical realities, funding uncertainty and growing inequality.

She thanked Brazil and the International AIDS Society for convening scientists, communities, policymakers, and activists in one room. She credited Brazil specifically for demonstrating, over decades, that universal access to health care is not an aspiration but a decision that governments can make.

That spirit, she said, is what the moment now demands. The global order has shifted profoundly since the field last met at this conference two years ago, and there is no reversing it.

"We are not going back... We must build something new, an AIDS response for the world that we have today, not the world we wish existed, not the world of yesterday," she said. She pointed to the political declaration on HIV that UN member states adopted just weeks ago, despite deep geopolitical tension, as evidence that a shared global commitment to ending AIDS still holds, and as a roadmap the field now has to act on.

Geography, she argued, must never be what determines who lives and who dies.

She said every breakthrough in the response had come from confronting exclusion through science, human rights and global solidarity. However, she warned that many of those gains were now under threat. On rights, she argued that the AIDS response has always advanced by putting people and human rights at its center, driven by communities demanding dignity and treatment.

That progress, she said, is now under strain for the first time since UNAIDS began tracking rights globally; criminalization is rising rather than falling, with more countries criminalizing same-sex relationships last year alone. She pointed to Senegal, where she said fear has displaced trust and HIV services for the people who need them most are closing as a result. Facing that reversal, she said, will require broader coalitions than the field has built before, uniting the HIV response with women's movements, LGBTQI movements, and democracy movements, since she argued health, gender justice, and democracy will rise or fall together. "History tells us that organized people eventually defeat organized money," she said.

Such policies, she said, were already forcing vulnerable communities away from HIV services.

She praised researchers for transforming laboratory discoveries into life-saving medicines available around the world. But she said access to the latest HIV prevention technologies remained far too slow. Two years ago, at the same conference, trial results identified a twice-yearly injectable as the most effective HIV prevention tool yet developed. Today, she said, the rollout is moving far too slowly. She said the world should already be working towards reaching 20 million people rather than only a fraction of that number. She rejected the idea that the higher target is unrealistic.

"During COVID, 4.5 billion people received vaccines within a year... We can move just as urgently to deliver HIV prevention," said Byanyima.

Byanyima also called on pharmaceutical companies to expand licensing agreements and technology sharing so that low- and middle-income countries, particularly in Latin America and Africa, could gain affordable access to new HIV medicines. Her call to industry was direct: open access, scale production, and share the underlying technology.

"Open the gates. Scale production. Share technology," she urged. "Millions of lives depend on the speed of implementing this."

She also warned that the global HIV response was facing one of its greatest financial challenges in decades. She described the response as one of the largest acts of global solidarity in public health history, built through the Global Fund, PEPFAR, UNITAID, governments, and communities, and now under unprecedented pressure. International HIV financing fell by more than US$1.5 billion last year, she said, while many heavily affected countries were spending more servicing debt than investing in health. She said it cannot substitute for external funding cut abruptly.

"This is not economic inevitability. This is the result of political choices," Byanyima said, calling for debt restructuring, fairer international taxation and sustained international solidarity alongside increased domestic investment.

Despite the challenges, she said there were still reasons for optimism, pointing to renewed commitments by African governments, Brazil's leadership on regional pharmaceutical production and growing international efforts to reform global financing.

"The world has changed," Byanyima said. "But our values have not changed and will not change. We still believe that every person deserves dignity. We still believe that scientific progress must benefit everyone. And we still believe that inequality can be defeated."

She said ending AIDS as a public health threat remained within reach if governments matched scientific innovation with political commitment, equity and global solidarity.

Progress is real, but it's fragile

WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the global HIV response stood at a defining moment. He warned that decades of progress were under threat but could still be protected through renewed commitment to science, communities and stronger health systems.

Tedros praised Brazil's leadership, saying that Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva had demonstrated the power of political commitment to expand treatment access. He cited Brazil's defense of free HIV treatment, its work making medicines more affordable, its support for production partnerships in Africa, and its record on protecting human rights.

"For more than four decades, HIV has tested humanity - not only our science, but our solidarity," he said. "Again and again, when the world predicted failure, communities proved it wrong."

He said that scientists, working alongside affected communities, had transformed HIV from a fatal diagnosis into a manageable condition. Countries have expanded lifesaving treatment to millions of people. But he warned that the global response was now facing its most serious disruption in a generation. "We have not come to Rio to mourn what is at risk," he said. "We have come to defend it. And to build what comes next."

Close 

He said the conference theme, Rethink. Rebuild. Rise, reflected what was needed to keep the world on track to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.

"We must rethink how we deliver services, making them more integrated, more people-centered, and more resilient. We must rebuild partnerships that put countries and communities at the center of every decision. And we must rise, not by lowering our ambition, but by renegading it," he said. "The goal of ending AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 is still within our reach," Tedros said. "But only if we're willing to act differently."

Tedros launched WHO's progress report on its Global Health Strategy on HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections for 2022–2030, which he said tells two stories at once: evidence that new infections and AIDS-related deaths have fallen sharply where countries have invested in health, science, and communities, alongside proof of how quickly funding cuts, emergencies, and inequality can reverse those gains.

He also announced new WHO guidance on HIV surveillance and updated service delivery recommendations designed to help countries strengthen routine monitoring, improve long-term care, and integrate HIV services into broader primary healthcare systems. He committed WHO to continuing to fold HIV services into primary health care and universal coverage more broadly, and to accelerating access to innovations from long-acting prevention and treatment to diagnostics and digital tools.

He said that a scientific breakthrough only counts once it reaches everyone, not only those who can pay for it. That integration, he said, will extend to tuberculosis, viral hepatitis, sexually transmitted infections, sexual and reproductive health, mental health, and noncommunicable disease services, alongside continued work to eliminate mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B.

"A scientific breakthrough only matters when it becomes a public health breakthrough for everyone, everywhere - and not only for those who can afford it," he said.

None of it, he said, works without communities, whom he described not as optional partners but as the architects of the response. These are the ones who reach people health systems cannot, defend human rights, and hold everyone else accountable. Tedros urged countries to protect HIV financing, strengthen community-led organisations and repeal laws that criminalise key populations. "Progress is real, but it's fragile," he said.

"We have the science. We have the tools," Tedros said. "What we need now is what has always mattered most in this fight - the will to stay united and the determination to finish what we started."

World.title: Kenya: Ruto Vows Every University Student Will Get Full Govt Funding
World.content:
Nairobi — President William Ruto has reaffirmed his pledge that every student joining university will receive full government funding, saying education remains the country's biggest investment despite growing concerns over where the money will come from.

President Ruto said the government is refining its university funding model to ensure every learner has access to higher education regardless of their financial background.

"We have made very good progress with our new student-centered funding model, and I want to tell our Vice-Chancellors we will be engaging them as we now progress to even a better funding model that will make sure that every student has full funding for their education," Ruto said.

He added: "That is the commitment I have made."



The President acknowledged that many Kenyans are questioning how the government will raise the money needed to finance the ambitious plan.

"I know many people are asking me, 'Where are you going to find the money to fund these universities?' And I want to tell them... if you think education is expensive, try ignorance, and you will know which one is more expensive," he said.

Ruto insisted investing in education is critical if Kenya is to become a developed nation.

"It is the single most important thing that we must do. Because for us to move this country to a first-world status, knowledge, education is central to that journey," he said.

He added that no country can achieve meaningful development without investing in its people.

"I have said no nation can develop beyond its capacity to think. If you cannot imagine the future, you cannot get there."

The President's latest remarks come a week after he announced plans to replace the current needs-based university funding system with a universal model.

If approved by Parliament through the proposed amendments to the Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) Act, every student admitted to a university, college or the Kenya Medical Training College (KMTC) from September 2026 would qualify for 100 percent government funding, regardless of family income.

The proposal follows mounting pressure on the current student-centred funding model, which has faced criticism over affordability, funding gaps and financial challenges facing public universities.

Government figures show higher education institutions continue to face significant funding shortfalls even as student enrolment continues to rise sharply.

While Ruto has maintained that no deserving student should miss higher education because of lack of money, education stakeholders have questioned whether the government has the financial capacity to implement the plan.

Close 

Despite the concerns, Ruto remained optimistic about Kenya's future.

"So, I am very confident about the future of our nation, and I am very confident about the young people who will make sure that that future becomes our reality," he said.

World.title: Thousands swarm stunning mountain escape as selfie tourism backlash erupts online
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The pursuit of the perfect selfie is creating headaches for one of the Italian Alps' most recognizable landmarks.

Viral videos shared online in recent weeks show massive crowds stretching through shuttle queues as visitors wait to reach Tre Cime di Lavaredo, one of the most iconic destinations in Italy's Dolomites.

The videos have sparked outrage, with many online commenters arguing that visitors were more interested in taking photos than enjoying the mountains.

FAMOUS BEACH NOW REQUIRES VISITORS TO RESERVE SPOTS WEEKS AHEAD AND PAY FEES

"This video proves that people are no longer able to enjoy the journey," one commenter wrote on Instagram. "In their minds, the only thing that matters is the photo."

"Everyone lined up for a photo just to show people on social media how great their lives are," said another user. "Hours in line for one picture."

Tre Cime di Lavaredo is one of the most famous landmarks in the Dolomites. It draws visitors from around the world with its trio of mountain peaks.

The UNESCO-protected mountains are subject to the Enrosadira phenomenon, in which sunrise and sunset turn the rock walls a vibrant pink and orange, according to The Dolomites — UNESCO World Heritage Centre page.

Tre Cime di Lavaredo gets over 800,000 visitors per year, per the Tre Cime di Lavaredo Hike Guide.

CLICK HERE TO 

Hikers and climbers gravitate to legendary vertical rock faces in summer, while winter transforms the region into a massive and interconnected ski network, according to Dolomites.com.

In response to the growing crowds, officials are considering requiring reservations for shuttle passengers in addition to the reservation system already in place for drivers.

Drivers must reserve access to the Rifugio Auronzo parking area in advance, according to the reservation website.

Reservations cost €40 (about $45) for cars, €26 (about $30) for motorcycles and €60 (about $68) for camper vans.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Tre Cime is not the only destination in the Dolomites that's been grappling with issues caused by overtourism.

Landowners near Seceda, another popular mountain destination in the Dolomites, reinstated €5 (around $5.60) turnstiles to help manage growing crowds at one of the region's most photographed viewpoints, as Fox News Digital previously reported.

Carlo Zanella, president of the Alto Adige Alpine Club, previously told Fox News Digital that the turnstiles were installed by a local farmer after visitors repeatedly trampled meadows while flocking to the scenic overlook.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Zanella also criticized the role of social media in reshaping mountain tourism.

"I am against the influencers," he said. "They are only interested in making money [through] advertising."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Zanella encouraged visitors to explore lesser-known areas of the Dolomites, saying there are "other even more beautiful places to visit."

Ashley DiMella of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

World.title: Chevy Chase called out for being 'not so nice' to Billy Joel's ex-wife at a keg party
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Billy Joel's ex-wife has called out Chevy Chase for being "not-so-nice" during an old-school keg party.

Katie Lee Biegel addressed the incident on a recent episode of her podcast, "All on the Table." She explained that the incident with Chase happened while she was married to Joel. The former couple tied the knot in 2004 before divorcing in 2009.

"My celebrity run-in that was not so nice was Chevy Chase," Biegel began.

"So, I was having a party with my ex-husband. It was a keg party. I wanted to have like an old-school keg party. We had a house that we were going to tear down. And it was like this little — we called it ‘The Sugar Shack,’ and had a very fun summer there, staying with friends," Biegel said.

JOEL MCHALE DISLOCATED CHEVY CHASE'S SHOULDER WHILE FILMING 'COMMUNITY'

She continued, "But then at the end of the summer, we decided to have a kind of like, ‘Tear the House Down' party, a keg party, and I had jello shots, kegs. It was a very star-studded party."

Biegel went on to explain the moment Chase mistook her for a member of the staff and "shooed" her away.

"And my ex-husband was standing talking to Chevy Chase and his wife. And I had a tray of jello shots. And I went up with the tray of jello shots and said, you know, ‘Do you guys want a shot?’ and Chevy thought that I was the staff at the party, and he took his hand and shooed me away," she said.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"He just did this," she said, making a shooing motion with her hand.

Chase has long had a reputation in Hollywood for being difficult to work with, with multiple former co-stars and collaborators alleging abrasive, confrontational and inappropriate behavior over the years.

Once-private diary entries written by Dr. Anthony Fauci have set social media ablaze with critics mocking the former White House COVID advisor’s fixation on emerging from the global pandemic as a celebrity and condemning his behavior.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., made the diaries public as part of the committee's ongoing oversight investigation. The journals chronicle Fauci's day-to-day role during the COVID-19 crisis through conversations with President Donald Trump, governors and world leaders, while detailing his media appearances and personal observations.

While much of the mainstream media initially ignored the shocking diary entries, there was no shortage of backlash on X. Outkick founder Clay Travis urged his followers to read the diary, calling Fauci "one of the true villains of American history."

ABC, NBC, CBS, CNN AND MS NOW IGNORE FAUCI DIARY ENTRIES THAT REVEAL FIXATION ON FAME DURING COVID

Grabien Media founder Tom Elliott, who spent hours digging into the diary, found that the word "award" was mentioned 80 times, "hero" appeared 49 times, "press" appeared a staggering 641 times and Fauci never wrote anything about "peer review," "meta-analysis," "risk-benefit," "learning loss" or "mental health."

Dana Loesch was stunned, calling the diary "one of the most infuriating things I’ve ever read."

Piers Morgan added, "These diaries are very damning. Fauci comes across as a fame-hungry narcissist who regularly said different things in private about Covid to what he told the world publicly."

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

Others put a spotlight on Fauci's apparent love for the TV camera.

XX-XY founder Jennifer Sey unearthed an old Politico appearance in which Fauci simply read flattering tweets about himself.

"Hard hitting stuff here," Sey snarked. "Could you kiss his butt anymore?"

FAUCI'S DIARY SHOWS HE FED QUESTIONS TO JOURNALISTS, BUILT FRIENDSHIPS WITH MEDIA FIGURES

The senator shared an AI-generated image of Fauci sitting on a bed while writing in a diary. In the background are posters and toys in a humorous attempt to suggest the doctor was like a self-obsessed teenager. World.title: Patriots receiver Mack Hollins’ barefoot escapades reach a new plateau in second New England season
World.content:
Mack Hollins has turned the proverbial corner as a New England Patriots wide receiver, but not in the ordinary way one might think, like his speed is improved or he reads defenders better now. This is more about his feet.

His habitually unapologetic bare feet.

Hollins reports that in his second year on the Patriots roster, his life habit of walking everywhere in his bare feet has gained acceptance locally. He knows this because restaurants are welcoming him in and allowing him to dine – sans shoes.

MACK HOLLINS ENTERS STADIUM WITH NO SHOES OR SHIRT

"I love it," Hollins told reporters at Patriots training camp during an interview session conducted barefoot. "It's really great because now they're kind of letting me slide being barefoot in restaurants and stuff because they know who I am.

"At first, it was like, some homeless guy coming in here, but now it's like the mechanic homeless guy so it's all right. So yeah, it's been great."

Let this marinate.

If you're pretty much disgusted by somebody else's bare feet on display anywhere but a beach, you're not going to be a fan. If you're thinking this is an attention-seeking move, well, maybe. Hollins has been known to stand out and not shy from attention.

ROB GRONKOWSKI OFFERS ADVICE FOR PATRIOTS TO SILENCE NOISE AROUND MIKE VRABEL CONTROVERSY AHEAD OF 2026 SEASON

But if you're a Patriots' fan and watched last season when Hollins unexpectedly started 13 regular-season games and two postseason games, and scored the team's only touchdown on a 35-yard reception in the Super Bowl LX, you might be more accepting of the guy's eccentricities.

And Hollins has a few.

He doesn't, for example, use forks or spoons or chopsticks or any other eating utensils. He uses his hands to eat because, he says, it helps him correctly gauge the temperature of the food which prepares his mouth for what's coming.

So, these New England restaurants are showing love to the barefoot guy who eats with his hands.

"Every team I've been on, you ask them who's the weirdest guy they're going to say Mack," Hollins once admitted.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

But this isn't aloof weird.

Or disruptive weird.

It's perhaps endearing weird.

"Yeah, yeah, it's not like a bad weird," Hollins said.

It's weird like Hollins showing up to NFL games in Buffalo's frigid temperatures shirtless. Also barefoot, of course, despite the ice and snow on the ground.

It's weird like him arriving to the 2025 AFC Championship game between the Bills and Kansas City Chiefs wearing an Animal Muppet character — you know, the red thing that plays drums — mask.

All that aside, shoeless Mack Hollins is gaining traction in New England. And he has an explanation why he prefers to do without footgear when he's not actually in a game.

"I think shoes are a tool and people have made them a part of their body," Hollins once said. "I wouldn't walk around with a hammer just because I might need a hammer sometimes."

World.title: What a fourth-generation fishing captain has learned from nearly 100 years on the Gulf
World.content:
For Dylan Hubbard, fishing is the easy part.

The harder part is carrying nearly 100 years of family history on his shoulders while figuring out how to keep the operation alive through hurricanes, federal regulators and a rapidly changing Florida tourism industry.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK

Hubbard is the fourth generation of his family to run Hubbard's Marina in Madeira Beach, Fla. The business traces its roots to 1928, when his grandfather started with five rowboats and 40 cane poles.

Today, Hubbard is vice president of the company and has begun the process of purchasing it from his father. But stepping into the family business was never as simple as inheriting a title.

"Oh, you have no idea," Hubbard told OutKick Outdoors when asked whether he had to earn his place before calling himself captain.

His grandfather, Wilson, originally ran the operation before leaving to serve during World War II. Hubbard's great-grandfather stepped in during that time, which is why the family considers it a fourth-generation business. His father later purchased the company from the family in 2004. Now, Dylan is preparing to carry it forward.

"It's also really cool to have that layer of: it's a family business. I'm fourth generation," Hubbard said. "Not only am I working, but also it's that legacy. So it's just an added layer of maybe responsibility or honor or blessing — whatever you want to call it — that really makes it even that much more special."

Watch Dylan Hubbard's full interview with OutKick Outdoors here:

That responsibility means knowing when to hold onto tradition and when to embrace change.

Hubbard's Marina began in Pass-a-Grille, back when Florida's barrier islands looked very different. But as new bridges changed traffic patterns and Pass-a-Grille became increasingly residential, Hubbard's grandfather recognized that the business needed a new home. Even though he was nearing 70 years old, he uprooted the operation and moved it north to John's Pass.

"He saw the writing on the wall," Hubbard said.

It was the kind of decision that probably felt risky at the time but proved essential in the decades that followed. John's Pass eventually developed into a major tourism destination, and Hubbard's grandfather also worked with the city to establish the boardwalk that now runs through the area.

That willingness to adapt has remained necessary — especially when nature delivered its worst, twice in less than two weeks.

In September 2024, Hurricane Helene brought nine feet of water into Hubbard's Marina. The main office was completely submerged, the main dock was destroyed, and the business lost infrastructure, inventory and equipment. Before the water had even fully receded, Hurricane Milton was bearing down as a Category 5, forcing the family to brace for a second direct hit while still standing in the wreckage of the first.

"It was pretty numbing," Hubbard said, "just a wild situation to go through."

Still, the boats survived. More importantly, so did the people.

Before official rescue crews could even reach the barrier islands, Hubbard and several crew members set out before daylight to assess the damage at John's Pass. What began as a trip to inspect the business quickly became something else entirely.

"We were the first boat out there," Hubbard said. "No one was out there — no fire, no EMS, no emergency folks. It was just us."

As they navigated through the damaged area, residents stood along seawalls crying, waving and begging for help. Some had stayed behind during the storm, become trapped, and then emerged to find they had lost everything.

"So what was supposed to be a search and find out what we needed to do and what got damaged turned into a rescue mission," Hubbard said.

Other members of the fishing community soon joined in, deploying their own boats to move people and supplies to and from the barrier islands — even as police tried, unsuccessfully, to keep boaters off the water given the debris and damage.

"We were essentially pirates for a week," he said.

For Hubbard, reopening quickly was never primarily about preserving the business's reputation or getting tourists back on boats. It was about his employees. At the time, the company had 84 staff members. Fifteen had lost everything in the storm.

"If I had just sat there and waited and not got to work, those people would not only have lost their homes and their vehicles and everything they owned, they would have also lost their jobs and not had income," Hubbard said. "So to me, it was imperative to open up as quickly as humanly possible."

The team rebuilt the dock in two days and had trips running again five days after Helene — faster than the barrier islands themselves officially reopened. The community later raised nearly $75,000 to help affected staff members.

In the year that followed, Hubbard's kept growing rather than pulling back: the company acquired a pirate ship, a dolphin tour boat and a shark tour operation in November 2025, adding to a portfolio that already includes a seafood market, a fuel dock and a boat-building operation. A new ghost tour just launched, and a Tampa Bay ferry service is next.

Capt. Hubbard may prefer being offshore, but much of his job now happens behind a desk, in meetings, or fighting battles that never make it onto a dock report.

Hubbard is heavily involved in fisheries management, serving as president of the Florida Guides Association and sitting on Gulf Council advisory panels covering reef fish, data collection and outreach.

A few years ago, that involvement got personal. After Hubbard publicly criticized weak enforcement against illegal charter operations at a federal meeting, NOAA's Office of Law Enforcement took a closer look at his own business — and told him the way Hubbard's Marina operated was against federal regulation.

It took him roughly 85 days to get the regulation itself changed, preserving his business model in the process.

"If you're not in the room, you're on the menu," Hubbard said of why he keeps showing up to meetings most people would find, in his words, "mind-numbing and boring."

CHARTER CAPTAIN JONATHAN MOSS EXPLAINS HOW TO GET KIDS HOOKED ON FISHING FROM AN EARLY AGE

It's not the only wild thing nearly 100 years on the Gulf has produced. Ask Hubbard for his strangest moment on the water and the answer comes without hesitation: "We've found dead bodies. We've come across boats on fire. We've saved people." His grandfather ran across great white sharks; his father, orcas; Hubbard himself has crossed paths with pilot whales, a right whale and one of the largest leatherback turtles he's ever seen.

"People always ask me, 'Do you still get to go fishing?'" Hubbard said. "I do, and I make time for it, and I definitely get out on the water as much as I can."

But he also understands that spending all his time fishing wouldn't necessarily serve the larger operation.

"If I spent my time offshore, that's definitely where I would rather be and enjoy a lot more," he said. "But I definitely wouldn't be in the position we are today if I did that all the time."

Hubbard hopes his grandfather would approve of where the family business stands today.

"I hope he would be happy," Hubbard said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The pirate ship, the ferry, the federal meetings — none of that existed when Wilson Hubbard started with five rowboats. But the motto he built the business on hasn't changed.

"If you're too busy to go fishing, you're just too darn busy."

Still true, four generations later.

World.title: ESPN’s favorite insider accidentally explained why most Americans don’t trust the media
World.content:
"Write what you know, not what you think."

Andrew Marchand offered that lesson to other reporters while discussing ESPN’s decision to part ways with NFL analyst Ryan Clark. The sports-media columnist for The Athletic, a New York Times-owned outlet, was responding to what he described as inaccurate opinions circulating online about Clark’s dismissal.

He thought he was explaining the difference between responsible journalism and uninformed speculation. Instead, Marchand accidentally explained why so many Americans distrust the press.

ESPN PARTING WAYS WITH NFL ANALYST RYAN CLARK AHEAD OF NETWORK'S FIRST SUPER BOWL BROADCAST

To be clear, his advice was perfectly sound. The problem came when Marchand revealed what he knew, how long he had known it and why he had not told his readers.

On his own podcast, Marchand claimed he had anticipated Clark’s departure since February. He went so far as to assert that he had "a story prepared in February" and received a "very strong indication" roughly one week before ESPN let Clark go.

So why didn’t he publish the report?

"Like others, you want to allow ESPN to tell him first," Marchand explained. He said he eventually reported that Clark was expected to be dismissed because the scoop became "competitive."

In other words, Marchand says he knew ESPN was preparing to part ways with Clark but he withheld the information while ESPN followed its preferred timetable. Then another outlet threatened to make the information public, and he published.

Marchand apparently believed that account enhanced his reputation as a responsible journalist.

It actually exposed the access-journalism game.

Before going further, it's important to make clear that the point is not Marchand personally, or who published one Ryan Clark story first.

Legendary sports radio host Dan Patrick recently brought up another situation that exposed why access-journalism serves the people involved, but often not the public at large.

After the San Francisco 49ers disclosed that head coach Kyle Shanahan had suffered serious injuries in a car accident 11 days earlier, ESPN’s Adam Schefter posted the news one minute later. ESPN quickly followed with a detailed report.

Patrick wondered whether ESPN and Schefter already knew what had happened but waited until the 49ers authorized its release.

"This isn’t journalism. Not really reporting," Patrick said. "They’re giving you the information" and then effectively saying, "Okay, now you can tell everybody."

Patrick didn't prove ESPN had been sitting on the story. But he identified the central problem with the modern insider economy: What is the public value of privately knowing something if the institution involved decides when the public may know it?

That's not journalism. It's public relations.

And while we don't know exactly what happened between Schefter, Kyle Shanahan, ESPN, the NFL and the San Francisco 49ers, we do know exactly how the Marchand-Clark situation played out and it illustrates Patrick's point.

As I detailed last week, my colleague Bobby Burack and I developed separate lines of reporting that ESPN was preparing to part ways with Clark. Four sources in total confirmed the information.

We contacted ESPN at 4 p.m. ET on Monday and gave the network until 5 to respond. ESPN asked us to delay publication until 5:45 while it was "trying to chase this down." We declined but offered to add anything the network provided.

Clark then disappeared from "NFL Live," ESPN unexpectedly told us at 4:49 that we could "stick to" our original timeline, and Marchand published a two-paragraph report 14 minutes later. OutKick’s more detailed story followed one minute after that.

That looks damning because it appears Marchand rushed out a short and incomplete story just to beat OutKick to the news.

Marchand has now explained his side, and his explanation makes the sequence harder to defend.

Recall that Marchand claimed he had "a story prepared in February." But his initial report didn't resemble a completed article that had been waiting since February. It consisted of two hurried paragraphs and included a typo.

Whatever "prepared" meant, his comments in a separate interview with Puck’s John Ourand established the more important point: Marchand had the information, intentionally waited on ESPN and published only after OutKick’s reporting forced the company to act.

"ESPN knew, I knew," Marchand told Ourand, explaining that the network had been trying to keep the Clark decision "close to the vest."

Then, Marchand said, "another entity called up" with the information and informed ESPN that it intended to publish. According to Marchand, ESPN became concerned and decided to tell Clark immediately rather than risk having him learn about the decision online.

CNN PANELIST BLAMES 'CULTURE WAR' RETRIBUTION AS REASON FOR RYAN CLARK'S ESPN DEPARTURE

Marchand didn't identify the other outlet, but he was describing precisely what OutKick had done. Our inquiry didn't merely make the story abstractly "competitive." By Marchand’s own account, it forced ESPN to accelerate its timetable.

Once ESPN had informed Clark, Marchand rushed out his two-paragraph report and made sure to note afterward that he had "reported it first," while the other outlet published "a little bit after."

Marchand didn't explain who alerted him that OutKick was preparing to publish or who told him Clark had been informed. Nor does his account prove ESPN asked us to wait specifically to help another reporter publish first.

And there is nothing inherently improper about giving a company a brief opportunity to notify an employee before he learns online that he has been let go. Reporters should consider the human consequences of publication.

But Marchand didn't describe granting ESPN a few minutes of courtesy. He said he possessed strong information for roughly a week and waited until competition threatened the arrangement.

Marchand went further in his interview with Ourand. He described himself as "being respectful" by waiting for ESPN and said he tries to wait "as long as you can" before publishing layoff news.

He then suggested that being a good reporter and being a good person "go hand-in-hand."

Marchand isn't simply admitting that he honored ESPN’s timetable. He is presenting that deference as evidence of his moral and journalistic superiority.

But OutKick didn't recklessly publish unconfirmed information or deny ESPN an opportunity to respond. We independently confirmed the story through four sources, contacted the company and gave it a firm deadline.

Marchand’s definition of responsible journalism appears to require something more: allowing the corporation at the center of the story to determine when the reporting may become public.

Responsible journalism means giving the subject of a story an opportunity to respond, as OutKick did when we offered ESPN one hour to comment.

But it does not mean giving the subject control over when the story becomes public. And it especially doesn't mean allowing the subject to dictate the framing of the news.

That's the difference between responsible journalism and access journalism. It seems that Marchand and many other insiders confuse the two quite frequently.

Access reporters receive strategically selected information from powerful sources, honor the source’s preferred timetable and publish when the institution decides the information can be released.

The reporter receives exclusives and status. The institution receives a predictable messenger.

Marchand demonstrated that predictability during the interview with Ourand.

Although he called ESPN’s execution "horrendous," he repeatedly insisted the company was "trying to do the right thing" and that its "hearts were in the right place."

ESPN put Clark on live television despite planning to part ways with him, removed him only after an outside outlet threatened to publish and created the humiliating spectacle Marchand was discussing.

Yet even while criticizing the result, a reporter who benefits from staying in ESPN’s good graces rushed to defend management’s intentions. The execution was bad, Marchand conceded, but ESPN’s motives, in his view, remained pure.

That instinct points to the second half of the access bargain. It's not only about allowing a source to control the timing of information. It's also about how aggressively a reporter is willing to scrutinize the people providing it.

A reporter who depends on one corporation for a steady stream of scoops has a powerful incentive not to challenge that corporation too aggressively. The next exclusive depends on the same executives and communications officials continuing to take his calls.

Marchand does criticize people associated with ESPN. But notice who draws his criticism and when they draw it.

His most sustained criticism has focused on Pat McAfee, an independently powerful personality whom ESPN does not fully control and who has repeatedly clashed with people inside the network. One Marchand report contained several petty and embarrassing details about McAfee that clearly came from ESPN insiders. Sports Illustrated described it as a "pretty brutal inside job."

That was technically reporting critical of an ESPN personality. It also demonstrated how an insider can serve one faction of a corporation against another.

Marchand criticized Ryan Clark after ESPN had decided to fire him. He wrote that "Around the Horn" had lost its way during the show’s final week, months after ESPN publicly announced its cancellation.

Even Marchand and Katie Strang’s substantial investigation into former ESPN executive Lee Fitting arrived after ESPN had let him go, when scrutinizing Fitting no longer threatened his standing inside the network. The report documented conduct that employees said went unchecked for years, but its target was already outside the building.

The discarded executive received scrutiny. The executives who still controlled access received credit.

That doesn't prove a formal quid pro quo. But it doesn't need to.

The institution supplies information. The reporter supplies predictability and favorable coverage.

The same arrangement becomes far more consequential when the subject is not a sports network but a government official helping shape national policy.

Newly released diary entries from Dr. Anthony Fauci showed just how cozy relationships between powerful officials and the journalists covering them can become.

Fauci wrote that he was building a friendship with CNN’s Jake Tapper and documented dinners at each other’s homes. He wrote that he "gave Jake some questions to ask" another health official during a CNN interview.

Dana Bash sent Fauci an encouraging message after a confrontation with a Republican lawmaker. George Stephanopoulos praised Fauci privately after an interview, while Andrea Mitchell called to apologize for failing to book him.

Reporters need sources, and friendly relationships can produce important information. None of those described interactions is a problem in a vacuum.

The problem arises when access, ideological sympathy and personal friendship erase the necessary distance between reporter and subject.

During a historic public-health crisis, the press was supposed to scrutinize one of the most powerful and influential officials in the country. Fauci’s diaries raise a different possibility: that some journalists covering him had begun to view him less as a subject requiring skepticism and more as an ally whose access and approval they valued.

INSIDE FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY: WHAT HE WROTE ABOUT TRUMP, TV PERSONALITIES AND CELEBRITIES

The Marchand-ESPN sequence shows the access bargain in sports media. The Fauci diaries show what happens when that same bargain reaches national policy.

That's the access bargain in its most dangerous form.

The information can be accurate and still function as PR. It can be selectively leaked, strategically timed and framed to benefit the institution or official providing it.

That's why many insider scoops provide limited public value. Firings, trades, contract extensions and television assignments generally become public anyway. The insider’s product is often not discovery, it's speed.

And in today's social media world, how much value does that even hold?

The Founding Fathers didn't enshrine freedom of the press in the First Amendment so reporters could distribute corporate announcements a few minutes early or launder government messaging from powerful officials.

They protected it because a free press was supposed to stand between the public and concentrated power.

That freedom carries a purpose: expose what powerful institutions want concealed, demand answers they would rather avoid and publish truths they would prefer remain buried.

When reporters instead allow corporations and government officials to control the timing, framing and scrutiny of the news, they are not fulfilling that founding role.

They are surrendering it.

My own career has often involved seeking access where I was not wanted. Nike stonewalled questions about a study on "transgender" youth athletes, the WNBA denied game credentials several times because they didn't want me asking questions and reporting on a Michigan high-school volleyball controversy led to harassment and required me to have a personal security detail at several games.

OUTKICK REPORTER HARASSED COVERING GIRLS VOLLEYBALL, TRANS PLAYER, AS PRINCIPAL DOES NOTHING

That resistance didn't make all of my conclusions correct, but it established that the subjects weren't controlling the reporting process. Quite the opposite, in fact.

Only 28% of Americans told Gallup last year that they trusted newspapers, television and radio to report the news fully, accurately and fairly, the lowest figure Gallup has recorded.

Media organizations often blame polarization, misinformation, social media and politicians for that collapse.

They should also examine the system they created.

Marchand thought he was establishing his superiority over reporters who lacked his access. He knew earlier, had better sources, supposedly had a story ready months before and then simply waited because that was the "responsible" thing to do.

Instead, his defense revealed the unspoken arrangement.

A powerful institution gives information to a favored reporter. The reporter protects the institution’s timeline and rarely makes himself a threat to the people providing access. When an outside outlet disrupts the arrangement, the insider rushes out the news, preserves his reputation and continues receiving information from the same sources.

Then he lectures everyone else to "write what you know, not what you think."

Marchand should add the unofficial second half of that rule: Write what you know... as long as the corporation that told you says it is okay.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

Dan Patrick identified the problem.

Andrew Marchand accidentally showed the entire process in action.

World.title: House committee passes Foreign Funding Transparency Act to expose foreign donations to nonprofits
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Lawmakers are seeking to expose foreign nationals who may be funneling money and donations through tax-exempt organizations to political committees as the House Ways and Means Committee passed a bill that would revise reporting requirements for tax-exempt groups.

The Foreign Funding Transparency Act, which passed 23-18 in the committee last Wednesday, would require tax-exempt organizations to collect and report to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) donations received from foreign nationals.

"For far too long, foreign influence and interference have plagued our tax-exempt sector," committee Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., said in a statement. "Foreign donations have no place in American politics, particularly when the sole goal is to manipulate our public discourse, promote propaganda and support violence."

Smith noted that many of the protests and demonstrations that take place across the U.S. appear to be grassroots but are actually well-organized and well-funded, often by groups within what he described as "shadowy networks."

"As the Ways and Means Committee conducted its investigation into the nation’s tax-exempt sector, it became clear that shadowy networks of well-funded organizations have been enjoying lucrative tax benefits for decades, while simultaneously accepting donations and direction from foreign nationals," Smith added. "From the outside, it looks like a movement, but once you see how the money flows, it becomes clear that this is a machine," he added.

The bill’s passage came just a week after Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for global cooperation at a summit in Washington to combat far-left political terrorism.

SHANGHAI SABOTAGE: INSIDE SINGHAM'S SECRET STRATEGY TO DEMONIZE AMERICA

"For far too long, however, our counterterrorism doctrine has had a blind spot – a blind spot when it comes to extremist violence from the political left," Rubio said. "Even today, the very idea that far-left terrorism could be a serious threat is treated as a right-wing fever dream, or worse, as a dangerous fascist conspiracy."

While Rubio didn’t mention any organizations or individuals by name, the House Ways and Means Committee noted Marxist Neville Roy Singham in a statement about the bill’s passage.

Singham, a 72-year-old American now based in Shanghai and who sold his tech company for $785 million in 2017, is known to fund pro-Chinese Communist Party groups operating in the U.S. He has funneled $278 million into the broad network of nonprofits since 2017, according to a Fox News Digital investigation.

The funneling of funds through nonprofit networks has been a key point of concern for lawmakers and the Trump administration. Major contributors, including Singham, often have dispersed funds through shell 501(c)(3) nonprofits, which subsequently contributed to various tax-exempt organizations.

RUBIO'S CALL TO COMBAT GLOBAL FUNDERS OF FAR-LEFT TERRORISM COULD PUT SINGHAM IN CROSSHAIRS

During his address to more than 60 countries earlier this month, Rubio noted that networks have been coordinating across multiple countries, providing training instructions and using encrypted communication to facilitate unrest. He said international cooperation was critical to disrupting the financing of dangerous organizations, some of which were working with hostile foreign states.

World.title: Kaylee Goncalves' mother says family ready for trial after Bryan Kohberger seeks to withdraw guilty plea
World.content:

Idaho student killer Bryan Kohberger is seeking to withdraw his guilty plea in a bid for a trial, but the family of victim Kaylee Goncalves says they're ready if he gets his wish.

"We knew we'd be hearing from him again, and September was coming up and that would be the end of his appeal, so we weren't really shocked," Kristi Goncalves, Kaylee's mother, said Monday.

Speaking with Fox News' Sean Hannity, Goncalves said her family has remained confident in the overwhelming evidence against Kohberger and would welcome the opportunity to present the case before a jury.

IDAHO MURDERS: NEW BOOK ON KOHBERGER REVEALS PREVIOUSLY UNSEEN EVIDENCE, CLAIMS SHEATH COULD BE INADMISSIBLE

"Honestly, either way this goes, whether the judge dismisses it right out the gate, fantastic, or if we wind up in court, we still feel like we wanted to go [to trial] in the first place," she said.

"We are very confident in the evidence in this case and, hopefully, if we do go to trial this time, he will be convicted and sentenced to death."

Kohberger, 31, pleaded guilty to murdering four University of Idaho students last year and was sentenced to four consecutive life sentences.

BRYAN KOHBERGER'S MOTHER CALLED HIM 'MY ANGEL' AND INSISTED POLICE MADE A 'REALLY, REALLY BAD MISTAKE': BOOK

Court records show that he filed a handwritten petition for post-conviction relief Monday. In the petition, Kohberger argued that he was "convinced to falsely confess," claiming his high-profile defense team of Anne Taylor, Elisa Massoth and Bicka Barlow didn't tell him about "exculpatory discovery" — evidence mentioned in the recent "Broken Plea" book but never vetted in court.

The news circulated after Kohberger called a New York Times reporter and claimed that he has an "absolute claim of innocence."

Reacting to the petition, former prosecutor and "Crime Stories" host Nancy Grace said Kohberger's effort to undo his plea deal should be met with exactly what he is asking for.

"Bring it on," Grace said on "Hannity."

"I agree with one thing Bryan Kohberger said in his self-styled petition. He says justice was not served. And amen, brother. It was not served because he needs the death penalty."

World.title: Washington says goodbye to Sen. Lindsey Graham
World.content:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump, congressional colleagues and world leaders Tuesday will say their final goodbyes to Sen. Lindsey Graham, the influential and colorful foreign policy hawk whose sudden death this month at age 71 stunned Washington and reverberated in capitals around the globe.

Two days of ceremonies and funeral services began Tuesday morning when Graham’s American flag-draped casket arrived at the Capitol for a special ceremony in the rotunda — his last visit to a building where he served for more than three decades.

In honor of the senator’s long military career, an armed forces body bearer team slowly carried his casket up the Capitol steps. Graham served as an Air Force judge advocate general, or JAG, officer and retired from the Air Force Reserve in 2015 with the rank of colonel.

The casket of late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham during a ceremony in the rotunda of the U.S. Capitol on July 28. Frank Thorp V / NBC News

Senate colleagues, past and present, Cabinet members and Graham’s family and staffers packed the Rotunda. Among those paying tribute were former Sens. Bob Corker and Lamar Alexander, both Tennessee Republicans; Rob Portman, R-Ohio; Richard Burr, R-N.C.; Jeff Flake, R-Ariz.; Pat Toomey, R-Pa.; and Kelly Ayotte, now New Hampshire’s GOP governor.

“It’s such a loss in terms of his voice on foreign policy and America’s role in the world,” Ayotte, who traveled regularly with Graham on Senate trips around the world, told NBC News, adding: “He loved life, he had so much fun, and no one could make you laugh more than Lindsey Graham.”

Vice President JD Vance, who also served with Graham in the Senate, remembered the late senator’s “swashbuckling, infectious laugh” and called him a “true American original.”

Graham, Vance said, had a common touch, likely from his humble upbringing in western South Carolina, and could connect with all people, whether it was political leaders or the waitstaff in the Capitol.

“Lindsey Graham loved people from all walks of life. … He was fascinated in the waitstaff in the Senate dining room. He was fascinated in the people who made the food. He was fascinated in the lowest staffer who had been hired three days earlier,” Vance said at the Capitol ceremony. “He was fascinated by, of course, the very leadership of our country, and I think he was fascinated in people because he loved people.”

Others on hand were former South Carolina Rep. Trey Gowdy, a Fox News host; acting Attorney General Todd Blanche; Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former senator; and White House budget director Russell Vought.

“It’s difficult to believe that we’re here today to say a final farewell to Lindsey as he leaves the Capitol for the last time. My heart is heavy,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said at the ceremony.

“Lindsey was a towering figure here in the Senate and on the international stage. ... Lindsey will be remembered as a senator and as a statesman,” Thune said. “But for me, most of all, I will remember him as my friend. It’s hard to think that there will be no more Senate dinners with Lindsey.”

Graham’s sister and only sibling, Darline Graham, who was appointed to replace him in the Senate, walked tearfully up to the casket alone, then placed her hand on the casket. Backed by Trump, she is running for a full term in an Aug. 11 primary.

She was joined by her family. Then a parade of Trump officials, senators and Senate staffers paid tribute. Former Sen. Burr kissed the casket “to say goodbye.”

“He was one of our close friends,” Burr said.

From the Capitol, Graham’s casket departed for the Washington National Cathedral for an invitation-only funeral service at 2 p.m. ET. That will be livestreamed.

Trump is expected to speak at the funeral. Cabinet officials and congressional and military leaders are expected to be on hand, as are global leaders who viewed Graham as a key American ally on defense and foreign policy matters, including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Graham didn’t come close to winning the presidency when he ran against Trump in 2016, but Tuesday’s send-off in the nation’s capital was fit for a president, with Trump, Vance and world leaders personally honoring Graham.

Graham did not lie in state or honor in the Capitol rotunda, but few other lawmakers have received such a ceremony.

It was a testament to Graham’s political influence and longevity. In addition to his 33-year military career, Graham had previously served as Senate Judiciary Committee chairman and was Budget Committee chairman when he died. He was also one of the most quoted members of Congress; he was a regular on Fox News and had logged 63 appearances on NBC’s “Meet the Press.”

“He’s been one of a kind, irreplaceable. dedicated his life to this country. I mean, in the end, gave his life to this country. I mean, all the arduous travel took a toll on him,” said Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who succeeded Graham as Budget chairman upon his death.

“Nobody had a quicker wit ... and he used that wit to really convince people to do things,” Johnson said.

Ayotte recounted the day during the 2015 presidential campaign when Trump read aloud his then-rival Graham’s personal phone number at a televised campaign event. Shortly after, Graham went with Ayotte’s young family to watch “Minions.”

“So my son, who was probably 5 or 6 years old, Lindsey had him on the phone answering the calls, and so Jake would pick up the phone and say, ‘Oh, hey, who is this? Why are you calling?’” Ayotte said. “So we had a lot of laughs over that.”

Remembrances will continue at the South Carolina State House on Wednesday morning. Graham’s casket will be carried by a South Carolina State Guard horse-drawn military wagon, known as a caisson, followed by an F-16 flyover to mark his more than three decades in the Air Force and Air Force Reserve.

A funeral service, open to the public, will be held at First Baptist Church of Columbia. A private family burial will take place in Pickens County, where Graham was born and raised.

World.title: Netanyahu joins Trump for high-stakes meeting at the White House
World.content:
This month, the U.S. carried out strikes for nearly two straight weeks, while Iran struck ships and American targets in the region. The sit-down will be their first face-to-face meeting since Axios reported last month that Trump had called Netanyahu “f---ing crazy” during a heated phone call. Trump confirmed the report was accurate in an interview with the New York Post. “I was a little bit perturbed at his constantly fighting with Lebanon,” Trump said.

Asked about the confrontation, Netanyahu said he and Trump sometimes have “tactical disagreements.” “We always find a way to work them out, and we do so as great friends,” he said.

Trump has declined to say whether he supports Netanyahu for re-election. Earlier this month, he dodged a question, saying that Netanyahu has been “a great wartime president.”

“He’s been a great wartime prime minister,” Trump said this month. “I don’t know anything about his politics, I’m not sure. I would think he should be popular, because he did a very good job.”

The meeting also comes amid scrutiny from lawmakers over the administration’s handling of the war since the U.S. and Israel launched it in late February. Four U.S. soldiers were killed in recent days, bringing the total number of American troops killed during the war to 18.

NBC News has also previously reported that U.S. weapons stockpiles are diminishing and that U.S. military commanders are allowing some Iranian missiles and drones to pass U.S. defenses to preserve the weapons supply. At the same time, the Defense Department is requesting that Congress approve an additional $67 billion in supplemental funding to expand weapons production and speed up delivery.

Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, argued in an interview on “Meet the Press” that the U.S. “has everything that it needs to conduct this campaign as effectively as it needs to be.”

Asked whether Trump had decided against escalating attacks on Iran, Waltz said that the president was giving talks between the two nations “some space” but that all options remained on the table.

In an interview Sunday on Fox News’ “Sunday Morning Futures,” Netanyahu said that the U.S. and Israeli intelligence services “are working so close together that it’s not that I’m going to present new information, but I think it’s a good thing to have the opportunity to sit with our good friend President Trump and to hear what he has in mind, because I think in many ways it’s his decision.”

“But let me say one thing, and I think that I should say it very, very clearly: If Iran attacks Israel, either directly or through proxies, either with ballistic missiles or UAVs or killer drones, it will make a terrible mistake, because our response, Israel’s response, will be very, very forceful,” Netanyahu said.
