World.title: “Who is that guy?”: Lula's response to Milei's remarks in São Paulo
World.content:
“Who is that guy?”: Lula's response to Milei's remarks in São Paulo

28th Tuesday, July 2026 - 10:55 UTC Full article

The remarks led to the sharpest diplomatic response between the two countries in years

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva addressed for the first time the remarks made against him by Argentine President Javier Milei, with a brief and ironic response that avoided escalating the controversy. Asked by reporters while preparing to receive South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, he replied: “Who is that guy?”

The reaction contrasts with that of the rest of the Brazilian government, which took a firmer stance. Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira described the Argentine president's remarks as “serious and unacceptable” and said they “constituted interference in internal affairs, in national affairs.” Speaking to TV Globo, he nonetheless defended the diplomatic route: “We must work to achieve understanding between nations, and diplomacy is based on that, on dialogue,” he said.

Finance Minister Dario Durigan questioned the Argentine leader's economic argument and compared the two countries' situations. In a radio interview, he said Milei had spoken about Brazil's situation despite Argentina posting a higher country risk, a larger public debt, and higher inflation. “One cannot fall for the narrative of those who claim the situation will become apocalyptic,” he said.

The episode began on Saturday, when Milei took part in São Paulo in the event formalizing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro's presidential candidacy for the October 4 elections. In a speech of about 25 minutes, the Argentine president avoided naming Lula and referred to him with terms such as “thief” and “convict,” while also using crude language about the region's left-wing governments. He argued that Brazil could face an adverse economic scenario if it does not change its political course.

The remarks led to the sharpest diplomatic response between the two countries in years. On Sunday, the Brazilian government recalled its ambassador in Buenos Aires, Julio Bitelli, whose return has no set date, and summoned Argentina's ambassador in Brasília, Daniel Raimondi, for explanations at Itamaraty. The president of the Supreme Federal Court, Luiz Edson Fachin, also issued an institutional note after Milei disparaged one of the court's justices.

In Argentina, a group of lawmakers filed a motion of censure over the remarks in the Chamber of Deputies. Argentina's foreign ministry had not issued an official response to the Brazilian statements as of this writing. Brazil and Argentina are Mercosur's two largest members and each other's main trading partners.

World.title: Fujimori's inauguration brings Southern Cone and Andean presidents together in Lima
World.content:
Fujimori's inauguration brings Southern Cone and Andean presidents together in Lima

28th Tuesday, July 2026 - 10:30 UTC Full article

Fujimori will become the first woman to reach Peru's presidency through the ballot box

The presidents of Bolivia, Paraguay, Chile, and Honduras arrived in Lima on Monday to attend the handover ceremony at which Keiko Fujimori will assume Peru's presidency for the 2026-2031 term. The leaders of Argentina, Javier Milei; Uruguay, Yamandú Orsi; Panama, José Raúl Mulino; and Ecuador, Daniel Noboa, are also expected to take part.

Interim President José María Balcázar hosted an official dinner for the delegations on Monday night at the Government Palace in the capital's historic center, and on Tuesday will hand the presidential sash to Fujimori on the anniversary of Peru's independence.

Several delegations arrived with defined bilateral agendas. Bolivia's Rodrigo Paz, on his first visit to the neighboring country, will hold a meeting with Fujimori with the stated aim of “restoring diplomatic dialogue between the two countries,” according to Foreign Minister Fernando Aramayo. La Paz's priorities include setting up a binational cabinet in the short term and advancing the use of the Peruvian port of Ilo, which for landlocked Bolivia holds “commercial, tourism and energy” significance.

Chile's José Antonio Kast had already held a video call with the president-elect on July 10, in which they discussed migration and coordination against transnational organized crime. The two also agreed on the need to revitalize the Pacific Alliance, a bloc in which both countries are full members and which they see as a key mechanism for commercial projection toward Asia-Pacific markets.

Paraguay's Santiago Peña, who arrived with his wife, has bilateral and business meetings scheduled, while Honduras's Nasry Asfura will meet with business leaders and officials to promote cooperation opportunities, according to their respective governments.

Fujimori will become the first woman to reach Peru's presidency through the ballot box, after winning by a narrow margin of 49,641 votes over left-wing candidate Roberto Sánchez in the June 7 runoff. She takes office on her fourth attempt, following three consecutive runoff defeats.

The incoming president assumes office facing two main challenges: citizen security, the population's foremost concern, and political stability in a country where no president has completed a five-year term over the past decade. Her electoral rival turned to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights alleging irregularities, a request the National Elections Board dismissed before proclaiming the results.

World.title: Trump asks the Supreme Court to allow his mail-voting restrictions before the midterms
World.content:
Trump asks the Supreme Court to allow his mail-voting restrictions before the midterms

27th Monday, July 2026 - 22:26 UTC Full article

Trump has repeatedly maintained that mail-in voting facilitates electoral fraud

The US government on Monday filed an emergency request with the Supreme Court seeking authorization to implement President Donald Trump's executive order restricting mail-in voting, which lower courts have blocked. The request comes 99 days before November's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.

The filing followed by two days a decision by the First Circuit Court of Appeals, based in Boston, which refused by a two-to-one vote to stay the injunction issued on June 25 by a district judge. That ruling keeps the order blocked in twenty-three Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia, which sued the administration.

The order, signed in March, tasks the director of Citizenship and Immigration Services and the commissioner of the Social Security Administration with drawing up a list of eligible voters, and bars the Postal Service from sending ballots to anyone not on it. The plaintiff states argue that the Constitution reserves the conduct of elections to the states and Congress, not the executive branch, an argument accepted in the earlier rulings.

In its filing before the high court, the administration framed the order as “general policy guidance” and stressed that the Postal Service has not finalized any regulations. The appeals judges had noted, by contrast, that the measure sets rapidly approaching deadlines requiring states to reorganize their procedures immediately, while also ensuring that officials and the public understand the rules governing the September and November votes. A White House spokesperson said the lower courts' decision “is not the final say” and that the administration expects a favorable outcome.

Trump has repeatedly maintained that mail-in voting facilitates electoral fraud. Election officials, courts, and federal agencies concluded that there was no evidence of widespread fraud in the 2020 elections, when that method saw unprecedented use during the pandemic, and noted that the system includes multiple verification and audit mechanisms.

The initiative is part of a broader set of government actions on electoral matters. The administration is pressing Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register on the federal roll and remains stalled in the Senate, and has sued twenty-nine states to obtain copies of their voter registries, which include dates of birth, driver's license numbers, and portions of social security numbers. Courts have blocked access in three states and have yet to rule in the rest.

World.title: Milei announces Starlink deal to bring satellite internet to 6,000 rural schools
World.content:
Milei announces Starlink deal to bring satellite internet to 6,000 rural schools

27th Monday, July 2026 - 22:20 UTC Full article

At the time of the announcement, neither the text of the agreement nor any public statement from the company about its terms had been released

Argentine President Javier Milei announced an agreement between the National Communications Agency (Enacom) and Starlink to provide satellite connectivity to 6,000 rural schools that currently have poor internet access or no connection at all. The announcement was made on Sunday during the main event of the 138th International Livestock, Agriculture and Industry Exhibition in Buenos Aires.

According to the president, Elon Musk's company will donate 6,000 complete satellite kits along with 24 months of its highest-capacity service, which includes priority access of up to five terabytes per month per site. “Yes, it's a huge amount. Thank you, Elon,” he said during the speech.

Once that period ends, the equipment will remain at the schools and the regulator will take on the cost of the service for an additional year, covering the subscription, installation, technical support, and monitoring. Enacom sources said those resources will come from the Universal Service Fund, made up of contributions from the telecommunications sector and earmarked for extending access to areas not covered by commercial provision.

At the time of the announcement, neither the text of the agreement nor any public statement from the company about its terms had been released. The president also said the initiative adds to the three million users who, he said, already use the company's services in the country.

Starlink accelerated its expansion in Argentina following the easing of the regulatory framework for satellite services introduced by the current government, and now operates across the entire territory. The Argentine market accounts for about 25% of the company's Latin American operation and ranks among the countries with the highest service penetration, with weekly user growth of around 2%. Most customers are households, a concentration that has led to episodes of saturation in certain areas, such as greater Buenos Aires, Córdoba, and the Vaca Muerta region.

The agreement fits into the relationship Milei has maintained with Musk since the start of his term. The two met in February 2025 in the United States and have kept in frequent contact since. In parallel, Tesla is advancing its commercial entry into the local market, after formally incorporating in the country and appointing its first manager for Argentina and Uruguay.

In the same speech, the president projected an expansion of agricultural output and said the country is in a position to double its grain harvest, though he announced no decisions on export duties, one of the sector's main demands.

World.title: Uruguay prepares protocols for the risk of El Niño flooding in the spring
World.content:
Uruguay prepares protocols for the risk of El Niño flooding in the spring

27th Monday, July 2026 - 22:00 UTC Full article

“The challenge we face now is preparing for what may happen in the spring as a result of this climate phenomenon,” the president said

Uruguay's government is drawing up a set of contingency protocols for the flooding risk associated with the El Niño phenomenon, which climate projections indicate will have its greatest impact on the region during the southern hemisphere spring. President Yamandú Orsi announced at the Congress of Departmental Governors that the measures will be presented in August, ahead of what may occur from September and October.

“The challenge we face now is preparing for what may happen in the spring as a result of this climate phenomenon,” the president said. He indicated that the protocols drawn up by the departmental emergency coordination centers will be put on the table and that a coordination space will be created with the National Emergency System. “We have a record, going back to 1998, of how floods play out and we know where they will hit hardest and where less. It will not affect every area in the same way,” he added.

The available projections are probabilistic. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center puts the probability of El Niño conditions during the June-July-August quarter at close to 100%, persisting at least through the end of the year. Uruguay's Meteorological Institute does not forecast specific flooding, but projects a higher probability of above-normal rainfall in the country's northeast, with that signal expanding toward the north and part of the center during the spring. Brazilian consultancy MetSul estimates a probability above 80% that accumulated rainfall will substantially exceed historical averages in southern Brazil, northeastern Argentina, and across Uruguay, placing the period of greatest risk between September and December.

A central concern is the effect of rainfall in southern Brazil on the flow of the Uruguay River, which runs along the country's western edge. Rio Grande do Sul has already recorded flooding episodes this month. National Party senator Sebastián Da Silva said management of the binational Salto Grande dam will be decisive and warned about the situation of the Río Negro dams, while identifying the Merín Lagoon basin, the Estero de Pelotas, and the Treinta y Tres lowlands as sensitive areas. He called for machinery and shelter space for potential evacuees to be arranged in advance.

Meteorologist José Serra said the movement of moisture from the equator toward southeastern Brazil and Uruguay has already begun to affect dams in the country's north, and put forward, as his own hypothesis, that a convergence between El Niño and a cooling of North Atlantic waters could amplify the phenomenon's effects.

The region is already going through a season of extreme events. Last week, Chile declared a state of catastrophe in the north of the country over a storm that left at least ten dead.

World.title: De la Espriella to close Colombian embassies in 14 countries and cut ties with Cuba and Nicaragua
World.content:
De la Espriella to close Colombian embassies in 14 countries and cut ties with Cuba and Nicaragua

27th Monday, July 2026 - 20:14 UTC Full article

The announcement draws a distinction between two situations. With Havana and Managua, the president-elect said there would be “no link whatsoever”

Colombia's president-elect, Abelardo de la Espriella, announced that his government will close the country's embassies in fourteen nations and will not maintain relations with Cuba and Nicaragua, which he described as “tyrannies.” The measure, released on Sunday night in a video on his social media accounts, will take effect from his inauguration on August 7.

The announcement draws a distinction between two situations. With Havana and Managua, the president-elect said there would be “no link whatsoever.” For the remaining twelve cases he cited budgetary reasons and made clear that the decisions “do not mean breaking diplomatic relations”: those countries will instead be covered through concurrent representation from other embassies in the region. “We cannot maintain such a costly structure, which produces no concrete results for the country,” he said.

The move reverses much of the diplomatic expansion pursued by the outgoing government of Gustavo Petro, which had opened missions in Africa, the Middle East, and Eastern Europe to diversify foreign policy. Colombia will close the missions inaugurated under that administration in Senegal, Ethiopia, Haiti, Barbados, the Czech Republic, and Romania, along with pre-existing ones in Algeria, Azerbaijan, Cuba, Ghana, Hungary, Malaysia, Nicaragua, and South Africa. On the African continent only the delegations in Kenya, Egypt, and Morocco will remain.

The shift regarding Cuba and Nicaragua carries significant history. The island acted as a guarantor of the negotiations between Juan Manuel Santos's government and the FARC that culminated in the 2016 peace agreement. With Nicaragua, Colombia maintains a decades-long dispute over the San Andrés and Providencia archipelago and fishing rights in surrounding waters, largely settled before the International Court of Justice.

The plan also includes merging the dual representations in Paris and Rome, where a single ambassador will take on duties before both the host country and the international bodies based there, the closure of fifteen consulates, and the cancellation of the planned mission in Ramallah, announced by Petro in 2023 but never established. Conversely, the incoming government will reopen the embassy in Israel, with which the outgoing administration severed relations.

The decision drew opposing reactions. Former trade minister Luis Carlos Reyes, a columnist for the Spanish newspaper EL PAÍS, argued the savings will be marginal, since total spending on foreign affairs accounts for 0.35% of the national budget. Governing-party senator Johana Osorio warned about the impact on ties with the global south. Former foreign minister Julio Londoño, by contrast, defended the measure, saying that “the proliferation of embassies and consulates has lent itself to paying political favors,” while acknowledging it is not decisive in budgetary terms.

The announcement adds to other foreign policy decisions by the incoming administration, which confirmed its intention to join the regional security alliance promoted by the United States.

World.title: IMF chief says Argentina is in "a strong position" despite missing its fiscal target
World.content:
IMF chief says Argentina is in “a strong position” despite missing its fiscal target

27th Monday, July 2026 - 19:59 UTC Full article

It is Georgieva's first visit to the country since taking over the institution in 2019 and the first by a top IMF official to Buenos Aires in eight years

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva on Monday endorsed the economic program of Javier Milei's government during a visit to Buenos Aires and ruled out that the country will need additional financing from the institution next year, when presidential elections are due. “Argentina today is in a strong position,” she said at a press conference alongside Economy Minister Luis Caputo.

It is Georgieva's first visit to the country since taking over the institution in 2019 and the first by a top IMF official to Buenos Aires in eight years. Her agenda included meetings with Caputo, central bank president Santiago Bausili, and a meeting with Milei at the presidential palace.

Among the indicators she said reflect an improvement, Georgieva cited the shift from a fiscal deficit to a primary surplus, inflation falling from 210% annually to around 30%, and the accumulation of some $13 billion in reserves since the start of the year. “I am not worried about Argentina having the money to pay its debt. Keep buying,” she said, referring to the central bank's currency purchases. Asked about the possibility of additional funds to navigate the election year, she replied: “There will be no need for extra financing.”

The endorsement comes, however, at a difficult moment on the fiscal front, the program's central pillar. Falling tax revenue during the first half of the year led in June to the first primary deficit of the current administration and to a breach of the fiscal target agreed with the institution for that period. While reserve accumulation targets have ceased to be a source of tension, the Fund's concerns have shifted toward the public accounts.

Georgieva placed at the center of the discussion the need for growth, currently concentrated in oil, gas, mining, and agriculture, to be “shared more widely.” Sectors tied to domestic consumption, such as construction, industry, and commerce, are in a weaker position. A recent central bank report shows household loan arrears tripled in a year, to 12.8%, their highest level in two decades. She spoke of the need to improve credit conditions for small businesses and families, manage those arrears, and accelerate infrastructure investment.

Argentina is the IMF's largest debtor: it accounts for about 35% of the institution's outstanding loan portfolio, with some $58 billion pending, far ahead of Ukraine, second with $15.4 billion. The current relationship dates back to the agreement signed in 2018 under Mauricio Macri's government, refinanced in 2022, to which a new $20 billion understanding was added in April 2025, the 23rd program between the country and the Fund. According to the financial program presented this month, Argentina faces maturities of nearly $45 billion between this year and next.

Small left-wing parties called a protest against the visit. On Tuesday, the delegation is scheduled to travel to Neuquén to tour the Loma Campana field in the Vaca Muerta formation, before continuing on to Uruguay.

World.title: Mercosur's two largest partners in their worst diplomatic crisis as Brazil recalls its envoy
World.content:
Mercosur's two largest partners in their worst diplomatic crisis as Brazil recalls its envoy

27th Monday, July 2026 - 09:14 UTC Full article

Milei defended his government's alignment with the United States and Israel and again criticized Brazil's judiciary for barring him from visiting Jair Bolsonaro

Brazil on Sunday recalled its ambassador in Buenos Aires, Julio Bitelli, for consultations and summoned Argentina's ambassador in Brasília, Daniel Raimondi, to provide explanations at the Foreign Ministry, in the sharpest diplomatic response between the two countries in years. The measures, taken by Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, follow the speech Argentine President Javier Milei delivered on Saturday in São Paulo at the convention that formalized Flávio Bolsonaro's presidential candidacy.

A spokesperson for the Brazilian foreign ministry said the ambassador was recalled “over President Milei's insults” at that event, where he referred to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva using terms such as “thief” and “convict” and disparaged a Supreme Federal Court justice. Bitelli was expected to arrive in Brasília between Sunday night and early Monday. A recall for consultations is a formal signal of displeasure through which a government temporarily brings its representative home.

Hours after the measure became known, Milei broadened his accusations in a radio interview from the Palermo Rural Exhibition. There he accused the Brazilian government of having financed part of what he called an “anti-Argentine campaign”: “Do you know who put the most money into this anti-Argentine campaign? The government of Brazil. Twenty-five percent of the resources came from the government of Brazil,” he said. He extended the accusation to Mexico and to the US Democratic Party. He offered no evidence and did not specify which campaign he meant, and the claim is not supported by any known public documentation.

In the same interview, Milei defended his government's alignment with the United States and Israel and again criticized Brazil's judiciary for barring him from visiting Jair Bolsonaro, sentenced to more than 27 years for the attempted coup and currently under house arrest. The Supreme Federal Court had prohibited visits for political or electoral purposes until the end of the electoral process.

The episode also drew reactions within Argentina. Buenos Aires province governor Axel Kicillof said the country “respects sister nations and is committed to regional integration.” Argentina's foreign ministry had not issued an official response as of this writing.

The crisis involves Mercosur's two largest members, which are also each other's main trading partners. Milei's visit, his third to Brazil since taking office, included no contact with the federal government. There is a precedent from July 2024, when Bitelli was also summoned to Brasília after an exchange between the two presidents, though of lesser intensity.

World.title: Is Mexico a safe place for the gay community? A recalibration of a first impression
World.content:
I still remember sitting on my couch years ago watching a CONCACAF Gold Cup soccer game when I was in high school. It was a Mexico game. I was not a soccer fan at that time, and the game was mostly just background noise for whatever social media app I was more engaged with on my phone.

I heard the Mexican fans begin to wind up a chant, and I started to pay more attention. I watched as the fans built into a unifying crescendo while waving jazz hands in the air. Their harmony became louder and louder until it stopped, and they all shouted puto (male prostitute) so loud that it echoed throughout the stadium. The ref stopped play and warned the Mexican fans to stop the chant or risk a forfeit.

That was my introduction to the “puto” chant, a homophobic slur that has marred Mexico’s fan culture in controversy as it has become a staple at El Tri games around the world.

To me, chants from fans of national teams are representations of a nation’s culture, both on and off the pitch. So this became my first impression of how queer rights were treated in Mexico. To an outsider, it looked like a country coming together to insult an opposing team using a homophobic slur, and that the force behind it had only become greater as the world has increasingly told them to stop.

I had never been to Mexico until I arrived in San Miguel de Allende in late June to start a nine-week journalism internship with Mexico News Daily. Now I found myself with a chance to find out what the queer experience was actually like in Mexico — a country famous for its entrenched Catholic beliefs that is incongruent and often intolerant of gay rights.

My first impactful experience came just 10 days after I arrived when I embarked on a four-hour bus ride to Mexico City to experience the Mexico vs. Ecuador round of 32 game. I was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of fans in the Zócalo, Mexico City’s main square, in what immediately became one of the most memorable experiences of my life.

Despite the eruptions after both of Mexico’s goals, the deafening national anthem and witnessing nearly 1.5 million people take to the streets in celebration, the “puto” chant still stuck out. Nearly all of the hundreds of thousands of attendees in the Zócalo — ranging from more stereotypically conservative young men to middle-aged women and even children — partook in the tradition. It made me, a gay 21-year-old who has only lived in progressive areas of the United States, a bit uncomfortable.

As a lifelong sports fan, I am no stranger to hooliganism, racism and homophobia at sporting events. It is almost expected among certain people and at some games, but when a chant like this is belted by women and children and by those young and old, it makes you feel like maybe the entire nation subscribes to outward intolerance.

I returned to San Miguel and was continuously reassured by my colleagues that the word had changed in interpretation throughout the years, and more vulgar speech was popular in casual conversation in Mexico. I understood, but the word clearly still had a negative connotation, as it is used directly at opposing teams and players. So even if the meaning is no longer a direct slur towards gay people, it still had a negative connotation that evolved from that word.

However, the next three weeks did not produce any evidence of homophobia, despite me keeping a keen eye out for it. At a watch party for the Mexico vs. England round of 16 game, a large crowd that gathered in front of the Parroquia de San Miguel Arcangel church barely uttered the chant. My daily life in San Miguel went on without ever feeling unsafe or witnessing any blatant acts of homophobia.

This past weekend I found myself with some free time, so I decided to go read a book in Parque Zeferrino, a newer park a little over a mile north of San Miguel Centro. I was enjoying the weather and watching fish dart around the pond, but I started to notice something every time I looked up. Seemingly every minute, more and more people were showing up at the park adorned in pride flags.

I went over to ask what was going on and found out that I had coincidentally stumbled upon the starting point of the San Miguel de Allende Pride Parade.

Nearly one thousand people — both locals and foreigners — marched from the park down to the Parroquia. It was a celebration filled with dancing, singing and chanting. People waved flags and folding fans. They brought skeptical onlookers watching from the sidewalks to join in. It was a beautiful and colorful scene, especially in one of the most conservative regions in Mexico known for its strong ties to the church.

From everything I had experienced at the Zócalo, it felt like onlookers could have treated the parade with disdain. But that word was never yelled. No one in the parade felt unsafe. No one seemed like they had to be hyper-aware of their surroundings. They were just expressing their pride.

Same sex marriage was legalized in all of Mexico’s 32 states in 2022. Mexico City first legalized it in 2009. The San Miguel Pride Parade has only existed for a few years, but it has since grown into a signature summer event.

I may have found it by accident, but the parade — and all the locals watching and supporting from the sidewalks — showed me that Mexico, despite its insistence on belting a homophobic chant and its entrenched catholic beliefs, can still be prideful and a space that feels welcoming to people from all over the world.

This does not forgive the chant at the Zócalo or the meaning behind it. But the United States — which has championed itself as a safe haven for gay rights — continues to move backwards as half the country vies to eliminate gay marriage. Mexico may be comfortable spewing a homophobic chant at its sporting events, but as of today, it just might be a safer place for queer people than its northern neighbor.

World.title: Sheinbaum hits back at Miller’s ‘Mexico’s systems don’t work’ claim: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📍 Miller, Ruffo and fracking: President Sheinbaum used her Tuesday press conference to respond to provocative remarks from White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller about Mexico, while also addressing the Ernesto Ruffo case and giving an update on the fracking feasibility assessment.

President Sheinbaum used her Tuesday press conference to respond to provocative remarks from White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller about Mexico, while also addressing the Ernesto Ruffo case and giving an update on the fracking feasibility assessment. 🎙️ Sheinbaum won’t debate Miller: Asked about Miller’s claim that Mexico’s justice, political and legal systems “don’t work” because parts of the country are “controlled and occupied by terrorist organizations,” Sheinbaum insisted there is “good coordination” between Mexico and the U.S. and asserted that “the people govern” in Mexico.

Asked about Miller’s claim that Mexico’s justice, political and legal systems “don’t work” because parts of the country are “controlled and occupied by terrorist organizations,” Sheinbaum insisted there is “good coordination” between Mexico and the U.S. and asserted that “the people govern” in Mexico. 🗳️ Midterms cited as motive: Asked why the U.S. official made the remarks, Sheinbaum pointed to November’s U.S. midterm elections.

Asked why the U.S. official made the remarks, Sheinbaum pointed to November’s U.S. midterm elections. ⚖️ Ruffo case is “criminal, not political”: Responding to a statement from 25 former Spanish and Latin American leaders — including ex-presidents Vicente Fox and Felipe Calderón — who called ex-Baja California Governor Ernesto Ruffo’s prosecution “political persecution,” Sheinbaum said the signatories should read the Attorney General’s evidence, calling it purely “a matter that has to do with a crime.”

Responding to a statement from 25 former Spanish and Latin American leaders — including ex-presidents Vicente Fox and Felipe Calderón — who called ex-Baja California Governor Ernesto Ruffo’s prosecution “political persecution,” Sheinbaum said the signatories should read the Attorney General’s evidence, calling it purely “a matter that has to do with a crime.” 🔥 Fracking assessment nearing completion: Sheinbaum said the expert committee studying “sustainable fracking” has reached internal agreements and is finishing its final assessment of energy needs through 2035–2040, with results expected within one to two weeks.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Today’s mañanera was important as President Claudia Sheinbaum responded to provocative remarks made by a senior Trump administration official. Given that the Mexico-U.S. relationship is currently strained, particularly in the areas of security and trade, any friction between the neighboring countries draws heightened scrutiny.

Also of note at the Tuesday morning press conference was Sheinbaum’s response to the view expressed by 25 former Spanish and Latin American political leaders regarding the criminal charges faced by a former governor of the northern state of Baja California.

In addition, today’s mañanera was significant as Sheinbaum provided an update on an expert group’s assessment of the feasibility of “sustainable fracking” in Mexico, a practice that, if approved, could allow Mexico to reduce its heavy reliance on natural gas imports from the United States. The results of the group’s assessment were initially expected in June, but now look likely to come in August.

Sheinbaum responds to Stephen Miller’s remarks about Mexico

A reporter asked the president about the Mexico-related remarks made on Thursday by Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff for policy and a homeland security adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump.

Stephen Miller: There is a reason why, in Mexico, the justice system doesn’t work, the political system doesn’t work, and the legal system doesn’t work. It’s because you have territory controlled and occupied by terrorist organizations who kill or kidnap anybody who gets in the… pic.twitter.com/zCyp7aRnsV — Clash Report (@clashreport) July 27, 2026

Miller said that Mexican criminal organizations “not only export massive death in the form of narcotics to our country, but they also export sophisticated criminal enterprises whose objective is to destabilize our democracy and to end the rule of law in our country.”

“There’s a reason why in Mexico, the justice system doesn’t work, the political system doesn’t work [and] the legal system doesn’t work. It’s because you have territory controlled and occupied by terrorist organizations who kill, extort, kidnap or murder anybody who gets in the way,” he said, referring to Mexican cartels that have been designated as foreign terrorists organizations by the U.S. government.

Sheinbaum’s first response to Miller’s remarks was a declaration that “we’re not going to get into a debate.”

She subsequently said there is “good coordination” between Mexico and the United States, and declared that “they” — i.e., Trump administration officials — know that “the people govern” in Mexico.

“Nobody else governs, the people rule,” Sheinbaum said.

“We’re a government of the people. … We work every day for security and peace in our country and there are results,” she said.

“I’m not going to get into a debate with him,” Sheinbaum added, referring to Miller.

Asked what she attributed the U.S. official’s remarks to, the president noted that midterm elections will be held in the United States in November.

“We’ve always said that Mexico should not be a defining element in their campaign,” Sheinbaum said, apparently referring to the U.S. Republican Party.

“… The United States has to look at itself, particularly with regard to the issue of drug use and the distribution [of narcotics] and money laundering in the United States,” she said.

Sheinbaum: Ruffo case is a ‘criminal issue,’ not a political one

A reporter noted that a group of former Spanish and Latin American political leaders issued a statement regarding the criminal charges faced by ex-Baja California Governor Ernesto Ruffo, who is accused of organized crime, fuel theft and tax evasion.

In the statement, the ex-leaders who belong to the “Democratic Initiative for Spain and the Americas” (Grupo IDEA) — among whom are former Mexican presidents Vicente Fox and Felipe Calderón — claim that the situation of Ruffo, National Action Party (PAN) governor of Baja California between 1989 and 1995, displays “unmistakable features of a political persecution orchestrated by those in power.”

Sheinbaum said “it would be very good” if the signatories of the statement “informed themselves” about the ex-governor’s situation by reading the information released by the Federal Attorney General’s Office.

“I repeat, it has nothing to do with a political issue. It’s a criminal issue,” she said.

Ruffo is “a person who allegedly, according to all the evidence, committed serious crimes,” Sheinbaum said.

“… Those who signed [the statement] saying that it’s a political matter are mistaken,” she said.

“It’s a matter that has to do with a crime,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum provides an update on the fracking feasibility assessment

Sheinbaum told reporters that a group of experts tasked with assessing the feasibility of “sustainable fracking” in Mexico has been expanded.

“The committee was expanded with two additional points of view,” she said.

“One from people who have historically had opinions against the exploitation of unconventional gas,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that another “group of people from different academic institutions” was added to the fracking assessment committee in order to develop an “energy planning scheme considering other sources of energy.”

“This second part is what has slightly delayed the committee’s ability to come to the mañanera to provide a result [of the fracking assessment],” Sheinbaum said.

She said that the committee has made a lot of progress, adding that its members have “even reached “agreements” among themselves.

“What’s missing is the final assessment regarding the growth of energy use and energy sources to 2035, 2040,” Sheinbaum said, explaining that the assessment considers how natural gas can be replaced by “other energy sources.”

She said that assessment is likely to be completed next week.

Sheinbaum said that next week or the week after next, the government will be in a position to announce the committee’s “guidance” regarding the feasibility of sustainable fracking in Mexico.

The president said she believed that the committee’s conclusions will be “satisfactory for everyone.”

The experts, she added, “will also propose that other studies are needed.”

Sheinbaum said those studies would be carried out this year.

The president has acknowledged her previous opposition to fracking, but now asserts that it can take place safely via the use of new technologies.

A decision to allow fracking in Mexico — a practice that was largely paused by former president Andrés Manuel López Obrador — would increase domestic production of natural gas, a fuel that Mexico currently imports from the United States in large quantities.

World.title: In canceling La Parota dam, Sheinbaum details a different water plan for rural Acapulco
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum announced Sunday the cancellation of the La Parota hydroelectric dam to instead double down on an alternative plan featuring radial wells, rehabilitated pumping systems and elevated tanks to supply water to the Acapulco area.

“Yesterday I informed the entire rural area of ​​Acapulco that we are no longer going to do [the dam project] because it would have greatly affected the communities,” Sheinbaum said.

The Federal Electricity Commission’s (FCE) proposed 900-megawatt La Parota dam was expected to flood between 14,000 and 17,000 hectares of land, impacting the municipalities of Acapulco, Juan R. Escudero, San Marcos, Chilpancingo and Tecoanapa. However, concerns over the land expropriation process and a lack of agreements with local communities drove Sheinbaum to cancel the project.

Sheinbaum’s water strategy for Acapulco includes three radial wells along the Papagayo River, the rehabilitation of aqueducts, the repair of the pumping system, the construction of elevated tanks and the replacement of leaking water lines.

The works were initially included in the January 2025 federal program “Acapulco Transforms with You,” established in response to the damage caused by Hurricanes Otis and John.

The radial wells are being built on tall towers — high enough to keep them safe from flood waters — and will draw from the Papagayo River through underground collection systems.

In addition, Sheinbaum said, the government will replace drinking water lines in the upper part of Acapulco, starting in the neighborhood of Renacimiento.

Cleanup work is now underway in the Papagayo River, and dredging is taking place to remove sediment and increase the capacity of the riverbeds.

The aim is to reduce obstructions and reduce the flood risk during heavy rainfall as part of Acapulco’s reconstruction and adaptation efforts following the two severe hurricanes.

Residents of towns bordering the river have voiced their concern that the water works will directly serve beachfront Acapulco, instead of increasing their supply.

With reports from El Imparcial, Expansión Política and Infobae

World.title: Formal and informal employment slumped during the first half of 2026
World.content:
Participation in the workforce declined by nearly 300,000 during the first half of 2026 as June employment figures were the second-worst of the year, according to the National Survey of Occupation and Employment (ENOE) carried out by the national statistics agency INEGI.

ENOE data indicates that 319,633 jobs were lost last month and said the decline was linked to a contraction in both formal and informal employment, although more pronounced in the latter.

The negative June figures — topped only by the loss of 705,427 jobs in January — resulted in a deficit of 293,227 jobs through the first half of the year. Economists say Mexico needs to create 1.2 million jobs annually just to keep pace with labor force growth.

The June report is particularly disappointing as there were high expectations for the economy since Mexico was co-hosting the FIFA World Cup.

“Employment figures show the labor market remained weak, despite … the World Cup, which failed to boost job creation, even temporarily,” the financial group Banco Base stated in an analysis. “The event’s effect was marginal and likely concentrated only in the host cities.”

ENOE said Mexico’s unemployment rate stands at 2.9%, its highest figure since September 2025. At the same time, the economically inactive population (EIP) increased by 285,856 people in June compared to May.

Banco Base interpreted the rise in the EIP as an indicator that “some of those who stopped working stopped looking for employment,” suggesting that “the unemployment rate alone does not reflect the magnitude of the deterioration in the labor market.”

The official employment rate for the population aged 15 and over registered at 58.8%, according to seasonally adjusted figures. This represents declines for both month-to-month (–0.2%) and year-on-year (–1.0%).

The economic think tank México ¿cómo vamos? Identified another significant structural challenge: low female participation. In June 2026, the labor force participation gap between men and women stood at approximately 28.3%.

With reports from El Economista and México ¿cómo vamos?

World.title: Sheinbaum denies Milei’s ‘anti-Argentina campaign’ claim: Monday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🇦🇷🇲🇽 Sheinbaum denies Milei’s ‘anti-Argentina campaign’ claim : Responding to weekend remarks by Argentine President Javier Milei accusing Mexico, Brazil and the U.S. Democratic Party of financing a campaign against his government, Sheinbaum was blunt: “There’s no [Mexican] campaign against any country in the world, nor against any government in the world.”

: Responding to weekend remarks by Argentine President Javier Milei accusing Mexico, Brazil and the U.S. Democratic Party of financing a campaign against his government, Sheinbaum was blunt: “There’s no [Mexican] campaign against any country in the world, nor against any government in the world.” 🎖️ Militarized schools ‘not authorized,’ says Education Ministry (SEP) : Amid fallout from the case of a student’s death at a so-called “militarized academy” in Tamaulipas, Education Minister Mario Delgado said such schools fall outside SEP and Defensa jurisdiction and that military-style education in schools is incompatible with Mexico’s constitutional education principles.

: Amid fallout from the case of a student’s death at a so-called “militarized academy” in Tamaulipas, Education Minister Mario Delgado said such schools fall outside SEP and Defensa jurisdiction and that military-style education in schools is incompatible with Mexico’s constitutional education principles. ⚠️ Zacatecas cartel threat video ‘isn’t real,’ Sheinbaum says : Asked about a video in which armed men claiming to be part of a Sinaloa Cartel faction threatened Zacatecas Governor David Monreal, the president said the Security Cabinet determined the same day it surfaced that the audio had been dubbed.

: Asked about a video in which armed men claiming to be part of a Sinaloa Cartel faction threatened Zacatecas Governor David Monreal, the president said the Security Cabinet determined the same day it surfaced that the audio had been dubbed. 🌎 Self-determination principle invoked again: Sheinbaum tied her response to Milei to Mexico’s long-standing approach to foreign policy, saying Mexico asks other nations for the same respect for internal affairs that it offers them.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum took the opportunity during her Monday morning press conference to share advances of her administration’s investigation into the impact of social media and artificial intelligence on Mexico’s young people.

Education Minister Mario Delgado brought in two experts — Lucía Magis Weinberg and Tania Jiménez García — to present findings on how excessive screen time and social media use affect young people’s cognitive and emotional development.

“We are compiling this information so that it is available to parents,” Sheinbaum said.

“And so that, together, we make a series of decisions to protect children and adolescents during this formative stage of their lives,” the president said, before connecting the issue to the development of the country at large.

Sheinbaum also shared results of a recent survey indicating that 71% of parents consider it necessary that the government regulate minors’ cell phone use in schools.

Other issues at today’s mañanera touched on headlines from Zacatecas to Argentina.

On the international front, reporters pressed Sheinbaum on Milei’s accusation that Mexico had helped fund a campaign against Argentina during the 2026 FIFA Men’s World Cup.

Milei’s accusation didn’t come out of nowhere. The president of Argentina has leaned on similar claims before: in May, a leaked call between him and pardoned former Honduran president Juan Orlando Hernández surfaced, in which Milei was said to have put up $350,000 for a media operation to spread information against leftist governments in Mexico, Colombia and Brazil — an episode that became known as “Hondurasgate.”

Sheinbaum was also asked on Monday about a video threatening Zacatecas Governor David Monreal, which she dismissed as fake.

That video surfaced in the wake of a real and still-unsolved multihomicide. Ten people — among them businesspeople and former officials — were found killed in several Zacatecas municipalities earlier this month, with five bodies located along the Zacatecas-Saltillo highway. State and federal authorities are still investigating who was responsible, with one line of inquiry examining whether some of the victims had ties to extortion by organized crime.

Sheinbaum rejects Milei’s ‘anti-Argentina campaign’ accusation

A reporter asked Sheinbaum to respond to remarks made Sunday by Argentine President Javier Milei, who told the Buenos Aires-based Radio Mitre that Mexico, Brazil and the U.S. Democratic Party had bankrolled a “campaña antiargentina” — an anti-Argentina campaign — aimed at undermining his government ahead of elections.

Milei’s comments came hours after Brazil recalled its ambassador from Buenos Aires over separate remarks in which he called Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a “presidiario” (convict) and a “ladrón” (thief). Milei alleged Brazil had funded 25% of the supposed campaign and labeled Mexican and U.S. Democratic officials “progressive heads” seeking to derail his economic agenda.

Javier Milei acusó a México y Brasil de financiar una presunta “campaña antiargentina” para desacreditar a su administración Esto previo a las elecciones presidenciales en Argentina 📹 Radio Mitre pic.twitter.com/2l5jYD1zti — Manuel Lopez San Martin (@MLopezSanMartin) July 26, 2026

“There’s no [Mexican] campaign against any country in the world, nor against any government in the world,” Sheinbaum said, adding that if anything, “here there is a campaign” against Mexico’s own government, from multiple fronts.

She stressed that Mexico “doesn’t tend to get involved with other countries” and tied her response to Mexico’s constitutional principle of self-determination, a doctrine she has repeatedly invoked this year in response to frictions in foreign relations.

Education Ministry: Military-style schooling ‘not authorized’

Monday’s mañanera also addressed fallout from the case of Dafne Quintos, a student whose recent death has been linked to a “militarized academy” in Tamaulipas. Quintos, 13, reportedly died on July 17 at Academia Militarizada “Doenitz” where she was taking a summer course. According to her mother, Alejandra Quintos, the crime is being investigated as a femicide with drowning as the cause of death.

Education Minister Mario Delgado reiterated a position his ministry first stated Friday: schools branded as “militarized” fall under neither the Education Ministry (SEP) nor the Defense Ministry (Defensa), and delivering military-style instruction in educational institutions is “incompatible with the constitutional aims, principles and objectives” governing Mexican education.

Delgado said Tamaulipas authorities have since identified five additional schools operating under the same model. He said he remains in contact with the Tamaulipas state government and has tried to reach Quintos’s mother directly.

Sheinbaum debunks video threatening Zacatecas governor

A roughly two-minute video circulating on social media shows nine masked, armed men posing behind a tenth who reads out a message on camera claiming responsibility for the killing of 10 men in Zacatecas earlier this month on behalf of a Sinaloa Cartel faction.

The spokesperson asserts — without evidence — that the murders were carried out at the state government’s request. The same message then turns to a direct threat against Zacatecas Governor David Monreal, warning him to “honor and respect the agreements his cabinet has with our organization” or face consequences that would extend to his family.

Asked about the clip, Sheinbaum said the recording is not authentic. She said the federal Security Cabinet informed her the same day the video surfaced that it contained technical inconsistencies, chiefly that the voice track doesn’t match the person shown speaking.

“It’s not a real video — the voice doesn’t even match what the person is saying,” she said, adding that the case is still being investigated.

She said federal authorities are working to determine who produced the video, who distributed it and what the purpose of publishing it was, and that any evidence linking public officials to organized crime would be investigated under the law regardless of the outcome.

Monreal has not commented directly on the video but said separately that Zacatecas maintains permanent security operations involving the army, the National Guard and state police. Last week, state authorities announced the arrest of five people in connection with the homicides.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Ensenada’s Isaac del Toro makes history at Tour de France
World.content:
Isaac del Toro has delivered Mexico’s best result ever in the Tour de France, taking third place overall and crossing the finish line Sunday in the white jersey — indicative of the race’s best young rider.

Competing in his first Tour de France, the 22-year-old from Ensenada, Baja California, stood on the podium in Paris alongside Slovenian Tadej Pogačar, who rode to a record‑equaling fifth Tour title, and Belgian Remco Evenepoel.

Isaac del Toro, winner of the white jersey at the Tour de France 👏👏😭🇲🇽🤍#TDF2026ᴿᴾ 💛 pic.twitter.com/w6DZFk3tvi — Fan Club Isaac del Toro 🐂🇲🇽 (@ToritoFanClub) July 26, 2026

Del Toro finished the three-week race 9 minutes, 42 seconds behind Pogačar, but comfortably ahead of his closest rival for the youth classification after a grueling final week in the Alps.

Evenepoel was 6:26 behind in second place following the last of 21 stages.

Early in the race, on a 168.5-kilometer stage held entirely in Spain, del Toro made history as only the second Mexican rider ever to win a stage of the Tour de France — and the first since Monterrey native Raúl Alcalá in 1989 and 1990.

On Sunday, ESPN compared Del Toro’s breakout in road cycling to Mexican pitcher Fernando Valenzuela, who won two top National League awards — the Cy Young Award, as the league’s best pitcher, and Rookie of the Year — in 1981, his first full season in the major leagues.

Del Toro battled illness in the final days but leaned on team support and Pogačar’s help on key climbs, including the summit finish to Alpe d’Huez. The two ride for the eight‑man UAE Team Emirates‑XRG squad.

“It’s not easy to finish on the podium being sick, so I’m really delighted and very grateful to the team for having done this for me,” he told Eurosport.

His performances — including the Barcelona stage win in which Pogačar eased up to let his young teammate take the victory — have turned him into a national figure. According to ESPN, murals have gone up in his honor, hills have been renamed in his native Ensenada, and cycling shops in Mexico are reporting rising demand for bikes and gear.

President Claudia Sheinbaum hailed Del Toro’s achievement on social media.

“Many congratulations to young Isaac del Toro,” she wrote Sunday on X. “Mexico is very proud of your effort, dedication and this great moment that inspires an entire country. Congratulations, Isaac! May your success continue.”

Del Toro’s Tour de France finish cemented his No. 3 status in the current Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI) world rankings, behind only Pogačar and Jonas Vingegaard of Denmark.

💛 The Final Top 10 of the #TDF2026. Only two riders have managed to hold onto a place in the Top 10 between 2025 and 2026: 🇸🇮 Tadej Pogacar and 🇫🇷 Jordan Jegat! 💛 Le Top 10 Final du #TDF2026. Seuls deux coureurs ont su garder une place dans le Top 10 depuis 2025 : 🇸🇮 Tadej… pic.twitter.com/eisjQXutup — Tour de France™ (@LeTour) July 27, 2026

His breakout 2025 season produced 16 victories across stage races and one‑day events, including several stage-race titles and second place overall at the prestigious Giro d’Italia.

Vingegaard, a two-time Tour de France champion, crashed out of this year’s race, suffering a broken collarbone during Stage 15 when he was in second place.

His departure opened the door for Pogačar, 27, whose fifth title tied him with Belgian Eddy Merckx, Spaniard Miguel Indurain and Frenchmen Jacques Anquetil and Bernard Hinault for the most Tour de France titles. American Lance Armstrong was stripped of his seven titles following doping investigations by cycling authorities.

With reports from ESPN, El Universal, Cycling News and the Associated Press

World.title: Hurricane Genevieve gathers strength offshore, casting stormclouds over most of Mexico
World.content:
Hurricane Genevieve briefly reached Category 5 in the early hours of Monday, becoming the first cyclone of this magnitude recorded in the eastern Pacific since Hurricane Kristy in 2024, the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC) reported.

As of 9 a.m. CST on Monday, the NHC said Genevieve was located approximately 855 kilometers south-southwest of the southern tip of Baja California Sur, with maximum sustained winds of 250 kilometers per hour and wind gusts up to 305 kilometers per hour.

The system was moving northwest at 20 kilometers per hour on a track that kept it offshore and parallel to the Mexican coast, and is expected to maintain a west-northwest to northwest track over the next two days, gradually slowing its speed.

Despite the hurricane’s strength, forecasters have ruled out any direct impact on Mexican territory, with no coastal watches or warnings in effect.

However, the generated swells are already affecting Mexico’s southwest coast and are expected to reach southern Baja California, with the risk of potentially dangerous rip currents.

Rainfall forecast for most states

According to the National Meteorological Service (SMN), cloud bands from Genevieve in the Pacific Ocean will increase the likelihood of heavy to very heavy rains in western Mexico, coinciding with the Mexican monsoon in the northwest and Tropical Wave Number 21 in the south, which will intensify the storms.

The SMN said very heavy rains are expected on Monday in at least 17 states, with particular intensity in Sonora, Oaxaca and Chiapas.

Here’s the rain forecast for Monday afternoon:

Very heavy rain with isolated intense downpours (75 to 150 millimeters): parts of Veracruz, Oaxaca, Chiapas and Tabasco.

Heavy rain with isolated and very heavy downpours (50 to 75 millimeters): parts of Sonora, Chihuahua, Durango, Sinaloa, Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, Guerrero and Puebla.

Showers with isolated heavy downpours (25 to 50 millimeters): parts of Hidalgo, México state, Mexico City, Tlaxcala, Morelos, Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo.

Periods of showers (5 to 25 millimeters): parts of Baja California, Baja California Sur, Tamaulipas, Zacatecas, San Luis Potosí, Guanajuato and Querétaro.

Isolated rain (0.1 to 5 millimeters): parts of Coahuila, Nuevo León and Aguascalientes.

With reports from Radio Fórmula and the Associated Press

World.title: MND Local: Experiencing a taste of Oaxaca at its annual mezcal festivals
World.content:
July sees hundreds of thousands of visitors arriving in Oaxaca to celebrate (and photograph) the traditions of Guelaguetza. Many are on the hunt for the best mezcal, and there are many events to provide just that, ranging from tasting seminars to street parties.

The principal event in Oaxaca City is the Feria del Mezcal, hosted at the Centro Cultural y de Convenciones de Oaxaca (CCO) in Santa Lucía del Camino. This is a multi-day extravaganza concluding July 28. Although many treat the event like the world’s largest open bar, it is much more than that. It is an agro-industrial, cultural exhibition where you can find rare mezcals and meet the producers who make them.

Oaxaca’s mezcal sipping and sampling festivals

Glynn Pegler runs two bars in Oaxaca City and says he has seen a “noticeable increase in the professionalism of the Feria this year. There is a full program of entertainment and seminars, and stricter controls on the quality of the products and their authenticity. From the quality of the displays and decorations in each of the mezcal stands this year, it is clear that everyone in the Feria has upped their game.”

Santiago Matatlán is a Oaxacan town known as “the World Capital of Mezcal.” The town recently hosted its own “Grand Mezcal Festival,” held from July 23-26, 2026. The dates coincided with the state celebration of Guelaguetza, as well as the town’s saint’s day (July 25) honoring Santiago Apóstol.

This year, the fair took place just a few blocks from the town square. Stalls showcased local mezcal brands, as well as traditional crafts and food. Over the course of the event, experts including Mabi Cuish, Carmen Vásquez and Cynthia Villalobos gave lectures. Music and dancing were featured in the form of a calenda, a cabalgata (horseback procession) and a jaripeo (rodeo).

An education in mezcal

The celebration integrates the mezcal tradition with other elements of Oaxaca’s cultural identity, strengthening the tourist offerings of Santiago Matatlán and its connection with Guelaguetza activities.

On Saturday, organizers presented awards, cheered on by the festival crowd. These included diplomas for students who completed a course in mezcal production through the “University of Mezcal.” The main event was the Largest Agave Heart Contest, sponsored by ProMez. The contest recognizes the quality and effort of the producers, highlighting two fundamental aspects of the agave: its sugar content, measured in degrees Brix, and the weight of the hearts.

Although the Grand Mezcal Festival in Matatlán has finished, you can still visit the community and the mezcal producers who work there. You can do this by reaching out to mezcalerías such as Quiote or by contacting local guides.

Anna Bruce is an award-winning British photojournalist based in Oaxaca, Mexico. Just some of the media outlets she has worked with include Vice, The Financial Times, Time Out, Huffington Post, The Times of London, the BBC and Sony TV. Find out more about her work at her website or visit her on social media on Instagram or on Facebook.

World.title: TIM Brazil Earnings Hit Record on Fiber, Mobile Growth
World.content:
Brazil · Business

TIM Brazil earnings reached a historic high in the second quarter of 2026, as one of the country’s largest wireless carriers reported a normalized net profit of R$1.036 billion (~US$203 million), a 6.2% increase from a year earlier and its strongest-ever result for a second quarter.

Key Facts —Record Net Profit. TIM Brasil’s normalized net profit reached R$1.036 billion (~US$203 million) in Q2 2026, up 6.2% year over year – its best-ever second quarter. —Net Revenue. Net revenue rose 5.5% to R$6.965 billion (~US$1.366 billion), led by mobile service revenue and fast-growing fiber broadband. —EBITDA & Margin. Normalized EBITDA climbed about 7% to roughly R$3.5 billion (~US$686 million), lifting the margin to 51.5%. —Shareholder Payout. The board approved R$400 million (~US$78 million) in interest on equity (JCP) for the quarter; 2026 remuneration guidance is R$5.3-5.5 billion (~US$1.04-1.08 billion). —Reported. The Profit Engine: Mobile and Fiber

TIM Brasil, the Brazilian arm of Italy’s Telecom Italia, saw net revenue climb 5.5% year over year to R$6.965 billion (~US$1.366 billion). Normalized EBITDA rose about 7% to roughly R$3.5 billion (~US$686 million), pushing the operating margin to 51.5% – among the highest in Brazilian telecom.

Management credited two engines. Mobile service revenue kept growing on the back of a higher-value postpaid customer base and disciplined cost control. At the same time, fixed broadband surged as customers adopted TIM’s ‘Ultrafibra’ fiber-to-the-home service, a segment the company is scaling to cut churn by bundling mobile and home internet.

The result extends a run of margin expansion for TIM, which has focused on premium postpaid users rather than chasing low-value prepaid volume. In a mature mobile market, converting revenue growth into record profit signals effective cost management.

Why the Record Matters

A record second-quarter profit lands as Brazil’s carriers compete on 5G coverage and fiber reach. TIM operates as one of the country’s ‘Big Three’ alongside Vivo (Telefonica) and Claro (America Movil), and its results broadly matched analyst expectations for the quarter.

The broadband push is central to the story. Fixed-line and fiber revenue has become TIM’s fastest-growing line, diversifying a business long dominated by mobile and giving it a second pillar as smartphone penetration matures.

Shareholder Returns

TIM’s board approved R$400 million (~US$78 million) in interest on equity (JCP) for the quarter – a tax-efficient form of dividend common in Brazil. For 2026, the company has guided to total shareholder remuneration of R$5.3 billion to R$5.5 billion (~US$1.04-1.08 billion).

For investors holding TIMS3, those recurring distributions are a core part of the stock’s total-return case, funded by TIM’s strong cash generation even as it keeps investing in fiber and 5G.

What It Means for Foreign Investors

TIM Brasil is majority-owned by Telecom Italia and listed on Brazil’s B3 exchange as TIMS3. For international investors, the record quarter underscores the appeal of Brazil’s large, data-hungry consumer market and TIM‘s shift toward a convergent mobile-plus-fiber model.

The usual caveat applies: returns for dollar-based investors depend on the Brazilian real. At about 5.1 reais to the US dollar, the quarter’s R$1.036 billion profit converts to roughly US$203 million, but sharp currency swings can amplify or erase gains when translated back into dollars.

World.title: LitioMX Lithium Plan Sets 2026-2030 Path for Mexico’s Battery Push
World.content:
Mexico · Business

Key Facts —LitioMX Lithium Plan LitioMX’s 2026-2030 program, published in Mexico’s official gazette, proposes a pre-industrial pilot battery plant. —Battery pilot plant LitioMX plans to install a small-scale industrial plant to produce battery packs and support pilot energy-storage projects. —Core objectives The program lists six objectives, including exploration, developing active battery materials, and strengthening the regulatory framework. —2026 budget LitioMX will remain without investment spending in the 2026 budget proposal, receiving only operating funds, according to Bloomberg Línea. —Sonora focus The lithium strategy is centered on the state of Sonora, though specific deposit development plans were not detailed in the published sources.

LitioMX lithium ambitions are taking clearer shape after Mexico’s state-owned company published its 2026-2030 institutional program on 24 July 2026, outlining plans for exploration, battery material development, and a small-scale battery pack plant.

Lithium production in South America; Mexico is building its own lithium industry (illustrative). Photo: Wikimedia Commons.

A State Monopoly on Lithium

For foreign investors, Mexico’s lithium landscape changed decisively in 2022 when the government nationalized the mineral, declaring it a strategic resource reserved exclusively for the state.

The decree created Litio para México, known as LitioMX, a decentralized public agency with the sole mandate to explore, extract, and commercialize lithium.

No private concessions for lithium mining are permitted. The legal framework bars foreign and domestic private companies from owning lithium reserves or production.

This model mirrors approaches in other resource-nationalist economies, but it leaves international investors watching from the sidelines unless mixed-investment or service-contract frameworks eventually emerge.

Inside the 2026-2030 Program

The newly published institutional program sets six objectives for LitioMX through the end of the decade.

First, the company aims to consolidate exploration, evaluation, and technical management of Mexico’s lithium resources.

Second, it will promote technology to produce active materials for batteries. Third, it plans to establish a small-scale industrial plant to manufacture battery packs.

Additional goals include developing energy-storage projects, advancing circular-economy and performance-improving technologies, and strengthening the regulatory framework for the lithium sector.

The document does not specify a total investment figure, a production capacity, or a concrete extraction flowsheet for any particular deposit.

The Sonora Deposits and Unrealized Potential

Mexico’s most promising lithium resources lie in the state of Sonora, primarily in clay deposits that are geologically complex and commercially untested at scale.

Unlike South America’s brine-based lithium or Australia’s hard-rock spodumene, Sonora’s clay deposits require processing technology that is still being developed globally.

The institutional program confirms a broader Sonora-focused strategy, but the published sources do not verify a finalized extraction plan for a specific deposit such as Bacadehuachi.

Analysts at Speyside Group have noted that Mexico has yet to unlock its lithium opportunity, citing technological hurdles and the absence of a clear path to commercial production.

Budget Constraints and the Pilot Plant

Despite the ambitious program, LitioMX faces immediate financial limitations. Bloomberg Línea reported that the company will remain without investment spending in the 2026 budget proposal.

El Financiero separately noted that LitioMX would only have budget for payroll in 2026, underscoring the gap between strategic rhetoric and fiscal reality.

The small-scale battery pack plant represents a tangible first step, but without capital expenditure funding, the timeline for construction and operation remains uncertain.

No confirmed project partners have been announced for the battery plant or lithium processing plans in the available official documents.

What Foreign Investors Should Watch

The 2026-2030 program signals the government’s intent to move beyond resource nationalism into downstream battery manufacturing, but execution capability is unproven.

Investors should monitor whether Mexico’s broader mixed-investment infrastructure plan, valued at roughly US$325 billion for 2026-2030, eventually creates openings for private participation in lithium-related projects.

Legal firms such as Jones Day have highlighted recent reforms that unlock private investment in strategic infrastructure, though lithium extraction remains firmly under state control.

For now, the opportunity for foreign capital is limited to potential service contracts, technology licensing, or participation in downstream energy-storage projects that do not involve ownership of the resource itself.

The Sonora deposits remain a long-term proposition. Any progress on extraction technology or pilot processing results will be critical signals for the market.

The Road Ahead

LitioMX’s institutional program provides a policy roadmap, but the absence of a dedicated investment budget for 2026 raises questions about near-term milestones.

The battery pack pilot plant, if funded and built, would mark Mexico’s first state-run step into battery manufacturing, a sector dominated by Asian and Western players.

International observers will also track whether the regulatory framework evolves to permit joint ventures or technology partnerships without violating the constitutional ban on private lithium concessions.

For expats and investors following Latin America, Mexico’s lithium story is still in its early chapters, with Sonora’s clay deposits representing both a strategic asset and a technical challenge that has yet to be solved.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is LitioMX and what does it do?

LitioMX (Litio para México) is a decentralized public agency created by the Mexican government in 2022. It holds the exclusive mandate to explore, extract, and commercialize lithium, which was nationalized as a strategic resource.

Can foreign companies invest in Mexico’s lithium sector?

Foreign companies cannot hold lithium mining concessions in Mexico. The constitutional framework reserves lithium exclusively for the state. Potential opportunities may exist through service contracts, technology licensing, or downstream projects that do not involve resource ownership.

Where are Mexico’s main lithium deposits located?

Mexico’s most significant lithium resources are in the state of Sonora, primarily in clay deposits. These deposits are geologically complex and require processing technology that is not yet commercially proven at scale.

World.title: Bolivia Investment: Paz Secures US$300 Million
World.content:
Bolivia · Business

Key Facts —Bolivia Investment President Rodrigo Paz announced about US$300 million for a highway, Amazon power and police, funded by CAF and the IDB. —Highway project Funds target the Santa Bárbara-Caranavi highway in the Los Yungas area of La Paz department, a key transport link in a rugged agricultural region. —Amazon electricity A portion of the financing supports electrical integration in Bolivia’s Amazon region, building on a prior US$204 million IDB loan for the same purpose. —Police modernization The package includes resources to modernize the Bolivian Police, though specific equipment or training details have not been released. —Broader context The announcement marks the Paz government’s first major investment push backed by multilateral lenders since taking office, amid a severe foreign-exchange shortage.

President Rodrigo Paz announced a roughly US$300 million Bolivia La Paz investment package on July 26, 2026, targeting a key highway, Amazon-region electrical integration, and police modernization. The financing, the new government’s first major push backed by multilateral lenders, comes from the CAF (Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean) and the IDB (Inter-American Development Bank).

What the US$300 Million Package Funds

The roughly US$300 million package covers three distinct areas. The first is the Santa Bárbara-Caranavi highway, located in the Los Yungas region of La Paz department, a mountainous, agriculturally important zone northeast of the capital city.

A Separate La Paz City Package

During a civic anniversary session for La Paz’s 217th year, President Paz also outlined a local investment package of roughly Bs 1 billion. This city-focused spending targets road infrastructure, including the Escoma-Charazani highway, completion of the Unduavi-Chulumani route, and bridges at four river crossings.

Economic Context for Foreign Readers

The roughly US$300 million multilateral package is the Paz government’s first big investment push since taking office. Bolivia faces a severe foreign-exchange shortage, dwindling gas exports, and inflation pressures that prompted an IMF agreement earlier in 2026.

Political Significance of the Announcement

Paz chose the sesión de honor for La Paz’s 217th civic anniversary to unveil the roughly US$300 million package. The timing underscores the political importance of the department, a traditional stronghold of opposition to the former ruling Movement Toward Socialism party.

What Comes Next for Investors

Foreign investors should watch for the finalized terms of the CAF and IDB financing agreements. The exact disbursement schedules, procurement rules, and project timelines will determine near-term opportunities.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is the Bolivia La Paz investment package worth?

President Rodrigo Paz announced roughly US$300 million in financing from CAF and the IDB for a highway in La Paz department’s Los Yungas region, electrical integration in the Amazon, and police modernization.

What does the Santa Bárbara-Caranavi highway project involve?

The project funds rehabilitation of the Santa Bárbara-Caranavi road in the Los Yungas area of La Paz department. It is one of three components in the roughly US$300 million multilateral financing package.

Is the La Paz city package the same as the US$300 million announcement?

No. The roughly US$300 million package is funded by multilateral lenders for a highway, Amazon electricity, and police modernization. A separate La Paz city package, announced in bolivianos, totals about Bs 1 billion for local roads, health, water, and other municipal projects.

World.title: Dominican Republic Electricity Demand Hits 4,203 MW Record
World.content:
Caribbean · Business

Key Facts —Dominican Republic Electricity Demand National electricity demand hit a record 4,203 MW on July 27, 2026, per the Energy Ministry. —Previous record 4,195.26 MW set on Wednesday, July 24, 2026, just four days earlier. —July records The July 28 peak was the fourth all-time demand record set during the month. —System stability The SENI grid met the record load without blackouts, maintaining stable nationwide supply. —Primary drivers Intense summer heat and increased consumption from economic growth.

Dominican Republic electricity demand surged to an unprecedented 4,203 megawatts (MW) on Monday, July 28, 2026, setting a new all-time high for the Caribbean nation’s power grid as a relentless summer heat wave and accelerating economic activity pushed the system to its latest peak.

Electricity transmission lines (illustrative). Photo: Wikimedia Commons.
