World.title: Montenegro Approves Paid Leave for Menstrual Pain Sufferers
World.content:
Rights groups have expressed satisfaction after Montenegro’s parliament amended the Health Insurance Law for women diagnosed with secondary dysmenorrhea – painful menstrual cramps – to grant two days of “menstrual leave” per month.

The measure, adopted by MPs on Monday, applies to women suffering such symptoms as a result of serious underlying conditions such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids, endometrial polyps, ovarian inflammation and polycystic ovary syndrome.

The initiative was submitted in March ahead of International Women’s Day by independent MP Jevrosima Pejovic. The bill previously received support from the parliamentary Health, Labour and Social Welfare Committee and the Legislative Committee.

The Women’s Rights Centre, an NGO, welcomed the adoption of paid menstrual leave, describing it as an important step toward recognising women’s health needs in the workplace. It also praised the persistence of MP Pejovic, who advocated for the measure.

“This is a valuable example of how the presence of women in politics helps give political significance to women’s experiences, which have long been pushed into the private sphere and treated as ‘secondary’ issues,” the NGO said on Tuesday.

The Centre recalled that it had proposed including this right into law two years ago, but the relevant ministry rejected the initiative at the time. “What matters now is that it does not remain merely a right on paper but becomes a concrete opportunity that provides women with safer, healthier and more dignified working conditions,” it said.

According to the explanatory note accompanying the legislation, the amendments are intended to properly regulate diagnosed pathological conditions, eliminate prejudice against women in the workplace and help balance their health needs with professional obligations.

The law defines the condition as symptoms caused by previously diagnosed gynecological disorders and lists symptoms including pain in intercourse, painful urination, infertility and unusually heavy menstrual bleeding. Diagnosis must be confirmed by a medical specialist.

Women seeking the new benefit will be required to renew their medical certificate by December 31 each year and submit it to their employer by January 30 of the following year.

The amendments also regulate compensation during leave. Under Montenegro’s Health Insurance Law, compensation for temporary incapacity for work is generally set at no less than 70 per cent of the salary base, while employers may provide a higher amount through collective agreements.

The law provides 100 per cent compensation for certain categories of illness and medical conditions, including occupational diseases and injuries, pregnancy-related complications, malignant diseases, haemophilia, cystic fibrosis, epilepsy, muscular dystrophy, cerebral palsy, paraplegia and quadriplegia, systemic autoimmune diseases, chronic renal failure requiring dialysis, HIV, psychoses and some other serious conditions.

The amendments do not say how the law will be implemented, including how employers and state institutions will verify eligibility and prevent possible abuses of the new entitlement.

BIRN was unable to reach MP Pejovic for comment on implementation of the law and safeguards against potential misuse.

The amendments are expected to enter into force after their publication in Montenegro’s Official Gazette.

World.title: Mayor Acquitted of Obstructing Justice in Kosovo War Crimes Trial
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



The defendants celebrate the acquittal at Pristina Basic Court, July 28, 2026. Photo: BIRN.

Pristina Basic Court cleared local wartime commander Sami Lushtaku and seven others on Tuesday of obstruction of justice, witness intimidation and participation in a criminal group.

Sami Lushtaku, a commander in the Kosovo Liberation Army, KLA, for the region of Drenica, was accused of having from 2013 until 2015 forced two defendants to change their testimonies in the so-called Drenica case, in which Lushtaku and other KLA commanders from the Drenica region were accused of committing war crimes.

Lushtaku was not present when the judge announced the verdict, which was applauded by the public in the courtroom.

“The court could not find any convincing evidence which would prove the guilt of the defendants,” Judge Leon Perlaska said, reading the verdict. “The court assessed the testimony of the witness codenamed ‘Witness C’ where he denied that he was forced to change his statement,” Perlaska added.

Lushtaku, now mayor of the Kosovo town of Skenderaj/Srbica, was sentenced in 2015 to 12 years in prison by the Basic Court in Mitrovica for a murder committed in 1998, although the victim’s name was unknown and no body was found.

He was cleared on appeal in 2016 but his conviction for “command responsibility for allegedly violating the [bodily] integrity and health of an undefined number of civilian Albanians held at the Likovc detention centre” was upheld.

His sentence was reduced from 12 to seven years in prison by the Appeals Court. He was cleared by the Supreme Court in July 2017.

World.title: Kosovo Retrial Confirms Serbian Police Ex-Inspector’s Ten-Year Sentence
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Sacir Lutvija in court om July 28, 2026. Photo: BIRN.



Sacir Lutvija, a 65-year-old ethnic Gorani former member of the Serbian police force, was sentenced to ten years in prison in a retrial at the Pristina Basic Court, for war crimes committed during the 1998-99 war in Kosovo.

Serbian police and military forces staged a campaign of arrests of ethnic Albanian civilians and 11 of them were taken to Prizren police station in southern Kosovo, where Lutvija was among the inspectors who questioned them, according to the indictment.

Prosecutors said those arrested were beaten during the interrogation and subjected to electric shocks on their hands and genitals. One civilian died and ten others sustained serious injuries.

Lutvija, who has both Kosovo and Serbian citizenship, was arrested in October 2023 and has been in detention since then. The time in custody will be counted towards his sentence.

The Kosovo Special Prosecution charged Lutvija with unlawfully arresting and beating civilians, inhumane treatment and murder in his capacity as an inspector and police officer in Prizren. Lutvija pleaded not guilty in September last year.

Judge Kujtim Krasniqi on Tuesday ordered Lutvija to pay a court fee of 400 euros as well as 100 euros to the crime victims’ fund.

The verdict can be appealed.

Lutvija was initially sentenced to 10 years in prison by the Pristina Basic Court in November 2025.

But the Court of Appeals sent the case to a retrial in June this year having concluded that the Pristina Basic Court had not “concretely clarified the actions attributed to the accused in relation to each of the injured parties”.

The Court of Appeal also said the Basic Court failed to explained the accused’s participation in committing the crimes and “did not clarify the evidence upon which the conclusions presented in the verdict were based”.

The Gorani are a small Slavic ethnic group who mostly follow Islam and inhabit a highland triangle between Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia.

World.title: Left High and Dry: Drought Exposes Central Europe’s Water Crisis
World.content:
Water management and retention

Described as the proverbial “roof of Europe”, Czechia sees all its rivers, streams and waterways flow out of the country – a systemic and geological drainage which makes the country particularly dependent on precipitation from above.

“This is a significant disadvantage, because most of the water we manage has to be retained: in the landscape, soil, hydrogeological structures or water reservoirs,” says Adam Vizina, head of the hydrology department at the Water Management Research Institute.

Water management and retention are, therefore, key for this landlocked country, yet the authorities appear short on solutions.

“Water will always flow away, but we can reduce our vulnerability,” argues Vizina, listing measures such as slowing runoff, interconnecting water supply systems, managing water reservoirs better, or protecting the quality and quantity of groundwater.

The state reportedly spent 75 billion crowns (about 3 billion euros) in the past three years on drought adaptation, yet experts – including a report by the Supreme Audit Office published last March – have criticised the slow pace and limited scope of the measures.

The Slovak Academy of Sciences recently released its “Vision for Slovakia 2040”, an extensive 90-page framework document commissioned by the government of Robert Fico laying out the key policy challenges for the next 15 years.

Among those, the forward-looking blueprint “identifies more frequent droughts as a key consequence of climate change and argues that strengthening water management, increasing landscape water retention and improving the resilience of agriculture and ecosystems should be central priorities for Slovakia’s long-term development.”

Whether the authorities will act on the recommendations is another matter, with experts long highlighting key shortcomings in Slovakia’s water management practices, from fragmented governance between different institutions and ministries, a lack of concrete follow-through, and scattered water data hindering real-time monitoring.

Czechia and Slovakia’s subpar water-management has deep roots dating back to decades of intensive farming that followed its collectivisation in the 1950s and 1960s under Communism – with all that entailed in terms of land consolidation, water erosion and reduced soil fertility, among other environmental impacts.

On the upside, the Czech Republic continues to receive roughly the same amount of rain on average every year as it used to, according to some estimates. But the way, time and place it does are changing, as must the measures meant to retain and manage it more effectively, experts say: less rainfall in the spring but more in the fall, more intense precipitation during storms, but less frequent episodes of long-term and widespread rain.

According to Milan Vitek from the local branch of Greenpeace, Czechia might soon be faced with the choice of keeping its scarce water either in the rivers or in its fields, but won’t be able to do both. “Adaptation is something that we are decades behind when we could’ve been much further ahead,” he previously told BIRN.

Water management or retention are also recently being cited as a silver bullet to solve Hungary’s problems. Although Hungary has a renewable water reservoir of 11,833 cubic metres per person, one of the largest in Central Europe (only Slovenia and Serbia have more in the region), 95 per cent of that originates from outside and simply flows through the country.

The building of dams or hydroelectric power plants has been a politically sensitive issue since the controversial plan to build the Bos-Nagymaros dam on the Danube helped trigger popular revolt against the Communist government in 1990. Since then, proposals for new dams and hydropower projects have remained politically off-limits in Hungary.

But times are changing. Laszlo Gajdos, the new Hungarian government’s environment minister, said at the height of the extreme heat at the beginning of July that “water is one of our most valuable resources for the future”.

Gajdos said the government must do everything it can to improve water retention, even with dam construction where necessary. “We should not let water flow through Hungary; it needs to be retained somehow. Personally, I don’t like this method, but it seems inevitable building some dams,” he told RTL.hu.

The government of Peter Magyar is working on a new climate and environmental law, expected by late autumn, which is set to address water management issues.

Gajdos, who became Hungary’s first environment minister in 16 years, stressed that water retention is a regional issue requiring cooperation with neighbouring countries.

Andras Szollosi-Nagy, who used to advise international organisations including the UN on water diplomacy and is the founder member of the World Water Council, could not agree more.

“Water retention is always somehow part of national sovereignty,” Szollosi-Nagy says. “The country upstream believes all the water is theirs, but if they retain it, neighbouring countries are affected. We need integrated water management in the region.”

He says there is no silver bullet to solve all the problems: dams, reservoirs, new technologies, satellite-based monitoring and controlled flooding could all play a role.

“Hungary’s water management system has been systematically dismantled in recent decades,” he says. “Now we need to rebuild it from scratch.”

World.title: Letter from Washington: US Seeks to Score Material Goals in the Balkans
World.content:
Greetings from America, which this month celebrated 250 years of independence from the British crown under a president who has called himself a king – and is also seen that way by the many thousands of people who have joined the “No Kings” protests in the US.

Donald Trump would not even allow the kings of football, the Spanish national team who won the World Cup, to enjoy their rightful moment on the throne this month. Instead, he lingered on stage after presenting them with the trophy at the stadium in New Jersey. An awkward situation was averted by Trump’s pal, FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who pulled the US leader aside, suggesting that it was time for him to step away.

Meanwhile, beside the footballing euphoria, the US-Iran memorandum of understanding has turned out to be more of a major misunderstanding. The war has escalated, bringing new American casualties and higher fuel prices, while reopening an uncomfortable question: what is the actual endgame? If the goal is to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons, to prevent further escalation in the Middle East, why is the United States simultaneously signing an agreement that would allow Saudi Arabia to develop the very same capability?

While all this has been happening, the Trump administration’s policy towards the Balkans has started to become increasingly clear. It is moving more aggressively into areas it considers important, such as energy, defence and infrastructure, while trying to push Russia, China and the European Union out of those spheres. Washington does not appear to be choosing its friends based on how developed their democracies are. Nor is it particularly troubled when someone in the Balkans talks about “ethnic cleansing”.

World.title: On Albania’s Adriatic Coast, Tourism Ambitions Put at Risk by Pollution
World.content:
Violeta was unimpressed by the rubbish blighting her summer holiday.

“It’s awful, isn’t it?” the 24-year-old said of the litter and construction waste strewn along beachfront at Golem Beach, a sandy stretch of Adriatic coast just south of the Albanian port city of Durres.

Golem is one of the most affordable holiday destinations in Albania, just 30 kilometres west of the capital, Tirana, and a relatively quick trip from neighbouring Kosovo. It is often packed with visitors, but Violeta said one week was enough.

“We’re going somewhere cleaner because of the pollution, like Ksamil,” she told BIRN, referring to a beach at the southern end of Albania. Pointing at rubbish, she said: “It bothers me because animals eat it and there are kids running around.”

World.title: What’s Driving the Real-Estate Price Surges in Eastern and South-East Europe?
World.content:
Rapidly rising real estate prices to the east and south of the Trieste-Szczecin line made existing dwelling owners happy - but potential buyers, especially younger people, less so.

According to Eurostat, in the first quarter of 2026, property prices in Bulgaria, Slovakia, and Croatia recorded price growth of 14 per cent over the first quarter of 2025. In a longer perspective of 3 and 10 years, the fortunes of individual countries have changed.

Generally, the total appreciation of housing real estate has been rapid, with Hungary in 10 years heading the list, followed by Bulgaria, Czechia, and Croatia.

However, Eurostat does not provide comparable data for countries southeast of Croatia, but Bosnia, Serbia, Montenegro, and others have followed similar paths. According to the Agency for Statistics of Bosnia, housing real estate prices increased by 20.4 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the first quarter of 2025. Nussubpekova recently reported a double-digit growth rate for Serbia.

World.title: North Macedonia Mourns Much-Loved Actor Goce Todorovski
World.content:
Goce Todorovski. Photo: Drama Theatre.

Actor Goce Todorovski has died aged 75, his family and the Drama Theatre in Skopje, where he spent most of his career, confirmed on Monday. The cause of death was not immediately announced.

Born in the western town of Kichevo in 1951, Todorovski graduated from the Faculty of Dramatic Arts in Skopje before joining the Drama Theatre in 1978. He went on to perform in more than 50 theatre productions, while also building a prolific career in television, radio and cinema.

His gift for comedy made him one of the country’s most enduring and popular actors.

For many Macedonians, Todorovski will be remembered above all for his appearances in the cult television series Macedonian Folk Tales (Makedonski Narodni Prikazni), whose humorous adaptations of traditional folklore became a fixture of family viewing for decades.

He was also a familiar face to generations of children through the educational television series “Scruffy Alphabet” (Bushava Azbuka), while radio audiences knew him from the long-running satirical comedy programme Hihiriku.

His film career included memorable roles in several classics of Macedonian and former Yugoslav cinema, including Happy New ’49 (Srekna Nova ’49), Weekend of the Dead (Vikend na Mrtovci), Trieste Via Skopje (Trst via Skopje), The Red Horse (Crveniot Konj), and many others.

Beyond his screen work, Todorovski was one of the leading comic actors of the Macedonian stage, collaborating with many of the country’s best-known theatre directors and helping shape the repertoire of the Drama Theatre for nearly five decades.

“Goce Todorovski never sought the audience’s affection. He won it from the moment he stepped onto the stage,” the Drama Theatre wrote in its farewell.

“His performances possessed a rare immediacy: a precise acting rhythm that seemed entirely effortless, expressive facial gestures, a distinctive stage presence, and the roguish charm with which he could effortlessly bridge the gap between the stage and the audience,” it said.

Todorovski’s performances earned numerous awards, including the state “23 October” prize for culture and the lifetime achievement award at the Vojdan Chernodrinski Theatre Festival in 2025, as well as the Presidential Order of Merit in 2023.

News of his death prompted an outpouring of tributes from fellow actors, public figures and audiences, many recalling the humour, warmth and distinctive characters that made Todorovski one of the defining faces of North Macedonia’s acting scene.

Actress Maja Andonovska Ilijevski wrote that Macedonian theatre had lost “a great man and a great actor”. Recalling their time filming the cult TV series Macedonian Folk Tales, she said Todorovski had been not only an acting legend but also a wonderful colleague, whose humour and warmth made those days unforgettable.

Andonovska said the countless characters Todorovski brought to life will remain part of the country’s collective memory, adding that “some people never truly leave – they live on through their roles, the memories of their colleagues and the love of their audience”.

Photographer Goran Anastasovski described Todorovski as “the man who made us laugh for decades” and “a giant on stage”, adding that his legacy of bringing smiles to various generations will endure.

World.title: Croatian Firefighters Continue Battling Bordeaux Wildfire
World.content:
July the 28th, 2026 – Croatian firefighters are continuing to battle the intense Bordeaux wildfire ravaging southwestern France, and which keeps being rekindled by problematic winds.

Croatian Air Force firefighting pilots are continuing their mission in southwestern France, where they are helping battle the massive wildfire near Bordeaux. Index reports that this intense operation has now entered its fifth day, with crews facing increasingly difficult conditions as strengthening winds threaten to reignite areas that had previously been brought under control.

The members of the 855th Firefighting Squadron are operating in the Saumos area, just west of Bordeaux. According to Major Ivan Dukić, conditions improved after overnight rain, but rising temperatures and stronger afternoon winds have caused the fire to become active once again.

“The situation is much better than it initially was thanks to some rainfall. However, temperatures are increasing, and as the day progresses the wind is strengthening. The fire has been waking up again, so we’ll see what the days bring,” Dukić said from France.

Since arriving in France, the Croatian crews have carried out 118 flights, logged 20 hours of flying time, and dropped 576 tonnes of water on the catastrophic French wildfires. They are working alongside French and other international crews as part of the rescEU civil protection mechanism.

Despite the demanding mission abroad, Croatia’s aerial firefighting forces remain heavily engaged at home during the peak wildfire season. Between the 15th of June and the 27th of July, the 855th Firefighting Squadron took part in extinguishing 39 wildfires along Croatia’s coastline and on the islands.

Commander Colonel Željko Bukvić said Croatia’s ability to respond both domestically and internationally is the result of careful planning, good organisation and the experience of its firefighting crews. He stressed that the squadron remains ready to assist both Croatia and its European partners whenever needed. The enormous wildfire near Bordeaux remains one of France’s most serious emergencies, with strong, problematic winds, high temperatures and dry vegetation continuing to fuel the blaze repeatedly despite efforts. Croatian pilots remain on the front line as authorities work to prevent the fire from spreading further.

World.title: July 1377: Dubrovnik Introduces Organised Isolation of Arrivals to Combat Plague
World.content:
July the 28th, 2026 – Turning the clock back to July 1377, we saw how the ever-diplomatic Dubrovnik organised the isolation of new arrivals in order to combat the plague.

In July of the aforementioned year, the former Great Council of the Republic of Dubrovnik adopted a decision requiring people arriving in the city (and then autonomous state of Ragusa) from plague-affected areas to undergo a period of isolation before entering the city or its surroundings.

trentina – strict isolation for a period of one month

Dubrovnik was one of the most important medieval trading centres on the Adriatic. Its wealth depended on shipping, merchants and goods arriving from across the Mediterranean and the European hinterland. Those same connections also carried infectious diseases. After the Black Death swept through Europe in the mid-14th century and caused catastrophic issues, the authorities faced a clear problem. A complete ban on foreign arrivals and goods would have protected the population but would also have severely damaged an economy based on trade. Instead they introduced a compromise.

Arrivals from infected regions were not allowed to enter Dubrovnik immediately. Index writes that they had to spend a fixed period separated from the local population so that any symptoms of disease could appear. The initial isolation period lasted 30 days and was known as the “trentina”.

dubrovnik tried to stop the disease at the city gates

Isolation was carried out at Cavtat and on nearby islets such as Mrkan; later Bobara and Supetar were also used. The underlying principle was that a person who showed no signs of illness after a sufficiently long interval posed a substantially lower risk of introducing infection. Medieval physicians had absolutely no knowledge of the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which was identified much later at the very end of the 19th century. They did, however, observe from experience that the disease spread through contact and the movement of people, and that symptoms could appear only after a delay. Dubrovnik therefore tried to stop the disease at the gates rather than respond only after an outbreak inside the city.

Rules were strict. People from affected areas had to complete the prescribed isolation, and contact between Dubrovnik residents and those in isolation was limited, creating a sanitary buffer.

dubrovnik’s decision eventually became a global practice in epidemiology

The period was later extended from 30 to 40 days. The modern word “quarantine” derives from the Italian quaranta (forty). The precise reason for choosing 40 days is not certain; explanations range from medical observation to the symbolic importance of the number in Christian tradition.

In subsequent centuries Dubrovnik developed a more elaborate system, including lazarettos where travellers, merchants and goods could complete the required period of observation before entry. The arrangement allowed trade to continue under controlled conditions rather than forcing a choice between an open city exposed to disease and a completely closed one without commerce.

The 1377 decision is regarded as one of the earliest organised applications of a practice that later became a standard method of epidemic control worldwide.

World.title: Split is Launching One of Croatia’s Largest Environmental Projects
World.content:
July the 28th, 2026 – Split is set to launch one of Croatia’s largest environmental projects as part of a massive 100 million euro investment.

Poslovni reports that construction works on this enormous project will last 28 months from the contractor being introduced to the site until the start of the plant’s trial operation. The total duration of the contract itself is 43 months, including the trial operation period and obtaining the operating permit.

One of the most important infrastructure projects in Croatia’s water management sector is now beginning in Split. On Tuesday, the 28th July 2026, the start of construction works on the Stupe Wastewater Treatment Plant (UPOV Stupe) will be officially marked. The project is a key part of the “Improvement of Water and Utility Infrastructure of the Split–Solin Agglomeration” initiative.

With the expansion of the Stupe wastewater treatment plant, Split will receive a modern wastewater treatment system that, once completed, will become the second-largest wastewater treatment facility in all of Croatia and the central point of a unified sewage system serving the Split–Solin agglomeration.

The value of the contract for the design and expansion of the facility amounts to 99,056,751.25 euros including VAT. The works will be carried out by a consortium consisting of WTE Wassertechnik GmbH (lead partner) and HERING d.d.

The future facility will have a capacity of 275,000 population equivalents, with secondary biological wastewater treatment. The construction of the Stupe wastewater treatment plant will provide modern treatment of municipal wastewater for Split and the surrounding area, helping to further protect the environment, preserve the quality of the Brač Channel, and improve the quality of life for residents.

As part of the second phase of the project, eligible costs amount to 243,149,745.48 euros. Of this, €165,365,077.30 euros will be financed through non-refundable European Union funds from the Cohesion Fund, while the remaining amount will be secured through Croatian national sources.

World.title: Approval Granted for Construction of Key Croatian Four-Lane Road Section
World.content:
July the 28th, 2026 – Approval has been granted for the construction of a key Croatian four-lane road section, and it is being hailed as one of the country’s most significant motorway projects.

Croatian drivers are a step closer to improved transport links after the government approved the construction of one of the country’s most important road projects. The decision clears the way for the development of a new four-lane section that is expected to improve traffic flow, increase road safety and strengthen connections between key parts of the national road network.

The approval relates to the 21.9-kilometre Podravska Expressway section between Pitomača and Virovitica, after the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition completed the environmental impact assessment and declared the project environmentally acceptable.

The project has received official approval following the completion of the necessary planning procedures, allowing preparations for construction to move forward. Poslovni reports that the new road section will be built with four traffic lanes, significantly increasing capacity compared with the existing road and helping to reduce congestion, particularly during periods of heavy traffic. According to the project plans, the upgraded route will form part of a wider transport corridor designed to improve connections between regions, shorten travel times and support economic development. The investment is also expected to enhance access for businesses, tourism and freight transport.

The planned road will include modern infrastructure designed to meet current safety standards, with features aimed at improving traffic efficiency and reducing the risk of accidents. Officials say the project represents one of the country’s most significant transport investments in recent years.

The approval marks an important milestone, but several stages remain before construction begins, including the completion of procurement procedures and the selection of contractors. Once the boots are actually on the ground, the project is expected to be carried out in multiple phases.

The new four-lane road is otherwise a large part of Croatia’s broader strategy to modernise its transport infrastructure and improve connectivity across the country. Once completed, it is expected to make journeys faster, safer and more reliable for both local residents and visitors, while supporting long-term economic growth.

World.title: Croatia Braces for Another Heatwave as Temperatures Could Reach 40°C
World.content:
July the 27th, 2026 – Following a brief but very welcome period of cooler, fresher and somewhat unstable weather, Croatia is set to face another heatwave with temperatures likely to reach 40 degrees.

After a brief spell of unsettled and sometimes stormy weather, Croatia is preparing for another intense heatwave, with temperatures expected to climb steadily throughout the week and potentially reach 40°C in some inland areas. Index reports that meteorologists are claiming that the hottest conditions are likely to arrive during the second half of the week.

above 35 degrees by the end of the week

Weather conditions are expected to stabilise on Tuesday and onwards. Daytime temperatures will rise each day, with much of the country seeing highs above 35°C by the end of the week. Forecasters say isolated locations could even record temperatures of around 40°C if current forecasts hold.

The Croatian Meteorological and Hydrological Service (DHMZ) has already issued an initial yellow heat warning for Thursday, cautioning that the heat could pose a risk to human health. Meteorologists warn that higher-level warnings may be introduced if temperatures continue to increase as expected.

The upcoming heatwave follows an unusual period of unstable weather that brought thunderstorms, strong winds and a series of strange meteotsunamis along parts of the Adriatic coast. Once the current weather system moves away, a strengthening area of high pressure is expected to bring prolonged sunshine and very little rainfall.

records were broken in june

Forecasters also pointed to this summer’s exceptional conditions. During June, fourteen of Croatia’s 35 main meteorological stations recorded new monthly temperature records, while Split reached an all-time record of 40°C at the Marjan weather station. Staggeringly, even sea temperatures climbed to around 30°C in some areas, highlighting the intensity of this year’s hot summer season.

Authorities are advising residents and visitors to stay hydrated, avoid prolonged exposure to the sun during the hottest part of the day and keep a close eye on vulnerable groups, including the elderly, young children and those with existing health conditions, as Croatia prepares for another spell of extreme summer heat.

World.title: Sea Floods Stari Grad on Hvar for the Third Time in Just 10 Days
World.content:
July the 27th, 2026 – The sea has created floods in Stari Grad on the island of Hvar for the third time in just 10 days due to repeated meteotsunamis.

Index reports that visitors and residents of Stari Grad on the island of Hvar have once again found themselves dealing with flooded streets after the sea overflowed onto the town’s waterfront, marking the third such event in just ten days. The repeated flooding has drawn attention to increasingly unusual sea level fluctuations affecting parts of Croatia’s coastline and islands.

Videos shared by residents showed seawater spilling over the promenade and into the historic centre, covering streets and public spaces before gradually receding. Although the flooding caused disruption, there were no reports of serious injuries or major structural damage.

According to meteorologists, the flooding was not caused by rainfall but by a combination of low atmospheric pressure, strong southerly winds and elevated sea levels. These conditions created what is known as a storm surge, pushing large volumes of seawater onto the shoreline and into low-lying coastal areas.

The phenomenon has affected Stari Grad several times over the past two weeks, with each event occurring under similar weather conditions. Locals say the repeated flooding has become a growing concern, particularly for businesses and residents along the waterfront who have had to repeatedly clear seawater from their properties.

Experts note that enclosed bays and historic harbour towns such as Stari Grad are especially vulnerable to this type of coastal flooding. When strong winds coincide with low air pressure, sea levels can temporarily rise enough to overwhelm quays, promenades and streets built just above normal sea level.

As weather conditions improved, the seawater gradually retreated and life returned to normal. However, the latest flooding serves as another reminder of how quickly changing weather patterns can impact Croatia’s coastal communities, with residents hoping calmer conditions will prevent another repeat in the coming days.

World.title: Sveti Ivan Beach: The Hidden Paradise That Requires a 50-Minute Hike
World.content:
July the 27th, 2026 – The entire island of Cres is stunning, but Sveti Ivan beach takes it a step further. If we’re being honest, it takes it many steps further, as a 50-minute hike is needed to reach this hidden paradise. Trust us, it’s so worth it.

Hidden beneath the ancient hilltop village of Lubenice on the island of Cres lies one of Croatia’s most spectacular beaches, Sveti Ivan beach. Putni kofer reveals that it is best known for its white pebbles, crystal-clear waters and particularly dramatic surroundings. It is very often considered one of the most beautiful beaches on the Croatian coast (and that’s a challenging title to receive in itself).

The beach sits in a secluded bay beneath the historic settlement of Lubenice, which is perched high on a cliff overlooking the Adriatic. Surrounded by steep rocks and untouched nature, Sveti Ivan offers the kind of peaceful atmosphere that is becoming increasingly rare on the Croatian coast.

Part of what keeps this beach so special is also what makes it difficult to reach. Visitors who choose to walk from Lubenice must follow a steep trail that takes around 50 minutes downhill, and the return journey can be even more challenging, especially during the intense summer heat. Proper footwear and enough water are essential, and we’d go as far as to discourage anyone doing this during the height of summer.

Because of the demanding access, even during the height of summer Sveti Ivan usually avoids the large crowds found at many other Croatian beaches. Those who make the journey are rewarded with incredible views, peaceful surroundings and some of the clearest waters on the Adriatic.

The beach can also be reached by sea, either with a private boat, organised excursion or water taxi. Nearby is another natural attraction, Plava Grota, a sea cave where sunlight creates beautiful blue reflections inside the cave.

Above the beach sits Lubenice, one of the oldest settlements on the Croatian islands. Located on a 378-metre-high cliff, the village has a history stretching back more than 4,000 years, with archaeological remains from the Bronze and Iron Ages found in the surrounding area.

Once one of Cres’ most important settlements, Lubenice is now home to only two permanent residents. However, during the summer months, visitors arrive to explore its ancient stone streets, admire the views and discover one of Croatia’s most breathtaking beaches down below.

World.title: Should Croatia Charge Tourists Who Need Emergency Help After Excessive Drinking?
World.content:
July the 27th, 2026 – Should Croatia be charging tourists who take it too far and require emergency medical help after excessive drinking or even illicit drug use?

Every single summer, Split in particular faces the same old problem, and that is tourists being found unconscious on city streets after heavy nights of drinking, with emergency services called to help them. The issue has sparked a debate over whether people who put themselves in danger through excessive alcohol consumption should contribute to the cost of medical interventions.

over 50 calls because of alcohol in june alone

During June alone, the Split-Dalmatia County Emergency Medical Service recorded more than 50 calls related to alcohol intoxication. Lukrecija Zderic reveals for Index that medical teams treated 44 people, while eight people were no longer at the location when emergency crews arrived. Among those who received help were also two minors.

Many of these cases involve young foreign tourists visiting Split during the summer season. Locals say it has become common to find intoxicated visitors lying on streets in the early morning hours after nights out and organised pub crawl tours.

The question now being raised is whether tourists who end up needing emergency medical assistance because of extreme alcohol consumption should help cover the cost. Some European countries already charge part of the expense in similar situations, but Croatia currently does not have such a system.

an abuse of already thin resources

Croatia’s emergency services are required to help anyone whose health is at risk, regardless of how the situation happened. However, every intervention requires medical staff, vehicles and resources.

The Croatian Health Insurance Fund explained that emergency medical teams are funded through contracted healthcare costs. A single emergency team consisting of a doctor, nurse and driver represents a significant annual expense for the healthcare system.

For foreign visitors, the final bill depends on their insurance situation. Tourists from EU countries, the European Economic Area and Switzerland with valid European Health Insurance Cards have their costs covered through international healthcare agreements. Visitors from countries without such agreements may have to pay themselves unless they have travel insurance.

irresponsible behaviour should face consequences

However, if a tourist leaves Croatia without paying a medical bill, the unpaid cost can ultimately fall on Croatian public funds. This means taxpayers may end up covering expenses that were never recovered.The debate comes as Split continues to balance the benefits of being one of Croatia’s most popular tourist destinations with the challenges that come from large numbers of visitors, particularly during the peak summer months.

As tourism grows, Croatia faces an ongoing question: should irresponsible behaviour surrounding alcohol and drug use that requires emergency medical intervention come with a financial consequence?

World.title: Iraq’s oil exports hit 526,000 bpd in May and June
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s average oil exports in May and June 2026 were roughly 526,470 barrels per day, compared to about 329,500 barrels per day in April, amid ongoing shipping and energy disruptions in the Gulf region.

The revenues generated from Iraqi oil exports saw an improvement over the last two months, supported by a relative increase in shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and the activation of alternative export routes.

Oil prices fluctuated, remaining high at around $100 per barrel during May before falling below that level in June.

The rising oil prices boosted Iraq’s export income in May and June 2026, when there were fears about supply constraints and increased Asian demand, notably from China and India.

Iraqi oil exports have been under growing strain since the beginning of March, following the suspension of loading operations at southern ports due to the US war against Iran, which had a direct impact on marine security in the Strait of Hormuz.

According to the State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO), Iraq’s total oil exports in May and June 2026 were roughly 32.11 million barrels, with a monthly average of over 16 million barrels.

The country’s oil exports reached 9.88 million barrels in April and around 18.6 million barrels in March.

Iraqi oil export earnings in May and June 2026 reached approximately $2.33 billion, averaging $1.16 billion per month, compared to $1.87 billion in April, $1.95 billion in March, and approximately $6.81 billion in February.

Experts believe that the current price levels of oil are likely to provide Baghdad with a better financial margin to mitigate some losses incurred from the significant decline in exports, even amidst ongoing security tensions in the region.

World.title: Iraqi PM arrives in Turkey on an official visit
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi arrived in the Turkish capital, Ankara, on Tuesday, for an official visit following an invitation from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Al-Zaidi said in a statement on X that his trip to Turkey will focus on investments, water, and development projects, as well as efforts to enhance stability in the region.

Turkish media highlighted the significance of the visit, as it is expected to broaden constructive collaboration between the two countries, particularly in the areas of water, energy, security, and economic cooperation, according to the state-run news agency (INA).

In addition to trade, security cooperation, and combating terrorism, al-Zaidi will discuss establishing a cooperative water management entity based on shared interests, as well as scientific collaboration and investment in advanced technology, to serve the interests of both Iraq and Turkey.

Al-Zaidi is scheduled to fly to Saudi Arabia on Thursday for an official visit, following his diplomatic trip to the Turkish capital, Ankara.

The trip is part of a larger regional diplomatic tour aiming to maintain regional balance and strengthen Iraq’s business connections.

The prime minister recently conducted high-level diplomatic visits to the United States on July 13 and Iran on July 23.

World.title: Ukraine rejects Iraqi official’s claims of Ukrainian cell operating in Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Tuesday dismissed statements by Iraq’s National Security Adviser Qasim Al-Aboudi, who claimed that Iraqi authorities had arrested a Ukrainian-linked cell responsible for carrying out attacks inside the country.

In an official statement, the ministry said the allegations were “groundless” and noted that no evidence had been presented to support the claims. It also pointed out that Al-Aboudi himself acknowledged during a televised interview that investigations into the matter were still ongoing.

According to the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry, Iraqi authorities did not communicate any information or concerns through diplomatic channels before the allegations were made publicly.

The ministry said that if Iraqi officials possessed credible evidence, the issue should have been raised through official diplomatic mechanisms rather than announced during a television interview. Instead, Kyiv said it first learned of the accusations through media reports.

Furthermore, Ukraine described the public remarks by a senior Iraqi official as “unacceptable and irresponsible” in the absence of supporting evidence. The ministry stressed that such statements contradict the principles of mutual respect between friendly nations and risk undermining relations between Iraq and Ukraine.

At the same time, Kyiv reaffirmed that it considers Iraq an important partner in the Middle East and remains committed to strengthening political, economic, and humanitarian cooperation between the two countries.

The Foreign Ministry also argued that the allegations mirror Russian propaganda narratives aimed at damaging Ukraine’s international reputation and weakening its partnerships across the Middle East.

Additionally, the statement suggested that the incident could have resulted from external information influence or formed part of a coordinated information campaign intended to disrupt Iraqi-Ukrainian relations.

Ukraine called on Iraqi authorities to address what it described as unfounded allegations and to prevent state institutions from promoting misinformation that could serve the interests of third parties.

The Ukrainian response follows remarks made on Monday by National Security Adviser Qasim Al-Aboudi during an interview on Dijlah TV. Al-Aboudi said Iraqi intelligence had identified what he described as Ukrainian interference inside Iraq and claimed security forces had arrested several individuals who allegedly carried out attacks on Iraqi territory.

He further stated that those detained confessed during questioning to working on behalf of Ukraine. However, Al-Aboudi did not identify the facilities allegedly targeted or specify whether the alleged operations extended beyond Iraq’s borders.

He also acknowledged that investigations into attacks carried out inside Iraq remain complex and require further examination before responsibility can be definitively assigned.

World.title: Iraqi PM expands powers as political deadlock delays cabinet completion
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – A dispute over Iraq’s remaining vacant cabinet positions has expanded beyond the selection of ministers, with political factions now focusing on the growing authority of the Office of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, according to a report published by Al-Mada newspaper.

The debate follows the leak of an official document indicating that Prime Minister Ali Falih Al-Zaidi has reactivated and expanded the powers of the Commander-in-Chief Office, placing several key security institutions under its supervision while the Ministries of Interior and Defense remain without permanent ministers.

According to Al-Mada, several political sources believe the expanded office significantly increases the prime minister’s direct oversight of Iraq’s security apparatus.

The report says the office now oversees the Ministries of Interior and Defense, the Counter-Terrorism Service, the National Intelligence Service, the National Security Service, the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), border crossings, military industries, and other security-related institutions.

Consequently, some political figures have described the move as a “quiet coup” against Iraq’s post-2003 political framework, arguing that it centralizes authority within the prime minister’s office while reducing the practical influence of future ministers.

Meanwhile, Iraq’s cabinet remains incomplete, with only 14 ministries currently filled while nine ministerial portfolios remain vacant. According to the report, political negotiations have become increasingly complicated, as disagreements now extend beyond candidate names to broader questions of political influence and institutional control.

Sources cited by Al-Mada said the State of Law Coalition has proposed rotating senior security positions as part of efforts to break the deadlock, particularly regarding the Interior Ministry, which traditionally falls under the Shiite political share, while the Defense Ministry is typically allocated to Sunni representatives.

However, negotiations have yet to produce a breakthrough.

At the same time, Al-Mada reported that U.S. objections have become one of the main obstacles preventing completion of the cabinet. Political sources quoted in the report claim Washington opposes appointing individuals affiliated with armed factions to ministerial positions or senior executive offices.

The report says these objections have complicated negotiations among members of the Coordination Framework, with some factions insisting that if their nominees are rejected, similar restrictions should apply to other political parties. As a result, discussions over the remaining cabinet positions have largely stalled.

Political analysts interviewed by Al-Mada argue that the continued delay in appointing ministers has allowed Prime Minister Al-Zaidi greater flexibility in managing state institutions through acting officials and appointments within his office.

According to the report, some political parties fear that prolonging the vacancies could further strengthen the prime minister’s influence over Iraq’s security establishment, making future ministerial appointments less significant.

The report also notes that recent anti-corruption campaigns and shifting political alliances have altered the balance of power within the Coordination Framework, adding another layer of complexity to negotiations.

Supporters of the government, however, argue that the current arrangements are necessary to maintain continuity while negotiations continue.

Officials quoted by Al-Mada said acting appointments and the reactivation of the Commander-in-Chief Office ensure that security institutions continue functioning despite the absence of permanent ministers.

They also expressed confidence that political forces will eventually reach an agreement to complete the cabinet, stressing that Iraq faces significant challenges, including anti-corruption efforts, security reforms, weapons control, and economic pressures linked to oil exports.

Nevertheless, the report suggests that political parties continue to use the vacant ministries as leverage in negotiations with the prime minister, making the timeline for completing the government uncertain.

World.title: US drone shot down in western Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – An unknown drone, first claimed by Iranian official media IRIB as a US surveillance one, crashed within a residential complex near the Haditha Dam in the western Iraqi province of Anbar.

Iraqi police and security agencies later indicated that the drone’s origin remains unknown, according to Al-Jazeera.

The debris was discovered blazing in a residential compound near the Haditha Dam in Anbar.

Local police stated that there were no recorded injuries or civilian deaths as a result of the collision.

Iranian state media swiftly released images of the smoking debris, claiming it was a US drone shot down amid broader regional activity.

The incident took place during a night of broad military conflict in Iraq, which included many drone attacks and defensive responses.

At least four Iranian drones attacked targets northeast of the capital of Iraqi Kurdistan, Erbil, sparking a huge defensive reaction, including over ten US jets and drones sent to inspect the skies.

Air defense systems were activated at Anbar’s Ain al-Asad Air Base in response to a drone strike.

Explosions, alleged suicide drones, and radar interruptions were also reported at Camp Taji, Balad Air Base, and Imam Ali Base in southern Iraq.

The US military has not publicly verified the loss of any aircraft in Anbar. Investigations into the model and operator of the crashed drone are still underway.

World.title: Al Zaidi: Iraq and Turkey can build a regional success story through economic integration
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi said on Tuesday that the Middle East needs new success stories built on economic integration rather than conflict, arguing that Iraq and Turkey have the potential to create a model regional partnership through joint investment, infrastructure, and trade.

The remarks came in an article published by Turkey’s Anadolu Agency ahead of Al Zaidi’s official visit to Ankara, where he is expected to meet Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and senior officials.

Al Zaidi said relations between Iraq and Turkey have traditionally focused on managing issues such as security, water resources, trade, and border crossings. However, he argued that regional changes require a more ambitious vision centered on economic cooperation.

He said Iraq has chosen a path of stability, reform, and development, prioritizing a stronger economy, an effective state, and balanced foreign relations that make regional cooperation a pillar of growth.

According to Al Zaidi, Turkey’s industrial base, strategic location, and expertise in infrastructure, energy, and transportation complement Iraq’s geographic position, creating an opportunity to establish one of the region’s most significant economic partnerships.

The prime minister highlighted the Development Road Project, describing it as more than an Iraqi initiative. He said the corridor could redefine economic connectivity in the Middle East by linking Gulf ports with Asian and European markets.

He added that the project would not only reduce shipping times but also create new cities, industrial zones, investment opportunities, and thousands of jobs, while establishing a new economic artery connecting ports to global markets.

Al Zaidi also stressed that security cooperation remains essential, saying Iraq’s and Turkey’s security are closely linked and require mutual respect for sovereignty as well as joint efforts to combat terrorism and organized crime.

On water issues, he said water is no longer simply a technical matter but a development challenge affecting millions of people. He called for a shared approach based on mutual interests, scientific cooperation, and investment in modern technologies to strengthen water and food security.

“The Middle East needs new success stories,” Al Zaidi wrote, adding that Iraq and Turkey can provide one if they move beyond traditional cooperation toward genuine economic integration.

He said every joint investment, factory, transport route, and energy project represents an investment in regional stability, arguing that lasting stability is built through shared projects rather than conflict.

Later on Tuesday, Al Zaidi departed for Ankara at the head of a high-level government delegation. According to the Prime Minister’s Office, the visit will focus on strengthening bilateral cooperation in the fields of economy, water, security, investment, and regional affairs.

The two sides are also expected to review the implementation of existing agreements and memoranda of understanding, while discussing progress on joint infrastructure projects, including the Development Road initiative.

World.title: Drone attack targets Khor Mor gas field in northern Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Drone attacks targeted the Khor Mor gas field in the northern Iraqi province of Sulaymaniyah in the early hours of Tuesday.

The attack on the field, which is Iraq’s largest gas field with reserves estimated at 8.2 trillion cubic feet, was part of a coordinated wave of suspected Iranian drone attacks against the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

Iranian official media reported an attack on the gas field, which is operated by the UAE-based Pearl Consortium that includes Dana Gas and Crescent Petroleum.

The gas field supplies the majority of the electricity in Iraqi Kurdistan.

According to reports, the strikes were carried out by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which targets Iranian Kurdish resistance groups and US interests in the region.

A few days ago, Iraqi Kurdistan’s Prime Minister Masoud Barzani stated that repeated security threats and drone attacks had caused energy companies to cut domestic output, seriously affecting the region’s electrical infrastructure.

The escalation takes place amid significant geopolitical challenges. On Monday, US President Donald Trump said he was ready to resume military action against Iran if diplomatic efforts to reach a nuclear deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz failed.

Trump stated that he has temporarily stopped military strikes against Iran to give negotiations a chance to work.

World.title: Iraq, Australia cooperate to sentence alleged drug trafficker to life imprisonment
World.content:
An Iraqi court has sentenced convicted drug trafficker Kazem Hamad to life imprisonment after finding him guilty of drug trafficking and links to transnational organized crime, in a case that involved close cooperation between Iraqi and Australian authorities.

The ruling marks a significant development in Iraq’s ongoing campaign against organized crime and narcotics trafficking.

In a statement issued on Monday, Iraq’s judiciary described Hamad as “one of the most wanted individuals by Iraqi and international courts.” According to the judiciary, Hamad was responsible for smuggling large quantities of heroin into both Iraq and Australia.

The statement also accused him of involvement with transnational criminal networks engaged in drug trafficking, money laundering, murder, kidnapping, extortion, and organized violence.

Australian authorities have identified Hamad as a key figure in Melbourne’s so-called “tobacco wars,” a violent conflict between organized crime groups competing for control of the illicit tobacco and vape market.

The turf war has been linked to more than 200 arson attacks, firebombings, and extortion incidents across the Australian city. Hamad was deported from Australia in 2023 and was arrested in Iraq in January 2026, where prosecutors charged him with smuggling narcotics into both countries.

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed earlier this year that it had provided operational information to support Iraq’s investigation. AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett said in February that the agency would continue cooperating with Iraqi authorities while pursuing its own investigation into Hamad and his alleged criminal network under Operation Carmen.

Australian investigators have also linked Hamad to several serious crimes, including allegations that he played a role in the December 2024 firebombing of Melbourne’s Adass Israel Synagogue, according to Australian media reports.

The life sentence comes as Iraq continues to intensify its fight against drug trafficking and organized crime. Despite imposing some of the region’s toughest penalties, including life imprisonment and the death penalty for major narcotics offenses, Iraq has experienced a sharp rise in drug trafficking and addiction since 2003.

Officials say authorities have arrested thousands of suspects in recent years as part of nationwide anti-drug operations. Iraq was recently ranked third globally in combating narcotics at the World Police Summit in the United Arab Emirates, reflecting the country’s expanding efforts to dismantle trafficking networks.

World.title: Jammu and Kashmir: Bus with Amarnath pilgrims slips into gorge, 39 hurt
World.content:
Security personnel gather near the wreckage after a bus carrying Amarnath Yatra pilgrims skids off the road and plunged into a gorge

SRINAGAR: At least 39 Amarnath pilgrims, including 21 from Madhya Pradesh and 19 Rajasthan natives, were injured after their bus skidded off the road in Ganiwan in J&Kâs Ganderbal district and slipped into a 50-foot-deep gorge on Tuesday morning. The fall was broken midway at around 25 feet by a house in a mountain hamlet below the road, preventing the vehicle from sliding further down the slope and averting a major tragedy, locals said.The devotees were heading back after visiting the holy cave shrine. The vehicle was moving from Baltal towards Srinagar when the accident occurred around 7 am near Ranga Morh, prompting a multi-agency rescue operation. Residents said the house belonged to Din Mohammad, who was away grazing sheep with his family at the time.J&K Police, CRPF, ITBP, health department and civil defence personnel rushed to the spot and launched a coordinated rescue operation, with assistance from locals. The injured were moved to SKIMS in Soura, Srinagar.J&K Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha visited SKIMS, where doctors briefed him about the health condition of those injured. In an X post, Sinha said he instructed officials to ensure the best possible treatment for the hospitalised pilgrims and arrangements for their safe return upon recovery.Health minister Sakeena Itoo also visited SKIMS and interacted with the injured pilgrims, assuring them of full govt support. She directed hospital authorities to monitor each patientâs condition and ensure round-the-clock availability of specialist doctors and essential healthcare services.This year's Amarnath Yatra began on July 3. The 57-day annual pilgrimage will conclude on Aug 28, coinciding with Raksha Bandhan. As of July 26, more than 4,14,000 pilgrims had completed the annual pilgrimage and offered prayers at the holy cave shrine.

World.title: CBI files chargesheet against 13 accused in NEET-UG paper leak case; hearing tomorrow
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) on Tuesday filed a chargesheet against 13 accused in connection with the NEET-UG paper leak case before the Rouse Avenue Court in Delhi.

The chargesheet, filed by the Economic Offences Wing of the CBI, will be placed before the special fast-track court constituted to hear paper leak cases on Wednesday.

According to the agency, the case has been registered under Sections 315(5), 318(4), 61(2), 238 and 303(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, along with Section 13(2) read with Section 13(1)(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and Sections 3, 4, 5, 10 and 11 of the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024.

As per the information shared by ANI, the accused named in the chargesheet are Yash Yadav, Mangilal Biwal, Dinesh Biwal, Vikas Biwal, Subham Khairnar, Dhananjay Lokhande, Prahalad Kulkarni, Tejas Harshad Kumar, Dr Manoj Shirure, Shivraj Raghunath Motegaonkar, Manisha Waghmare, Manisha Mandhare, and Manisha Sanjay Hawaldar.

All 13 accused are currently in judicial custody.

The alleged leak of the NEET-UG examination paper triggered nationwide outrage and led to multiple investigations into irregularities in the conduct of the medical entrance examination.





Dharmendra Pradhan also resigned on July 25 as Union education minister, following which the Cockroach Janta Party withdrew its 36-day agitation that had mobilised lakhs of people over alleged irregularities in competitive examinations and the NEET paper leak.

World.title: After SC order, West Bengal govt says no action against NEET protesters, except those with criminal records
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The West Bengal government on Tuesday announced that it would not take any coercive action against students who participated in recent demonstrations over the NEET (UG) paper leak issue.

However, the BJP-led state government clarified that the relief would not apply to individuals with criminal antecedents.

The directions are in line with the Supreme Court's interim order earlier in the day, under which states can continue investigations into registered FIRs but cannot take coercive action against students who participated in protests, provided they have no criminal antecedents.

According to an official press release, one case had been registered in West Bengal in connection with the NEET (UG) paper leak protest issue and 16 people had been arrested as of 6 pm on July 26.

Earlier, two other BJP-led states, Bihar and Assam,

the withdrawal of cases and legal proceedings against all protesters involved in demonstrations over the alleged NEET (UG) examination irregularities.

In Maharashtra, another BJP-led state, chief minister Devendra Fadnavis

the state home department to issue orders for the withdrawal of cases registered against students who participated in the protests.





The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online satirical outfit that led the main protests in Delhi, has warned of resuming its agitation if cases against all protesters are not withdrawn. The demand was among the conditions accepted by the Centre, following which the CJP called off its indefinite sit-in on July 25.

The CJP had been protesting at Delhi's Jantar Mantar since June 21.

World.title: Law on delayed birth registration to be more stringent; govt says birth certificate gives one legal identity
World.content:
NEW DELHI: A bill seeking to make the provision for delayed registration of births and deaths more stringent, is set to be introduced in the Lok Sabha, and shall require every birth or death reported to the registrar after two years of its occurrence, to be registered on only an order made by a judicial magistrate of the first class.

As per the statement of objects and reasons of The Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026, the proposal to make the law more stringent is based on consultations held with the state/UT govts and other stakeholders and âwill encourage timely reporting of events of birth and deathâ.

It added that âthe registration of births and deaths is mandatory under the Act and the birth/death certificate issued after such registration, provides legal identity to an individualâ and âis admissible as evidence for the purpose of proving the birth and death of a personâ.

Birth certificate is also the key document for determining a person's citizenship status. It is one of the documents accepted during the special intensive revision (SIR) electoral roll, as a proof of citizenship.

The bill seeks to add sub-section 3A to Section 13, requiring any birth or death intimated to the registrar after two years of occurence, to be registered only on the order of a first-class judicial magistrate, âafter verifying the correctness of the birth or death and on payment of such fee as may be prescribedâ.





The existing Section 13(3) mandates that a birth or death, of which delayed information is shared with the registrar after one year but within two years of its occurrence, will be registered only on order of a district magistrate, sub-divisional magistrate or an executive magistrate authorised by the district magistrate and appointed under Section 14(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).

The rules to implement Section 13(3A) â including determination of the prescribed fee for delayed registration â may be framed by the state govt, empowered under Section 30 to do so.

World.title: 13 Indians stranded aboard vessel in Ukraine amid repeated drone, missile attacks: Report
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Thirteen Indian seafarers are among 15 crew members stranded on board a cargo vessel at Ukraine's Chornomorsk port, where repeated drone and missile attacks have placed the crew in what has been described as a "life-threatening situation", according to the Forward Seamen's Union of India (FSUI).

In an urgent appeal posted on X, the union said the vessel, MV AMIR1, remains docked at Chornomorsk while hostilities continue in the surrounding area.

"MV AMIR1, currently at Ukrainian port Chornomorsk with 15 crew on board, including 13 Indian seafarers, is trapped in a terrible and life-threatening situation," it said.

The union alleged that drone and missile attacks were being carried out in the immediate vicinity of the ship, leaving the crew in constant fear.

"Repeated drone and missile attacks are being attempted in the immediate vicinity of the vessel. The crew is living under constant fear of a direct hit at any moment," it said.

The FSUI urged the shipowners, the vessel's flag state, the relevant authorities and the government to intervene immediately to ensure the crew's safety and facilitate their evacuation.

"We urgently appeal to all concerned authorities, shipowners, flag state, and the Government of India to immediately secure their safety and arrange prompt repatriation," the union said.





Calling for urgent action, it added, "Indian seafarers must not be left as sitting targets in conflict zones. Act now."

This comes a day after MEA raised concerns with Ukraine over the safety of Indian seafarers in the Black Sea. On Monday, the MEA summoned Ukraine's ambassador to India, Dr Oleksandr Polishchuk, following an attack on the merchant vessel MV OMORFI near the Ukrainian port of Odesa that had four Indian crew members on board.

The MEA said the strike resulted in the death of an Indian national and condemned attacks on commercial shipping in the "strongest terms", calling them a threat to maritime safety, freedom of navigation and international commerce. It also urged Kyiv to ensure that commercial vessels carrying civilian seafarers are not targeted.

World.title: Uttarakhand CM Dhami distributes subsidies to boost clean mobility; flags off 11 clean fuel vehicles
World.content:
Uttarakhand chief minister

on Tuesday distributed capital grant and incentive subsidy cheques to six primary beneficiary vehicle owners under the Uttarakhand Clean Mobility Transition Policy-2024 at the Mukhya Sevak Sadan, Chief Minister's Camp Office.

The Transport Department has also completed the subsidy approval process for five additional beneficiaries. On the occasion, the chief Minister flagged off 11 clean fuel-based vehicles.

Addressing the programme, the chief minister said that the assistance was not merely financial support but a symbol of the state government's commitment to building a clean, modern, and environmentally sustainable transport system in Uttarakhand.

He said the initiative would promote clean fuel-based public transport in urban areas, reduce pollution caused by diesel-powered vehicles, and strengthen environmental conservation efforts.

Dhami said the world is facing the serious challenge of climate change, making it essential to strike a balance between development and environmental protection. He emphasised that development is meaningful only when it remains in harmony with nature and ensures a safe and clean future for coming generations.





The chief minister said that under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, India is emerging as a global leader in green energy and sustainable development. He highlighted initiatives such as the country's target of achieving net-zero emissions by 2070, the Lifestyle for Environment (LiFE) campaign, the PM e-Bus Sewa scheme, and the expansion of solar and other renewable energy sources as evidence of India's commitment to environmental protection.

Dhami said Uttarakhand, nestled in the Himalayas and revered as Devbhoomi, is the origin of life-giving rivers such as the Ganga and Yamuna. He noted that the state's rich biodiversity, forests, rivers, and mountain ecosystems are invaluable national assets. Protecting the environment and maintaining ecological balance, he said, is a shared responsibility, adding that the state government's vision is to ensure that development and environmental conservation go hand in hand.

The chief minister said that with this vision, the government has implemented the Uttarakhand Clean Mobility Transition Policy-2024. The policy aims to modernise public transport in urban areas, reduce pollution caused by ageing diesel vehicles, and encourage the adoption of CNG and other clean fuel-based transport systems. He expressed confidence that the policy would lay a strong foundation for a cleaner, safer, and more sustainable transport network across the state.

Dhami further said that the state government is continuously expanding the operation of electric buses in Dehradun, Haridwar, and Haldwani. EV charging stations are also being established across Uttarakhand to provide the necessary infrastructure for clean mobility. He added that work is progressing rapidly on ropeway projects and modern urban transport systems, which will improve traffic management, reduce congestion and pollution in hilly regions, and make transportation safer and more environmentally friendly.

World.title: Two Army soldiers injured in mine blast in J&K's Uri
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Two

soldiers were injured in a mine blast near the Line of Control (LoC) in

's Uri sector on Tuesday, officials said.

The soldiers sustained injuries in the blast at a forward post in Kamalkote area of Baramulla district. They were provided first aid locally before being airlifted to the Army's 92 Base Hospital in Srinagar.

The cause of the explosion is being ascertained, officials added.

(With PTI inputs)

World.title: Latur municipal authorities explore Ambedkar memorial on study tour
World.content:
Corporators from the Latur Municipal Corporation, Maharashtra, visited Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Smriti Vanam and Ambedkar Kala Vedika in Vijayawada on Tuesday as part of a study tour.

The delegation, led by Mayor Jayashree Bhalchandra Sonkamble, inspected the facilities, the beautification work and the digital exhibitions of Dr. Ambedkar’s life at the memorial park. They also sought details about the advanced technology used in constructing the statue.

The delegation later visited Ambedkar Kala Vedika, where they examined the modern facilities on the ground and first floors, art galleries, and the architectural features of the complex.

Later, NTR District Collector G. Lakshmisha gave a comprehensive presentation on the design, technical aspects, and the cultural and educational significance of Ambedkar Smriti Vanam and Ambedkar Kala Vedika.

Following the presentation, Ms. Jayashree Bhalchandra Sonkamble expressed her gratitude to the district officials and Vijayawada Municipal Corporation for the warm welcome extended to her team. She invited Mr. Lakshmisha to attend the foundation stone-laying ceremony of Dr. Ambedkar’s statue in Latur.

Mr. Lakshmisha later presented the Mayor and the delegation with a replica of Dr. Ambedkar statue. Vijayawada Municipal Corporation in-charge Commissioner A. Ravindra Rao, Chief City Planner Sanjay Ratna Kumar, Latur Municipal Corporation officials and corporators were present during the tour.

World.content:
The Directorate of Technical Education (DoTE) has instructed principals of engineering colleges to not collect any fee from students admitted under the horizontal reservation category (7.5% reservation for students who studied in government schools from Class VI to Class XII).

A press release stated that DoTE has also instructed college principals to not admit students without following due procedure. Grievances, if any, may be addressed to tndote@tndote.com.

World.title: Parliament Monsoon Session Day 7 updates: Lok Sabha debates anti-paper leak Bill; punishment not enough deterrence, say Opposition MPs
World.content:
Ending a week-long logjam, the Lok Sabha on Tuesday (July 28, 2026) debated on the Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026. The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) on Tuesday (July 28, 202) renewed its demand for scrapping the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) in the Lok Sabha, arguing that the proposed amendments to the anti-paper leak Bill fail to address the “core issue” of the medical entrance examination itself. World.title: Girl who went missing from Aluva in Kochi traced to Pune
World.content:
A 12-year-old girl who went missing from Aluva was traced to Pune on Tuesday, reportedly in the company of a 25-year-old man, according to the police.

She had left home on Saturday on the pretext of borrowing a book from a friend. When she did not return, a police complaint was lodged that night.

When it emerged that she had boarded a train with a man, a joint operation was launched with the Railway Protection Force. It was discovered that the two were travelling to Pune. Eventually, the girl was found early on Tuesday.

The police have registered a case.

World.title: Non-payment of maintenance is economic abuse, constituting domestic violence: Kerala HC
World.content:
The non-payment of maintenance by itself is an economic abuse, which constitutes domestic violence, according to the Kerala High Court.

It held that claims of victims of domestic violence need no independent corroboration as usually the harassment happens inside the confines of a house.

Accordingly, the court dismissed a plea challenging an order of the Judicial First Class Magistrate, Chittur, directing a man to pay ₹10,000 as maintenance to his wife and child.

The court found no reason to interfere with the Magistrate’s order, which was upheld by the District Court, Palakkad. The man challenged the order before the High Court alleging that the maintenance amount was excessive, and that his wife had been employed as a teacher in a private college. He further denied the alleged incidents of domestic violence as unbelievable, without independent corroboration.

Justice Jobin Sebastian, who considered the case, noted that the woman had approached the Magistrate complaining of several acts of ill-treatment and harassment by her husband. She said she was forced to leave the house with her child due to the abuse and had been living separately for a year, during which time the man had not paid the maintenance.

She informed the court that the amount awarded was sufficient to meet the expenses of herself and her child.

The High Court found that there was no reason to disbelieve the allegations of domestic violence since the woman had categorically deposed before the Magistrate that she was subjected to mental and physical cruelty by her husband within their matrimonial home. She claimed that he had misappropriated her gold ornaments and used them for his business purposes.

The court held that the fact that she had worked in a private college for a short period on a nominal salary was not a reason to deny the relief of maintenance in her favour. It observed that the maintenance amount awarded was ‘just and fair’, and that the man was an able-bodied person, bound to provide sufficient maintenance to ensure a dignified life for his wife and child.

World.title: Maharashtra police flags ‘cross-border disinformation’ campaign on NEET protests
World.content:
The Maharashtra State Cyber Department on Tuesday (July 28, 2026) said it had found links to nearly 500 social media profiles allegedly involved in a “cross-border disinformation campaign” during the Cockroach Janata Party protests.
